**"Surely, their messengers came to them with clear proofs"**: the messengers brought commands, prohibitions and signs, plain miracles and evidence of the truth of their message. Allah punishes no one until He has sent a messenger to warn them (17:15).

**"but still they would not believe in what they had already denied."** They would not believe in the scriptures and messengers later, because they had denied the truth when it first came to them, even though they recognised it. This is how Ibn ʿAṭiyyah explained it, and the explanation is sound. A verse supports it:

> "What will make you ˹believers˺ realize that even if a sign were to come to them, they still would not believe? We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first" (6:109-110).

One explanation says they had denied it on the Day of the Covenant. Another says the last nations did not believe in what the first nations had disbelieved. So when the signs came to them they persisted in disbelief. Allah did not guide them to the truth, a just repayment for rejecting it the first time despite seeing clear signs and proofs.

**"This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers"**: Allah seals the hearts of those who disbelieve in Him and reject the truth, as is in His knowledge, so that they cannot accept good as good. In the same way that He closed the hearts of the peoples of these towns who rejected their prophets, He closes the hearts of those who reject Muhammad ﷺ, so that they are not guided to faith.

### Did every prophet have miracles?

This verse shows that all the prophets were given miracles. The Qur'an mentions the miracles of some prophets and not of most. That does not allow anyone to conclude that the prophets whose miracles are not mentioned had none. As for the claim of Hūd's people in Sūrah Hūd that he had brought them no clear sign, this verse shows it was sheer stubbornness. Or perhaps they thought his miracles of little account.

### Why do people cling to what they once said?

The verse describes a trait of the disbelievers: they held rigidly to ignorance simply to prove that what they had once said was right, ignoring every clear sign and proof of the truth. Many Muslims, and even some scholars, show the same habit, defending their mistaken statements in the face of clear proofs. This is a common cause of incurring Allah's anger.

### How does a heart become insensitive?

Allah has given human beings the powers of seeing, hearing and thinking, so that they may learn lessons and understand His signs. When a person does not use these powers for their purpose, the sensitivity of his heart slowly fades until his feelings are dulled. Then the seal of insensitivity is fixed on his heart and mind. He becomes like someone who does not see though he has eyes, does not hear though he has ears and does not understand though he has a mind. Though a human being, he has lost his humanity. Such a heart is kept off the path of guidance.

### In short

- These five stories are only some of the many that teach the same lesson, told to the Prophet ﷺ through Jibrīl.
- Every people received messengers with clear proofs, and every prophet was given miracles, mentioned or not.
- Those who reject the truth when it first comes are left unable to believe later, for Allah seals their hearts.
- Defending one's earlier word against clear proof, a habit even some Muslims share, invites Allah's anger.

102.text:
The stories end with a verdict on most of these peoples: "We did not find most of them true to their covenant. Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious". Most of the earlier nations did not keep their covenant. They were rebellious, turning away from obedience and compliance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We did not find most of them true to their covenant."** Allah found no loyalty in most people to the covenant made on the day of the pledge, the first covenant. Grammatically, the following "Rather, We found" uses a softened in, meaning "indeed".

**"Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious"**: most of them, or as one explanation puts it, all of them, were wrongdoers who broke their covenants and rebelled against Allah, not standing firm on what He commanded.

### Which covenant is meant?

The covenant mentioned here is the fiṭrah, the natural disposition Allah placed in people while they were still in their fathers' loins. He took their covenant that He is their Lord and King, and that none but He deserves worship. They affirmed it and testified to it against themselves. Then they broke it, threw it behind their backs and worshipped others besides Allah, with no proof or argument, and no support from reason or divine law. The pure fiṭrah rejects such acts, and every honourable messenger, from first to last, forbade them.

Two reports given under 7:30 make the same point. One hadith, in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, says that every child is born on the fiṭrah until his parents change his religion. In another, recorded by Muslim, Allah says He created His servants pure in faith (ḥunafāʾ), and then the devils led them away and forbade them what He had allowed.

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said this covenant is the covenant Allah made with the spirits of all creatures before creating them, when He asked, "Am I not your Lord?" Every human spirit answered "Yes" and so entered the covenant (7:172). After coming to earth most people forgot it and took to worshipping false gods. So the verse says that Allah did not find most people true to it.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said the covenant here is the covenant of īmān, faith, which another verse mentions when it speaks of one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful. On this reading, the verse means that most people turned away from their covenant with Allah.

### Why do people forget promises made in distress?

Nearly everyone, however sinful, turns to Allah when caught in some trouble. Often he promises Allah, aloud or in his heart, that he will be faithful, obey Him and avoid disobedience if only he is rescued. But once he is out of it, he goes back to his worldly desires with no thought for his covenant with Allah. The Qur'an mentions many such people.

The verse says "most of them", not "all of them". Some people are so perverse that they do not turn to Allah even in distress and never think of making Him any promise. Others keep their promise and stay obedient to Him. The verse ends by saying that most people were rebellious, turning from their covenant to stay obedient to Allah.

### How has history repeated itself?

The human race began with the followers of Ādam (Adam). When they fell into wrong ways, Allah's prophets came to warn them. Those who reformed themselves when the prophets came were saved, and those who refused were destroyed. Then the following generations forgot the vows of submission they had made to their prophets, and they suffered the same fate as the later generations of Ādam's followers. This has happened again and again, until the history of most of the human race has become a history of disobedience and broken pledges.

### What comes next?

These verses have described five events among earlier peoples, so that people today may learn from them and not follow the road that led their forerunners to ruin. The next account, of the Prophet Mūsā (Moses), is told in some detail. His miracles were more numerous and more striking than those of other prophets. His people, the Israelites, were also more stubborn and ignorant than other peoples. The verses that follow (7:103-110) also contain several rulings and points for discussion.

### The inner reading: loyalty to the covenant

Junayd said, "The finest of servants in state is the one who stands with Allah in guarding the limits and in loyalty to the covenants."

### In short

- Allah found most of the earlier peoples untrue to their covenant and rebellious against Him.
- The covenant is the fiṭrah and the pledge "Am I not your Lord?", or, in Ibn Masʿūd's view, the covenant of faith.
- People often promise Allah obedience in distress and forget it once relieved.
- After these five stories, the surah turns to Mūsā, whose miracles were greatest and whose people were most stubborn.

103.text:
After Nūḥ (Noah), Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ (Lot) and Shuʿayb comes the longest story in the surah: "Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors". It is told in detail because the miracles of Mūsā (Moses) were more numerous and more striking than those of other prophets, and because his opponents were so stubborn.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then after them We sent Moses"**: after the messengers already mentioned, Allah sent Mūsā.

**"with Our signs"**: with proofs and clear evidence, nine signs in all. The signs may be the verses of the Torah or the miracles of Mūsā.

**"to Pharaoh and his chiefs"**: Pharaoh (Firʿawn) ruled Egypt in the time of Mūsā. The word was the title of the Egyptian kings, and the Pharaoh of Mūsā's time is said to have been Mernephtah. His chiefs were his people, his council and his court.

**"but they wrongfully rejected them."** Literally, "they did wrong by them". Injustice and stubbornness drove them to deny the signs and refuse belief. Instead of thanking Allah and believing, they treated His signs with indifference and rejected them. The Arabic word for wrong (ẓulm) means using a thing for the opposite of what it was made for. Another verse says, "And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly. See then what was the end of the corruptors" (27:14).

**"See what was the end of the corruptors"**: see how destruction was the end of those who spread corruption through disbelief. The āyah means: look how Allah punished those who blocked others from the path of Allah and denied His messengers. He drowned every one of them while Mūsā and his people watched. The public drowning added disgrace to the punishment of Pharaoh and his people, and comfort to the hearts of Allah's party, Mūsā and those who believed in him. Allah condemned them in this world and in the next. Once again people are invited to learn from these events and think about their own end.

### Why does a prophet speak first to the leaders?

A prophet's message is first addressed to the leaders of his day, those who lead the thinking of their society. With their sharper minds, such people are better placed to grasp the message of truth in all its depth. Yet history shows that they have nearly always opposed the prophet's call. They use their mental gifts to give the message of truth a false meaning.

### In short

- After the five earlier prophets, Allah sent Mūsā with nine signs to Pharaoh, the ruler of Egypt, and his chiefs.
- They rejected the signs wrongfully, against their own inner conviction, putting them to the opposite of their purpose.
- Their end was a public drowning that disgraced them and comforted the believers.
- The leaders a prophet first addresses are best able to understand him, yet they have usually been his fiercest opponents.

104.text:
The scene opens on a debate between Mūsā (Moses) and Pharaoh, in which Mūsā answers Pharaoh with decisive proof and clear miracles before Pharaoh and his people, the Copts of Egypt: "And Moses said, “O Pharaoh! I am truly a messenger from the Lord of all worlds". It is a plain declaration, made to Pharaoh's face, that he is the messenger of Allah, the Lord of all the worlds.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And Moses said, “O Pharaoh!"**: Mūsā spoke when Allah sent him to Pharaoh (Firʿawn).

**"I am truly a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"**: my Sender is the Maker of all things, their Lord and King, who owns and sustains everything. Pharaoh denied him and said, "You are lying!"

### Why should Pharaoh have believed him?

Mūsā wanted them to believe him because his truthfulness was beyond question. He had never spoken a single lie. Besides, his miracles were clear proof of his claim to prophethood.

### In short

- Mūsā declared before Pharaoh and his court that he was a messenger of the Lord of all the worlds, Creator and King of all things.
- Pharaoh called him a liar, though Mūsā's honesty was beyond doubt and his miracles were plain proof.

105.text:
Mūsā (Moses) explains what his messengership requires of him, and makes his demand: "obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth. Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord, so let the children of Israel go with me.”" His rank as a prophet does not allow him to attribute anything but the truth to Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth."** It is my duty, and only fitting for me, to convey nothing from Him but the truth, because of what I know of His might and power. Since I have been sent by Allah, I can only speak the truth about Him. In one reading the Arabic says ʿalā, "obliged", and in another ʿalayya, "it is binding on me". In that second reading "it is right" (ḥaqīqun) is the subject, and its predicate is "that I say nothing but the truth about Allah".

**"Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord"**: I have brought decisive evidence that Allah gave me, to show that I am telling you the truth and that I am sent to you by Allah.

**"so let the children of Israel go with me.”"** Release them from your slavery and oppression, and from the misery you have put them through. Let them leave with me, with their belongings, great and small, so that they may worship your Lord and theirs. Some say he meant: send them with me to Syria. Pharaoh had enslaved them. They are the descendants of a noble prophet, Isrāʾīl, who is Yaʿqūb (Jacob), son of Isḥāq (Isaac), son of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the Friend (Khalīl) of Allah. In the light of such clear signs, Pharaoh should have believed him and freed the children of Israel from his unlawful control.

### Why must a messenger speak only the truth about Allah?

The message Allah gives His prophets is a sacred trust, and tampering with it is a great sin. All of Allah's prophets are free of sin and could never do such a thing. Allah is the Truth, so it is not fitting for anyone who comes forward in Allah's name to speak of anything but truth and justice. If he did otherwise, he would lose the right to speak for Allah and would earn punishment instead of reward.

### Why did Mūsā ask for the children of Israel?

Mūsā was sent both to the children of Israel and to Pharaoh and his Coptic people. At that time the children of Israel had many weaknesses, but they basically supported Mūsā. Pharaoh and his people, with a few exceptions, rejected him. In the end, after forty years of calling them to Allah's command, Mūsā was ordered to leave Egypt with the children of Israel. He asked Pharaoh to let them leave the country, so that they could worship the one God in the open air of the desert.

### In short

- As a prophet, Mūsā was bound to say nothing about Allah but the truth, for the message is a sacred trust.
- He came with clear proof from Allah and asked Pharaoh to free the enslaved children of Israel, descendants of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq, son of Ibrāhīm.
- After forty years of preaching, he was told to lead them out of Egypt to worship Allah freely.

106.text:
Pharaoh, in his stubbornness, would listen to nothing, and answered with a challenge: "Pharaoh said, “If you have come with a sign, then bring it if what you say is true.”" In effect he told Mūsā (Moses): I will not believe what you have said, nor grant your request.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Pharaoh said, “If you have come with a sign"**: if you have brought a sign, as you claim.

**"then bring it"**: show it to me, so that we can see it.

**"if what you say is true.”"** If you are telling the truth in this, and if you really are a messenger, produce your proof so that we can know whether your claim is true.

### What lay behind the demand?

Pharaoh did not ask for a sign in order to believe. He had already said he would neither believe nor grant the request. His demand was meant to put Mūsā on the spot, in front of the court, in the hope that he would fail. It gave Mūsā the opening to show the signs Allah had given him.

### In short

- Pharaoh refused to believe Mūsā or free the children of Israel, and demanded a sign if Mūsā was truthful.
- The challenge, meant to embarrass Mūsā, became the occasion for his miracles before the whole court.

107.text:
Mūsā (Moses) answered Pharaoh's demand at once: "So Moses threw down his staff and—behold!—it became a real snake". This was the first of the signs.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So Moses threw down his staff"**: he cast his staff down on the ground.

**"and—behold!—it became a real snake"**: the word thuʿbān means a huge serpent. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it was a male snake, and as-Suddī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same. One explanation describes it as a huge, yellow, male serpent. The word mubīn, "real" or "manifest", shows that the miracle happened openly before the eyes of Pharaoh's people. It was not done secretly in a hidden or private place, as magicians usually work. It was an enormous snake, there for all to see.

### What happened when the staff became a serpent?

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the staff became a huge snake that opened its mouth and rushed at Pharaoh. When Pharaoh saw it coming, he leapt from his throne and cried out to Mūsā to take it away, and Mūsā did. Another historical report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that as the serpent moved toward Pharaoh, he jumped from his throne and sought shelter near Mūsā, and many of his courtiers died of fright.

As-Suddī said the snake opened its mouth and went for Pharaoh to swallow him. Its lower jaw rested on the ground and its upper jaw reached the top of the palace wall. Pharaoh was so terrified that he jumped up and wet himself, which had never happened to him before. He cried out, "Mūsā, take it away, and I will believe in you and let the children of Israel go with you." So Mūsā picked it up, and it became a staff again.

### Is such a transformation impossible?

A staff turning into a real serpent is not as impossible as it may seem. It is astonishing only because it is unusual. A miracle must be something unusual, beyond the power of ordinary people. Allah shows miracles through His prophets so that people may understand that the prophets have powers from Allah and are His true prophets.

### In short

- Mūsā threw down his staff, and it became a huge serpent in full view of Pharaoh's court.
- Terrified, Pharaoh leapt from his throne and begged Mūsā to take it away, promising belief and freedom for the Israelites.
- A miracle is not impossible, only unusual. It is a sign from Allah that confirms His prophet.

108.text:
The second sign followed: "Then he drew his hand ˹out of his collar˺ and it was ˹shining˺ white for all to see". Mūsā (Moses) put his hand inside his garment and drew it out shining, not from leprosy or any sickness.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then he drew his hand"**: the verb nazaʿa means to pull something out of something else with force. It suggests that Mūsā drew his hand out with some effort. This verse does not say where he drew it from, but other verses do. One says, "Now put your hand through ˹the opening of˺ your collar" (27:12), and another, "And put your hand under your armpit" (20:22). So he drew his hand out either from under his arm or from inside his shirt, near his chest.

**"and it was ˹shining˺ white"**: the word bayḍāʾ means white. A hand can also turn white from disease. That is perhaps why other verses add "unblemished", literally "without harm" (28:32, 27:12), to remove any suspicion of illness. Ibn ʿAbbās said "without harm" means not from leprosy. When Mūsā put his hand back into his sleeve, it returned to its normal colour. Mujāhid and several others said the same. A tradition reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās says that the whiteness was no ordinary whiteness. It gave off a light that lit up everything around it. It was radiant, not the usual colour of his skin.

**"for all to see"**: the word nāẓirīn, "onlookers", suggests that the light so astonished people that they gathered to look at it.

### Why two miracles?

On this occasion, at Pharaoh's demand, Mūsā showed two miracles: the staff turning into a serpent, and the hand shining with light. The first served as a warning to the disbelievers, and the second as an invitation to the truth. The second also showed that Mūsā's message was a light, and that following it would lead people to lasting success.

### In short

- Mūsā drew his hand from his collar or from under his arm, and it shone white with a light that lit up its surroundings.
- The whiteness was not from leprosy or any illness, and the hand returned to normal when he put it back.
- The serpent was a warning and the shining hand an invitation, showing that his message was light.

109.text:
Pharaoh's court quickly found a label for what they had seen: "The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said, “He is indeed a skilled magician". When his fright had passed and he was back on his throne, Pharaoh told his chiefs that Mūsā (Moses) was a skilled magician, and they agreed. In Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ the same words are spoken by Pharaoh himself, so it is as if they said them in consultation with him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said"**: the word malaʾ means the influential chiefs, the notables and leaders. They spoke once they had seen the staff transformed and the hand turned white.

**"“He is indeed a skilled magician"**: a cunning sorcerer of great knowledge, outstanding and expert in magic. Knowing nothing of Allah's divine power, they could say nothing else. They believed Pharaoh was their god, and they had seen nothing in their lives but the tricks of sorcerers. Still, they added the word ʿalīm, "knowing", "skilled". This shows they felt Mūsā's miracles were of a kind no ordinary magician could perform. So they called him a sorcerer of great knowledge.

### How does a miracle differ from sorcery?

Miracles and sorcery differ so plainly in nature and effect that anyone with common sense can tell them apart.

- Sorcerers usually live in impurity, and the dirtier and more impure they are, the better their sorcery works. The prophets, by contrast, are by nature the cleanest and purest of people.
- A sorcerer never succeeds when he claims to be a prophet.
- The effects of sorcery have physical causes, like everything else, except that their causes are hidden from ordinary people, who therefore think they happen without any cause. Miracles are a direct display of Allah's power and have nothing to do with physical causes.

That is why the Qur'an attributes miracles directly to Allah and not to the prophets. The Qur'an says "but Allah threw" of the pebbles that the Prophet ﷺ threw at the Battle of Badr. In short, miracles and sorcery are entirely different. People of knowledge are never confused about this, and Allah has given clear signs of the difference so that ordinary people need not be confused either.

Even Pharaoh's people sensed that Mūsā's miracles were somehow unlike the usual work of sorcerers. So even while accusing him of sorcery, they admitted that he was "skilled", meaning his acts could not be compared with those of ordinary sorcerers.

### In short

- Pharaoh and his chiefs agreed in calling Mūsā a skilled magician, unable to imagine any power beyond sorcery.
- Calling him "skilled" admitted that his signs were beyond any ordinary magician.
- Sorcery works through hidden physical causes and impure practitioners. Miracles come directly from Allah through the purest of people.

110.text:
The chiefs went on to raise a political alarm, and Pharaoh asked for their advice: "who seeks to drive you from your land.” ˹So Pharaoh asked,˺ “What do you propose?”" They held a council to decide what to do about Mūsā (Moses). They plotted to put out the light he had brought, to bring down his word, and to paint him as a liar and a fraud.

### Phrase by phrase

**"who seeks to drive you from your land.”"** By this, they claimed, he means to drive you all out of the land of Egypt through his magic. They feared that he would win people over with what they called his magic, and so prevail over them and push them out of their land.

**"˹So Pharaoh asked,˺ “What do you propose?”"** Pharaoh asked his chiefs what they advised him to do about the matter. One explanation renders it, "So what do you command?"

### Did their fear come true?

What they feared did happen, as Allah says: "and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared" (28:6). After consulting about Mūsā they agreed on a plan, which the following verses describe.

### How do leaders discredit a call to truth?

The leaders of a prophet's day use their talents to give the message of truth a false meaning. They declare that a sign which came by Allah's intervention was produced by magic. Or, to belittle the prophetic movement, they give it a political colour and say that such preachers are only seeking power. The general public cannot analyse such matters, so this kind of talk makes them suspicious of the truth.

Levelling such empty charges at someone who brings the truth is a serious crime. In this way the leading figures of the day may keep their leadership, but only at the cost of the Hereafter. Mūsā was the representative of the truth, but Pharaoh took him for a mere magician and decided to defeat him with his own magicians.

### In short

- The chiefs accused Mūsā of plotting to drive them out of Egypt by magic, and Pharaoh asked for their advice.
- They plotted to brand him a liar, yet what they feared came to pass in the end.
- Calling a sign magic and a prophet a seeker of power are old tactics for turning the public against the truth.

111.text:
Having seen the staff turn into a serpent and the hand shine with light, Pharaoh should have been convinced and believed in Mūsā (Moses), as logic and sense required. But wrongdoers always look for false interpretations of the truth in order to hide it. Pharaoh and his people denied him, and his chiefs advised: "They replied, “Let him and his brother wait and send mobilizers to all cities". They had told the people that Mūsā was a great sorcerer who wanted to drive them from their homes and take over the country.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied, “Let him and his brother wait"**: Ibn ʿAbbās said "wait" here means "delay him for a time". Put off the case of Mūsā and his brother Hārūn (Aaron), and postpone any decision about them. One explanation adds: do not kill them.

**"and send mobilizers to all cities"**: send summoners, gatherers or soldiers to the cities, regions and provinces of your kingdom, O Pharaoh (Firʿawn). Send people to all the cities of Egypt to call every magician and gather them from many lands.

### Why did the chiefs suggest delay?

Pharaoh's people said there were many expert sorcerers in their cities who could defeat Mūsā. Some soldiers should be sent to gather them and bring them for the purpose. Rather than act against Mūsā at once, they wanted a public contest, sure that their magicians would show his signs to be nothing more than magic.

### In short

- Instead of believing after the two signs, Pharaoh's chiefs advised him to put off Mūsā and Hārūn for a while.
- They urged him to send men to every city of Egypt to gather the magicians, confident they could beat Mūsā.

112.text:
The chiefs complete their advice: "to bring you every clever magician.”" The gatherers would bring every skilled and powerful sorcerer to outdo Mūsā (Moses) in magic, and so they summoned them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"to bring you every clever magician.”"** They will bring you every expert and accomplished magician, cunning and well versed in sorcery. In the Arabic, "magician" is read sāḥir, and in another reading saḥḥār, a master of magic.

### Why did they think magicians could defeat Mūsā?

At that time magic was the trade of the day, widespread and popular, and sorcerers enjoyed high status among the people. Pharaoh and his court assumed that what Mūsā brought was the same kind of magic as the sorcerers of their age practised. On that mistaken assumption they gathered all the magicians to defeat the miracles he had shown them. Allah tells how Pharaoh set the meeting:

> "We can surely meet you with similar magic. So set for us an appointment that neither of us will fail to keep, in a central place.” Moses said, “Your appointment is on the Day of the Festival, and let the people be gathered mid-morning.” Pharaoh then withdrew, orchestrated his scheme, then returned" (20:58-60).

Mūsā had spent 40 years calling his people to Allah's command. Pharaoh still saw in him only a practitioner of magic, and decided to overcome him with his own magicians.

### Why do miracles match their age?

Allah sent Mūsā with the miracles of the staff and the shining hand so that people could plainly see the humiliation of the sorcerers once they took him on. It is Allah's usual way to send His prophets with miracles suited to what their age prizes.

- In the time of the Prophet ʿĪsā (Jesus), Greek philosophy and medicine were at their height. So his miracles were to open the eyes of people blind from birth, and to heal lepers at once by touching them.
- In the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the Arabs prided themselves on their eloquence and command of language. So the Qur'an was sent as the greatest of all his miracles.

### In short

- The chiefs proposed gathering every skilled magician in the land to outdo Mūsā, and Pharaoh set a public meeting on the day of the festival.
- In an age that prized magic, they took his signs for magic of the same kind.
- Allah gives each prophet miracles that surpass what his age excels in: magic for Mūsā, medicine for ʿĪsā, and eloquence for Muhammad ﷺ.

113.text:
Pharaoh's summons went out, and the magicians arrived from all over the country: "The magicians came to Pharaoh, saying, “Shall we receive a ˹suitable˺ reward if we prevail?”" Allah describes the exchange between Pharaoh and the magicians he gathered to defeat Mūsā (Moses).

### Phrase by phrase

**"The magicians came to Pharaoh"**: Pharaoh (Firʿawn) sent people to call the magicians, and they came. One explanation puts their number at 70. Historical reports differ widely on how many there were, giving figures from nine hundred to three hundred thousand. The staffs and ropes used in the contest are said to have filled three hundred camel-loads.

**"saying, “Shall we receive a ˹suitable˺ reward if we prevail?”"** They asked whether he would give them a reward, a gift, if they won and beat Mūsā with their magic. In the Arabic, "shall" (a-inna) may be read with both hamzahs pronounced, or with the second softened and an alif inserted between them.

### What does their first question reveal?

The first thing the magicians did was to secure a promise of payment for their performance. Worldly people are always after worldly gain, and they do nothing until they are sure of their profit. The prophets and their followers, by contrast, always declare, "I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds" (26:109). The prophets of Allah preach and deliver His message only for people's good and guidance, and seek no payment for it. They look for their reward from Allah alone.

After this exchange with Pharaoh, the time and place of the great contest were fixed. An open piece of land was chosen, and the time was set for after sunrise on their festival day, as Mūsā had said (20:59).

### In short

- The magicians gathered from all over Egypt, in numbers the reports give anywhere from 70 to many thousands.
- Their first concern was payment, the mark of worldly people. The prophets ask no reward from anyone but Allah.
- The contest was set for after sunrise on the festival day, in an open place.

114.text:
Pharaoh answered the magicians generously: "He replied, “Yes, and you will certainly be among those closest to me.”" He promised them a reward and great provision. He made them hope for whatever they wished, and to be among his inner circle and closest companions.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He replied, “Yes"**: yes, you will have your reward and a gift.

**"and you will certainly be among those closest to me.”"** On top of your reward, you will be brought near to me in rank and given important positions.

### Did Mūsā speak to the magicians first?

Some reports say Mūsā (Moses) had a short conversation with the chief of the magicians. He asked whether they would accept the faith if he defeated them. The chief replied that there was no question of their being defeated, for they had such great magical powers that no one could overcome them. Yet, he said, if Mūsā did defeat them, they would declare their faith openly before Pharaoh.

### What happened once they were reassured?

Once the magicians were assured of the cursed Pharaoh's promises, they turned to the contest itself, as the next verse tells. They came confident of victory and of the rich rewards Pharaoh had dangled before them.

### In short

- Pharaoh promised the magicians not only a reward but a place among those closest to him.
- Reports say their chief told Mūsā they would openly believe if he defeated them.
- Reassured of their reward, they went into the contest sure of winning.

115.text:
On the day of the encounter, the magicians challenged Mūsā (Moses): "They asked, “O Moses! Will you cast, or shall we be the first to cast?”" Proud and certain of winning, they offered him the choice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They asked, “O Moses! Will you cast"**: the Arabic word ilqāʾ means to drop something down. Will you throw your staff first? Choose, O Mūsā, whether you want to be the first to throw.

**"or shall we be the first to cast?”"** Or shall we throw what we have before you? In another verse they say, "O Moses! Either you cast, or let us be the first to cast" (20:65).

### What lay behind their question?

The question was perhaps meant to show how sure they were of their art. The way they worded it suggests that they wanted to go first. But to give the impression of strength to their opponent, they put it as a question. Since Mūsā had nothing to fear, he invited them to throw first.

### In short

- At the contest, the magicians offered Mūsā the choice of throwing first or letting them begin.
- Their wording showed their wish to start and their pride in their art.

116.text:
Mūsā (Moses) let them go first: "Moses said, “You first.” So when they did, they deceived the eyes of the people, stunned them, and made a great display of magic". Trusting in Allah to give him victory, he was not worried about them, and told them to throw their ropes and staffs.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses said, “You first.”"** Throw first whatever you are going to throw. This was a command permitting them to begin, as a means of bringing the truth to light.

**"So when they did"**: when they threw their ropes and staffs. One explanation says they threw 70 staffs and 70 ropes. Ibn ʿAbbās said they threw thick ropes and long sticks, which seemed to be crawling, an illusion produced by their magic.

**"they deceived the eyes of the people"**: literally "they bewitched the people's eyes". They deceived the eyes and made people think the trick was real, when it was only an illusion. They kept people from seeing the true state of those ropes and staffs. Things looked different from what they really were.

**"stunned them"**: they frightened and overawed the people, making the ropes and staffs look like slithering snakes.

**"and made a great display of magic"**: they produced a mighty sorcery. One explanation calls it a plain lie.

### Why did Mūsā let them go first?

The wisdom of letting them throw first may have been this, and Allah knows best: the people would see the magicians' sorcery first. Then, once the magicians had cast their spell and captured every eye, the clear and undeniable truth would come, just when everyone was waiting for it, and strike their hearts all the more. That is exactly what happened. It has also been said that Mūsā's courtesy in giving them the first turn had its effect, for they accepted the faith after their defeat.

A question arises here. Sorcery is forbidden, and when it is used to oppose a prophet of Allah it becomes disbelief. How then could Mūsā give the magicians permission by saying "You first"? A little thought gives the answer. It was certain that the magicians would show their magic in any case. The only question was who would begin, and Mūsā let them begin. This had a further advantage. The people could watch their whole performance while the magicians had all the time they wanted to make their staffs look like snakes. Then Mūsā's staff would become a serpent and swallow all their snakes, so that the defeat of magic would be displayed openly before everyone.

### Why does a prophet not strike first?

Prophets are given miracles suited to the mindset of their contemporaries. In ancient Egypt, magic held people's minds captive, so Mūsā was given a miracle that would outdo magic. As Pharaoh had planned, all the great magicians gathered at the national festival. When they asked Mūsā who should begin, he asked them to show their magic first, and they agreed.

This shows that a prophet never takes the initiative in moving against his enemies. Up to the last moment he leaves his opponents the chance to start hostilities. Only once they have taken that responsibility on themselves does he use every power at his command to overcome them. When it comes to setting out the teachings of Islam, the prophet is the one who begins. Where the first move could mean an attack, he never makes it.

### Was it real change or only illusion?

Allah describes what they did elsewhere:

> "So Moses concealed fear within himself. We reassured ˹him˺, “Do not fear! It is certainly you who will prevail. Cast what is in your right hand, and it will swallow up what they have made, for what they have made is no more than a magic trick. And magicians can never succeed wherever they go.”" (20:67-69).

This verse shows that their display was only a bewitching of people's eyes. It made them see the staffs and ropes as snakes leaping on the ground, while the ropes and staffs did not change at all. It was a kind of mesmerism that took hold of the onlookers' minds.

That does not mean sorcery is limited to this kind, or that it can never change one thing into another, for there is no proof either way. Many forms of magic have been taken as real. The words magic and sorcery are usually applied to anything that seems to happen in an unusual way. Sleight of hand, telepathic influence and mesmerism are sometimes called magic. Turning one thing into another by magic may be possible, but there is no sound reason or proof for or against it.

### In short

- Mūsā let the magicians throw first, and their ropes and staffs seemed to become slithering snakes.
- It was an illusion cast on the eyes. The ropes did not change, though people were deceived and frightened.
- Letting them begin let everyone see the magic fully before the truth overwhelmed it, and his courtesy is said to have helped win them to faith.
- A prophet never starts hostilities. He lets opponents begin, then overcomes them with what Allah gives him.

117.text:
At that tremendous moment, when Allah separated truth from falsehood, He sent a revelation to His servant and messenger Mūsā (Moses): "Then We inspired Moses, “Throw down your staff,” and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion". Thousands of staffs and ropes seemed to be snakes leaping all over the ground when Allah told Mūsā to throw down the staff in his right hand.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then We inspired Moses, “Throw down your staff,”"** Allah revealed to Mūsā: cast your staff, O Mūsā. And he threw it.

**"and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion"**: it swallowed up their lying show, their staffs and ropes. In the Arabic, "it devoured" is read talaqqafu, with one of the two original tāʾ letters of tatalaqqafu dropped. "The objects of their illusion" means what they were transforming by deception, the magic with which they made things look real though they were not real at all.

### How did the staff overcome the magic?

When Mūsā threw his staff, it became a huge serpent and at once began to eat up the magicians' snakes. Al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah described it as a huge serpent in plain view, its jaws open, gulping down the ropes and sticks of the magicians. Ibn ʿAbbās said Mūsā's staff swallowed every rope and stick the magicians had thrown. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said it went after the ropes and sticks one after another until nothing the sorcerers had thrown was left. Then Mūsā took it in his hand, and it became a staff again, just as before. The crowd stood bewildered and stunned. In no time the great serpent of Mūsā had eaten every one of their snakes, destroying the illusion that they were crawling snakes.

### In short

- Allah told Mūsā to throw his staff, and it became a great serpent that swallowed every rope and stick of the magicians.
- What the magicians had made to look real was exposed as illusion, and the staff returned to its form in Mūsā's hand.

118.text:
The contest was decided: "So the truth prevailed and their illusions failed". It became clear that Mūsā (Moses) was right and that the magicians' work was false.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So the truth prevailed"**: the truth came to pass, confirmed and made plain. It proved that what Mūsā said was true.

**"and their illusions failed"**: literally "what they were doing became void". Their sorcery came to nothing, fizzled away and was shown to be false.

### Why did the magicians' tricks collapse?

When the magicians threw down their sticks and ropes, people saw moving snakes because of an optical illusion. But when Mūsā's staff turned into a snake and moved along the ground, their sticks and ropes went back to being sticks and ropes. The magicians knew the limits of magic. They could see that what Mūsā's staff did lay far beyond anything their art could achieve.

### In short

- The truth of Mūsā's message was confirmed before everyone, and the magic was shown to be empty.
- Once the real sign appeared, the illusion lost its hold and the ropes were plain ropes again.

119.text:
The defeat was public and complete: "So Pharaoh and his people were defeated right there and put to shame". Mūsā (Moses) triumphed over them in the assembly, before the very crowd that had been gathered to watch his humiliation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So Pharaoh and his people were defeated right there"**: Pharaoh and his people, and the magicians with them, were beaten on the spot, at that very gathering, and Mūsā was victorious over them.

**"and put to shame"**: they were humiliated and left disgraced.

### Why does "right there" matter?

Pharaoh had chosen the time and place himself, a festival day with the people gathered, hoping to expose Mūsā before the whole nation. Instead the defeat fell on him in that same public setting. The stage he had built to shame Allah's messenger became the scene of his own disgrace.

### In short

- Pharaoh and his magicians were defeated at the very assembly they had called.
- The public contest meant to disgrace Mūsā ended in Pharaoh's own humiliation.

120.text:
Then came the most astonishing turn of the day: "And the magicians fell down, prostrating". The magicians realised that what they had seen came from heaven and was in no way magic.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And the magicians fell down"**: literally "were thrown down". The magicians were so overwhelmed by Mūsā's (Moses') miracle that they could do nothing but fall. It may also mean that Allah favoured them and placed them in prostration. One explanation says they went down so quickly that it looked as if they had fallen.

**"prostrating"**: they prostrated to Allah, having seen the greatness of His power and His clear signs. Al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah said they did not raise their heads until they had seen Paradise, the Fire and the reward of their inhabitants.

### How could magicians turn to faith in a moment?

Mūsā's mission in Egypt lasted about 40 years, and this contest took place in its final stage. So the magicians must already have known his message, though the veil over their eyes had not yet lifted. When they saw his superiority in the very field in which they were experts, every veil was torn away. They could see that this was not magic but divine prophethood. Of their own free will, without hesitation, they prostrated themselves before Allah.

### In short

- Seeing the staff swallow their work, the magicians knew it was no magic and fell down in prostration to Allah.
- As experts in magic, they recognised the sign at once. Their knowledge, which had served Pharaoh, now led them to faith.

121.text:
The magicians declared their faith openly: "They declared, “We ˹now˺ believe in the Lord of all worlds—". Muhammad ibn Isḥāq reported that they added, "Had Mūsā been a magician, he would not have defeated us."

### Phrase by phrase

**"They declared, “We ˹now˺ believe in the Lord of all worlds—"**: they cried out that they believed in the Lord of all creation. Pharaoh, it is said, asked, "Are you speaking of me?"

### What did the magicians come to see?

In this event the magicians saw how small human devices are, even at their most perfect, and how great and all-powerful Allah is. After that, Pharaoh, with all his authority, looked worthless to them. The same men who, before witnessing Allah's greatness, had longed for Pharaoh's rewards now brushed aside his threat of the worst punishment as if it meant nothing.

### In short

- The magicians declared their faith in the Lord of all worlds, knowing no magician could have defeated them.
- Having seen Allah's power, they lost all regard for Pharaoh's rewards and threats.

122.text:
The magicians completed their declaration: "the Lord of Moses and Aaron.”" They named the Lord of the worlds as the Lord whom Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron) worshipped.

### Phrase by phrase

**"the Lord of Moses and Aaron.”"** He is the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn, who alone deserves the worship of all people, while the false gods deserve none. They said this because they realised that what they had seen the staff do could not be done by sorcery.

### Why add "the Lord of Moses and Aaron"?

After saying "the Lord of all worlds", the magicians added "the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn". They did so to make it clear that the Lord whom Mūsā and Hārūn worshipped is the true Lord of the universe, and not Pharaoh, as he claimed to be. Since Pharaoh posed as their lord, this addition left no room for doubt about whom they now believed in.

### In short

- The magicians specified their faith in the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn, the one God worthy of worship.
- The addition shut out Pharaoh's claim to lordship, making plain that he was not the lord they meant.

123.text:
The magicians' public conversion was a disaster for Pharaoh, and he answered with threats and cunning: "Pharaoh threatened, “How dare you believe in him before I give you permission? This must be a conspiracy you devised in the city to drive out its people, but soon you will see". Some historical reports say that after the magicians declared their faith, six hundred thousand more people followed them. Before the contest only two people had believed in Allah. Now a great host had become Muslim. Like a shrewd politician, Pharaoh hid his state of mind from the people and turned the situation around by accusing the magicians of conspiracy and rebellion.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Pharaoh threatened, “How dare you believe in him before I give you permission?"** You have believed in the Lord of Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron) before I commanded you to! In the Arabic, "have you believed" (a-āmantum) may be read with both hamzahs pronounced, or with the second turned into an alif. The words were a threat to the magicians. They were also meant to convince his people that the magicians had decided in haste and fallen into the trap of Mūsā and Hārūn. Otherwise, he implied, he too would have believed if they had proved truthful.

**"This must be a conspiracy you devised in the city"**: what you have done is a plot hatched between you and Mūsā, a trick with which you have deceived the people. Pharaoh was saying that Mūsā had beaten them only because they had plotted with him and agreed to it beforehand. Elsewhere he says, "He must be your master who taught you magic" (20:71).

**"to drive out its people"**: so that you can all work together, by guile, to seize influence and power, replace the chiefs and masters of this land, and take control of the state.

**"but soon you will see"**: you will soon find out what I am going to do to you, and how I will punish you as a warning to others.

### Did Pharaoh believe his own charge?

Pharaoh knew perfectly well, as did every sensible person, that the accusation was baseless. From the moment he arrived from Madyan, Mūsā had called Pharaoh to Allah and shown him tremendous miracles and clear proofs of his truth. Pharaoh then sent agents to the cities of his kingdom and gathered the magicians scattered across Egypt. He and his people chose among them, summoned them and promised them rich rewards. The magicians were eager to beat Mūsā before Pharaoh and win his favour. Mūsā had never known, seen or met any of them before. Pharaoh knew all this, but claimed otherwise to fool the ignorant masses of his kingdom:

> "And so he fooled his people, and they obeyed him. They were truly a rebellious people" (43:54).

A people who believed Pharaoh when he said, "I am your lord, the most high!" (79:24), were among the most ignorant and misguided of Allah's creatures.

As-Suddī reported in his tafsīr, from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and several other Companions, why Pharaoh spoke of a plot. Mūsā had met the chief of the magicians and asked whether he would believe and testify to the truth if Mūsā beat him. The chief swore by Allah that he would, confident his magic could not be overcome. Pharaoh had seen the two of them talking, and that is why he said what he said.

### How did Pharaoh twist the event?

It was a clever scheme. Pharaoh tried to keep his people in their old ignorance and make them believe that the contest had been fixed in advance between Mūsā and the magicians. He twisted the plain fact that Mūsā's miracle and the magicians' open conversion had exposed his own ignorance and falsehood. He turned it into a political matter, telling his people that the whole affair was a plan to take over the country and drive them out.

Pharaoh treated accepting or rejecting Mūsā's call as a matter of his "permission", while the magicians treated it as a matter of a "sign" from Allah. A haughty person always lets his own opinion override argument and proof. Such people are never moved to accept the truth.

### In short

- After the magicians and many others believed, Pharaoh accused them of conspiring with Mūsā to seize power.
- He knew the charge was false, since Mūsā had never met them, but used it to fool his people.
- He turned a clear sign into a political plot, to keep his people in ignorance.
- Pharaoh saw faith as needing his permission, while the magicians saw it as answering Allah's sign.

124.text:
Having made his vague threat, Pharaoh now spelled it out: "I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then crucify you all.”" The magicians' support for Mūsā (Moses) had stung his pride. To side with Mūsā against him was to insult him before the whole nation, so he was enraged and resolved on harsh punishment, as any arrogant man in power would.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides"**: the right hand and the left foot of each of you, or the left hand and the right foot. The aim was to leave them completely crippled.

**"then crucify you all.”"** I will crucify every one of you, making an example of you to terrify all who see you. One explanation says on the river bank. Another verse says, "and crucify you on the trunks of palm trees" (20:71), where the Arabic preposition fī means "on". Ibn ʿAbbās said Pharaoh was the first to crucify people and the first to cut off hands and feet on opposite sides.

### What drove Pharaoh to such cruelty?

Both the magicians and Pharaoh had been beaten in the field of argument. The magicians admitted their defeat and so became worthy of Allah's lasting rewards. Pharaoh made it a matter of prestige. To satisfy his false pride, all he could do was persecute people who loved the truth, and in the Hereafter he himself would be given over to Allah's lasting punishment.

### In short

- Pharaoh threatened to cut off the magicians' hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them all.
- Ibn ʿAbbās said Pharaoh was the first to use these punishments.
- Defeated in argument, he turned to brutality to save face, as the arrogant in power do.

125.text:
The magicians' reply showed the power of faith: "They responded, “Surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return". Only a few hours before, they had been Pharaoh's worshippers. Now, with faith in Allah, they showed such strength and courage that their only answer to his threats against their lives was a calm "To our Lord we will return".

### Phrase by phrase

**"They responded, “Surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return"**: after their death, however it came, they would be restored to their Lord and return to Him in the Hereafter. Their return was to their Lord alone, so they did not fear what Pharaoh threatened them with.

### Why were they unafraid?

They were now certain they would go back to Allah. Allah's punishment, they knew, is harsher than Pharaoh's. His punishment for what Pharaoh was calling them to that day, and for the magic Pharaoh had forced them to practise, would be greater than anything Pharaoh could do. So they would bear Pharaoh's punishment patiently that day, to be saved from Allah's.

Faith in Allah, which the Qur'an calls īmān, is a great power. When it enters a heart, the person feels strong enough to face the whole world and every force gathered against him. That was the great change in the magicians.

They knew well Pharaoh's power and authority over them. They did not say he could not kill them for their new faith. Their answer meant that the whole of this passing life had no value in their eyes. They were content because they were sure of meeting the Lord of the worlds after leaving this world, where they would have an everlasting life of peace and comfort. Another reading of their reply is this: Pharaoh had the power to end their lives, but he too would soon be brought before the Lord of the worlds and called to account for his tyranny. In another passage their reply continues: "So do whatever you want! Your authority only covers the ˹fleeting˺ life of this world" (20:72). This too shows how little they cared for this temporary life.

### What does their sacrifice prove?

To give one's life for the truth is the final testimony that the truth is true. With Allah's help, the magicians were able to make that sacrifice. By offering themselves for the worst punishment, they proved that their faith in Mūsā (Moses) was no excuse or conspiracy. It was a genuine acknowledgement of the truth.

### In short

- Facing torture and death, the magicians calmly answered that they would return to their Lord.
- Faith had turned Pharaoh's worshippers into men who valued Allah's judgement above his punishment and this world above nothing.
- Their readiness to die proved their faith was no plot but a sincere witness to the truth.

126.text:
The magicians named the real reason for Pharaoh's rage, and turned to Allah in prayer: "Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺.”" This great change in their thinking and action came from true faith in Allah. Their faith also opened to them a door of knowledge and wisdom, as their prayer at that moment shows.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us."** You are finding fault with us, punishing us and taking spiteful revenge only because we believed in our Lord's signs when they came to us through Mūsā (Moses). If that is our crime, we stand by it.

**"Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance"**: pour out patience and steadfastness on us when we are crucified and mutilated, so that we may stand firm for the truth and hold to Your religion. Then we will not slide back into disbelief when what he threatens comes to pass.

**"and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺.”"** Take us to You as Muslims, people who have sincerely surrendered to You, obeying Your commands and following Your messenger Mūsā and his religion.

### What happened to the magicians?

They told Pharaoh:

> "By the One Who created us! We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us. So do whatever you want! Your authority only covers the ˹fleeting˺ life of this world. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord so He may forgive our sins and that magic you have forced us to practice. And Allah is far superior ˹in reward˺ and more lasting ˹in punishment˺.” Whoever comes to their Lord as an evildoer will certainly have Hell, where they can neither live nor die. But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done good, they will have the highest ranks" (20:72-75).

The magicians began the day as sorcerers and ended it as honoured martyrs. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj all said: they began the day as sorcerers and ended it as martyrs.

### Why is patience the key to victory?

Their prayer showed knowledge and wisdom, and it was also the best way out of their trial, because steadfastness and patience are the only keys to success against an enemy. Tafsīr al-Manār records a related finding. A commission formed to study the causes and effects of the World War remarked that Muslims who believe in Allah and the Hereafter are the bravest of people on the battlefield and the most patient in hardship, because of that faith. So German military experts urged that honesty and a sense of accountability in the Hereafter be instilled in their soldiers, as a great source of strength and courage.

### Was their change itself a miracle?

The magicians' instant and complete change of heart was no smaller a miracle than Mūsā's other miracles. Men who had spent their whole lives in disbelief and ignorance became, in a moment, the most aware and truthful of Muslims, ready to give their lives for their faith. It is a pity that Muslims and Muslim states try every other means to make themselves strong, while neglecting the real source of power and strength: faith, steadfastness and patience.

### Why did their prayer carry such force?

The strength the magicians showed at that critical moment came entirely from Allah's help, and the prayer on their lips was inspired. When a servant surrenders himself to Allah body and soul, he comes so close to Him that he begins to receive special blessings and speaks words that are inspired in the fullest sense. Their prayer meant: we have surrendered to You completely, O Allah. We have done all that was in our power, and we leave the rest to You. When a servant prays like this from the bottom of his heart, Allah is surely enough for him in all his difficulties.

### In short

- The magicians told Pharaoh his only grievance was their faith in Allah's signs, and they stood by it.
- They asked Allah for steadfastness under torture and to die as Muslims, and they began the day as sorcerers and ended it as martyrs.
- Faith and patience are the true sources of strength, a lesson even military experts have noted, though Muslims often neglect it.
- A servant who surrenders wholly to Allah is given inspired words and finds Allah sufficient for him.

127.text:
Allah describes the plotting of Pharaoh and his people, their evil intentions and their hatred for Mūsā (Moses) and his people: "The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people protested, “Are you going to leave Moses and his people free to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?” He responded, “We will kill their sons and keep their women. We will completely dominate them.”" With clever falsehoods, Pharaoh had managed to keep his ignorant people in their old ignorance. Yet they noticed something odd. All his fury fell on the magicians alone. He did not dare say a word against Mūsā and Hārūn (Aaron), his real opponents.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people protested"**: the leaders and notables of Pharaoh's people urged him on, provoking him to act against Mūsā and the believers with him.

**"“Are you going to leave Moses and his people free"**: will you not kill them? Will you let them go free?

**"to spread corruption in the land"**: spreading unrest among your subjects, changing their religion and worship, and calling them to worship their Lord, Allah alone, instead of you. How strange that these people worried about Mūsā and his people causing corruption! In truth, Pharaoh and his people were the ones spreading corruption, though they did not see it.

**"and abandon you and your gods?”"** and to leave you and the worship of your gods. In another reading: and to give up worshipping you as a god. Ibn ʿAbbās, as as-Suddī narrated from him, said their gods were cows. Whenever they saw a beautiful cow, Pharaoh would order them to worship it. That is why as-Sāmirī made for the children of Israel the statue of a calf that seemed to low. One explanation says Pharaoh had made small idols for them to worship, while telling them he was their lord and the lord of those idols. Their words also show that Pharaoh himself worshipped other gods, even while claiming to be his people's god.

**"He responded, “We will kill their sons"**: Pharaoh accepted his people's advice. We will slaughter their newborn sons, as we did the first time. The verb can be read nuqattilu, "we will kill in great numbers", or naqtulu, "we will kill".

**"and keep their women."** We will let their grown women live, to serve us as maidservants.

**"We will completely dominate them.”"** We have overwhelming power and supremacy over them. So they did this to them, and the children of Israel were filled with grief.

### Why did Pharaoh not threaten Mūsā himself?

Pharaoh had no convincing answer to his chiefs' question, and could only say he would kill the Israelites' sons and spare their women. It is explained that he tried to reassure his people this way. By killing the males and sparing the women, he would wipe out the Israelites over time, while the women would serve his people. In fact Pharaoh was so frightened by Mūsā's miracle that even while threatening to kill every Israelite man, he could not bring himself to utter one word against the two brothers. As Maulānā Rūmī put it, all humans and spirits stand in awe of the one who fears Allah and holds to taqwā.

### Did the old law work?

This was the second time the law of killing the Israelites' sons and sparing their women was proclaimed. The first time was before Mūsā's birth, so that Mūsā would not survive. The failure of that law was plain to see that very day, in the huge crowd of Israelites present. The opposite of what Pharaoh intended came about. The fate he planned for the children of Israel, to crush and humiliate them, fell on him instead. Allah gave the children of Israel victory, disgraced Pharaoh and drowned him with his soldiers. When Allah means to humble a people, everything they devise leads only to disaster, and this tyranny led Pharaoh and his people to their shameful end.

### In short

- Pharaoh's chiefs goaded him to act against Mūsā, calling him a spreader of corruption, when they themselves were the corrupters.
- Their "gods" included the cows they worshipped, which explains as-Sāmirī's later calf.
- Pharaoh renewed his old law of killing the Israelites' sons, yet was too afraid to threaten Mūsā and Hārūn themselves.
- The first law had already failed, and this one too would turn back on him.

128.text:
When Pharaoh pressed on with his evil plan, Mūsā (Moses) gave his people a remedy: "Moses reassured his people, “Seek Allah’s help and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. He grants it to whoever He chooses of His servants. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous.”" After his defeat, Pharaoh had enforced the law of killing the Israelites' sons, and they were terrified, remembering what they had suffered before Mūsā came. Mūsā was aware of their fear. Out of kindness he offered them two wise steps, and promised that the good end would be theirs and that they would prevail.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses reassured his people, “Seek Allah’s help"**: ask Allah alone for help, to remove hardship from you and bring you good.

**"and be patient."** Endure the trial you have been given, and their persecution, until things turn in your favour.

**"Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺."** The land, the land of Egypt, belongs to Allah, not to Pharaoh or anyone else to do with as they please.

**"He grants it to whoever He chooses of His servants."** He bequeaths it as an inheritance to whom He wills. By His will, He gives authority in the land to different peoples in turn.

**"The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous.”"** The praiseworthy end belongs to those who are mindful of Allah, who guard against disbelief, idolatry and indecency. One explanation says the end meant is Paradise. Those who believe, follow their Lord's commands and avoid what He forbids will reach the good end despite their tests and trials. So if they kept taqwā by acting on these two instructions, they would in the end rule the whole country.

### What is the remedy that never fails?

A little reflection on Mūsā's two teachings shows that together they are a sure remedy for every difficulty. The first ingredient, the heart of the remedy, is seeking Allah's help. If the Creator of the universe comes to someone's aid, who can stop Him? Maulānā Rūmī put it in a couplet: earth, air, water and fire are all Allah's servants, lifeless to you and me, but fully alive to Allah. A hadith says that when Allah wills something, everything turns to serve that purpose. No weapon against an enemy is stronger than turning to Allah for help with a sincere heart. Merely saying some formula is not enough.

The second ingredient is patience. The Arabic word ṣabr literally means holding oneself in check when unwelcome things happen. Everyone knows that nothing important is achieved without hardship. A person who readily prepares to face difficulty succeeds in most of his aims. The Prophet ﷺ said that no one has been given a greater blessing than patience. Abū Dāwūd recorded this.

### How does a prophet solve a people's problem?

Pharaoh's rule had created a problem for the children of Israel, and they asked their prophet to solve it. The solution he offered was to turn to Allah. This shows the difference between how worldly leaders and prophets approach a community's problems. Worldly leaders look for the answer at the level of government, either by compromising with the authorities or by clashing with them. The Prophet's solution was to bear what was happening patiently, seek Allah's help, and turn to Allah without expecting anything from the powers that be.

He also explained why his solution went against the usual thinking of his people. Their problems seemed to come from the ruling power and seemed solvable only by that power. But the more important question was how power comes to be held at all. No one holds power merely through clever strategy. Power is given or taken away directly by Allah. So the solution to the problem also lies with Allah.

### In short

- Facing Pharaoh's renewed persecution, Mūsā told his people to seek Allah's help and be patient.
- The earth belongs to Allah, who gives it to whom He wills, and the good end belongs to the mindful.
- Sincere reliance on Allah and patient endurance together are a remedy that never fails. Patience is among the greatest of blessings.
- Prophets solve a people's problems by turning them to Allah, the true giver and taker of power.

129.text:
The children of Israel could not see how patience alone would free them from Pharaoh's oppression, and they complained to Mūsā (Moses): "They complained, “We have always been oppressed—before and after you came to us ˹with the message˺.”" His answer held out hope: "He replied, “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land to see what you will do.”" Mūsā answered by reminding them of their present situation and how it would change.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They complained, “We have always been oppressed"**: we suffered at Pharaoh's hands. Pharaoh and his people humiliated and disgraced us, killing our sons, using our women and forcing us to labour, and you have seen some of it.

**"before and after you came to us ˹with the message˺.”"** Perhaps they meant that they had been waiting for a prophet to save them from Pharaoh's oppression, yet their lot was unchanged even after he came.

**"He replied, “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy"**: when Allah says "perhaps" (ʿasā), it carries certainty. Your Lord will destroy your enemy, Pharaoh and his people, through drought and hunger. Mūsā gave them hope of release from their trial.

**"and make you successors in the land"**: Allah will establish you in the land after them and make you its inhabitants, the land of Egypt.

**"to see what you will do.”"** So that He may see how you act in it, whether you obey Him, and whether you are thankful or ungrateful. Mūsā was encouraging them to value Allah's favour when the afflictions were lifted and replaced by blessings.

### Is power a reward or a test?

The last phrase of the verse holds a wise lesson. Sovereignty and rule are not goals in themselves. They are a means to make peace and justice prevail in the land, a sacred trust given by Allah so that good may overcome evil. The verse warned the Israelites that, if they were given this trust, they should not forget the fate of those before them.

The verse speaks directly to the Israelites, but indirectly it warns everyone entrusted with rule. Sovereignty belongs to Allah alone. He has made human beings His deputies on earth, giving them power and taking it away when He wills:

> "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O Allah! Lord over all authorities! You give authority to whoever You please and remove it from who You please; You honour whoever You please and disgrace who You please" (3:26).

So power is a test of how far rulers fulfil their duty to establish peace and justice and make good prevail over evil.

In this world, being powerful is as much a test as being powerless. Whoever has power today is being tested on whether he will grow arrogant and tyrannical, or act with justice and humility. If power is given to others instead, that too is to test them. If one group loses power through its own incompetence and it passes to another group, which also proves incompetent, power will be taken from it too and given to yet another. The prosperity and power people long for in this world can only be truly had in the Hereafter. In this world they are given only as a test, and in the Hereafter they will be given to the righteous as a reward.

### What did ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd tell the caliph?

Abū Ḥayyān records an event under this verse in his tafsīr, Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd once visited al-Manṣūr, later the second caliph of the Abbasid dynasty, before he came to power. He recited this verse to him, "Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land", as a kind of prediction that al-Manṣūr would come to the throne. Soon afterwards al-Manṣūr became caliph. When ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd came to him again, al-Manṣūr reminded him of his prediction. ʿAmr replied at once that the first part had come true, since he was now caliph. But the second part still remained: "to see what you will do". Gaining power, he meant, is nothing to be proud of, because afterwards Allah judges how those in authority use that trust.

### In short

- The Israelites complained that their suffering had not changed since Mūsā came.
- Mūsā assured them that Allah would destroy their enemy and make them successors in the land, to see how they would act.
- Power is a trust and a test from Allah, who gives and takes authority as He wills, and the powerless are tested too.
- ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd reminded a new caliph that the verse's warning, "to see what you will do", still lay ahead of him.

130.text:
The next verses tell of the calamities that struck Pharaoh and his people one after another, until they finally led to their death. The first punishment from heaven, after Pharaoh rejected Mūsā (Moses), was a famine: "Indeed, We afflicted Pharaoh’s people with famine and shortage of crops so they might come back ˹to their senses˺". According to historical reports, this famine lasted seven years.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We afflicted Pharaoh’s people"**: Allah tested and tried them, and seized them.

**"with famine"**: literally "with years", meaning years of drought and hunger, one year after another, with little produce.

**"and shortage of crops"**: the failure and disappearance of fruit and crops. Mujāhid said this was the lighter of the two. Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah said that a date palm would bear only a single date. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah said the drought struck the people of the countryside, while the loss of fruit struck those living in cities and towns.

**"so they might come back ˹to their senses˺"**: so that they might take heed and become believers. They might reflect, realise that this was a punishment from Allah for their disbelief, and repent to Him.

### Why does hardship come first?

The famine was a warning, not yet the final blow. As with earlier peoples, Allah first sent hardship so that they might humble themselves and return to Him. It gave Pharaoh's people the chance to recognise that their land, their harvest and their very survival lay in Allah's hands, not Pharaoh's. Whatever Pharaoh might say about his power, the failed harvests answered him.

### In short

- The first of the punishments on Pharaoh's people was years of drought and failed crops, lasting seven years by some reports.
- Drought struck the countryside and loss of fruit struck the towns, until a palm bore only one date.
- The aim was that they might take heed, recognise Allah's punishment and repent.

131.text:
When a people are marked by Allah's anger, they lose the ability to tell right from wrong. So it was with Pharaoh's people. They learnt nothing from the warning, and instead blamed their calamities on Mūsā (Moses): "In times of prosperity, they said, “This is what we deserve,” but in adversity, they blamed it on Moses and those with him. Surely all is destined by Allah. Yet most of them did not know".

### Phrase by phrase

**"In times of prosperity"**: whenever good came to them, a fertile season, plenty and comfort, wealth, good harvests and a thriving economy.

**"they said, “This is what we deserve,”"** This is ours by right, because we have earned it. And they did not give thanks for it.

**"but in adversity"**: whenever evil struck them, such as drought, famine, failed fruit, disease or other hardship.

**"they blamed it on Moses and those with him."** They took it as a bad omen from Mūsā and the believers with him, the children of Israel, and would say the hardship came because of them and what they had done. The Arabic word for omen, ṭāʾir, literally means a bird. The Arabs had a superstition that a bird flying to their right or left meant good or bad fortune.

**"Surely all is destined by Allah."** Literally, "their omen is with Allah". ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: their afflictions are with Allah and from Him. Their hardship and their plenty alike came from Allah, who brought it on them. The misfortunes happened by Allah's decree and permission. Neither they nor Mūsā had any hand in them, except for Mūsā's prayers against them.

**"Yet most of them did not know"**: most of them, or as one explanation puts it, all of them, did not know or believe that whatever befell them came from Him. They put down what happened to other causes rather than to Allah's decree.

### Is there any such thing as a bad omen?

The verse teaches that good and bad fortune come from Allah. Everything in this world happens by His will. No one can bring good or bad luck to anyone. It is sheer ignorance to believe in omens and to build one's actions on such baseless notions.

### How do words twist every warning?

Words have to be used to call a thing right or wrong, or a person innocent or guilty. But words are used by human beings, who in this world of testing are free to use them however they please. The most dangerous part of that freedom is the ability to justify calling truth falsehood, and falsehood truth. A person can label a prophet's plain miracle as magic and then ignore it.

If Allah gives him a blessing, he can describe it as though it came only from his own ability and effort. If Allah sends a warning to punish him for ignoring the truth, he is free to blame it on the bad luck brought by the very worshippers of Allah whom he mistreated, and on whose account the warning came. Everything comes from Allah so that people may learn from it. But with a few words, a person turns every warning upside down and so misses its lesson.

### In short

- Pharaoh's people took prosperity as their due and blamed every hardship on Mūsā and the believers.
- Their "omen" was with Allah: good and bad alike came by His decree, not from Mūsā.
- Belief in omens is ignorance, for nothing brings luck but Allah's will.
- By clever labels, people can explain away every blessing and every warning and so learn nothing.

132.text:
Pharaoh's people showed the depth of their rebellion, tyranny and stubbornness with an open vow: "They said, “No matter what sign you may bring to deceive us, we will never believe in you.”" Whatever miracle, proof or evidence Mūsā (Moses) brought, they would neither accept it nor believe in him or his message.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They said, “No matter what sign you may bring"**: whenever and whatever sign, evidence or proof you bring us, O Mūsā, even proof of the falsehood of our own beliefs.

**"to deceive us"**: literally "to bewitch us with", to dazzle our eyes or cast a spell on us.

**"we will never believe in you.”"** We will not believe in your message, they say. They said this out of stubbornness against the truth. So Mūsā prayed to Allah against them.

### Why can't some people see the truth?

Pharaoh's words show that even when the truth appears in the clearest and most complete form, only a person who is open to it receives it. The truth shows itself only to someone who is serious about it, willing to receive and accept it wherever and in whatever form it comes. Someone who is not serious, who is content with things as they are, cannot see the truth as truth, and so cannot accept it.

Being pleased with one's own condition makes a person blind to what lies outside himself. He is ignorant despite his knowledge, and deaf though he has ears.
