A person will surely find the truth if his mind is free of negative conditioning. But most people have been conditioned in this way, and that is why the truth escapes them.

### In short

- Pharaoh's people swore they would never believe, whatever sign Mūsā brought, and called his signs sorcery.
- Their vow drew Mūsā's prayer against them.
- The truth reveals itself only to those who are open and serious. Contentment with the status quo blinds people to it.

133.text:
Their vow brought a succession of punishments: "So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people". Mūsā (Moses) was given nine miracles during his time in Egypt, as warnings to Pharaoh's people. Two were shown before Pharaoh and his court, and the third was the famine. This verse names five more.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We plagued them with floods"**: the word is ṭūfān. Ibn ʿAbbās said it was heavy rain that ruined the crops and fruit. He is also reported to have said it means mass death. Mujāhid said it was water that carried plague everywhere. One explanation says it was continuous, unbroken rain, day and night, from one Saturday to the next. Another says it was a flood of water that entered their houses and stood up to people's necks as they sat, for seven days. Most of the great commentators say it was a flood.

**"locusts"**: the well-known insect, which they sent to eat everything the earth produced, plants and fruit, for seven days. Ibn Abī Najīḥ reported that Mujāhid said they ate the nails in their doors and left the wood. Locusts are lawful to eat. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Abū Yaʿfūr asked ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Awfā about locusts. He said that they took part in seven campaigns with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that locusts were part of their food. Ibn Mājah, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and ash-Shāfiʿī recorded, through ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam from his father, that Ibn ʿUmar reported the Prophet ﷺ as saying that two kinds of dead creature and two kinds of blood had been made lawful. The creatures are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are named in the report as the kidney and the spleen.

**"lice"**: the word is qummal. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is the grain weevil, or by another view small wingless locusts, and Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said the same. Al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said qummal are small black insects. Others compare it to woodworm or ticks, crawling creatures that ate whatever the locusts had left. The word is used both for lice and for an insect that eats grain. Possibly both were sent: small pests ate their grain while swarms of lice ate even their hair and eyelashes.

**"frogs"**: they swarmed into their houses and food stores and plagued them.

**"and blood"**: blood flowing in their water, filling their wells and rivers.

**"—all as clear signs"**: distinct signs, one after another. Ibn ʿAbbās said each punishment lasted a fixed time, followed by a period of relief and then the next punishment. One explanation says they came a month apart.

**"but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people"**: they were too proud to believe in Allah or in what Mūsā brought, and they were a sinful, criminal people, idolaters who would not give up falsehood or be guided to the truth.

### How did the plagues unfold?

Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr recorded Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's account. When Mūsā came to Pharaoh and demanded the release of the children of Israel, Pharaoh refused. So Allah sent the flood, a rain that went on until they feared it was a punishment. They asked Mūsā to pray to his Lord to stop it, promising to believe and let the children of Israel go. He prayed, and the affliction was lifted, but they neither believed nor let them go.

That year Allah made the earth bring forth crops, fruit and grass as never before. "This is what we hoped for," they said. So Allah sent the locusts, which began to eat the grass. When they saw what the locusts did to it, they knew no crop would survive. They made the same promise, Mūsā prayed, and the locusts were removed. Still they did not believe or release the children of Israel.

They gathered grain and stored it in their houses, saying they had saved their crops. Then Allah sent the qummal, the grain weevils. A man would take ten sacks of grain to the mill and get back three small bags. They made the same promise, Mūsā prayed, and the weevils were removed. Still they did not let the children of Israel go.

Once, sitting with Pharaoh, Mūsā heard a frog croak. He asked Pharaoh what he and his people would suffer from these creatures. Pharaoh scoffed at the idea that frogs could do anything. Yet by nightfall a man would sit in a mass of frogs up to his chin, unable to open his mouth without a frog jumping in. They made the same promise, Mūsā prayed, but they did not believe.

Then Allah sent blood, which filled their rivers, wells and water jars. They complained to Pharaoh that they had nothing to drink. He told them Mūsā had bewitched them. They asked how that could be, when every time they looked in their jars the water had turned to blood. They went to Mūsā with the same promise. He prayed and the blood stopped, but again they neither believed nor let the children of Israel go. A similar account is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, as-Suddī, Qatādah and several others among the Salaf.

### In short

- After the famine, Allah sent five distinct signs: flood, locusts, weevils or lice, frogs and blood.
- Each struck for a time, was lifted at Mūsā's prayer, and was followed by another when they broke their word.
- Locusts are lawful food, as the Companions ate them on campaign.
- Despite all these signs they stayed arrogant, a criminal people who would not believe.

134.text:
Each time a punishment fell, Pharaoh's people turned to Mūsā (Moses) with the same plea: "When tormented, they pleaded, “O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you." Then came their oath: "If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you.”" Whenever the flood, the locusts, the weevils, the frogs or the blood came on them, they made this promise.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When tormented"**: whenever the punishment fell on them.

**"they pleaded, “O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf"**: call on your Lord for us.

**"by virtue of the covenant He made with you."** Because of the prophethood He has given you, and His promise to you that He will lift the punishment if we turn to Him. One explanation says: because of what He has commanded you.

**"If you help remove this torment from us"**: the Arabic la-in, "if", carries the lām of an oath. They swore to it.

**"we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you.”"** We will release them from captivity and send them with you, with all their belongings.

### How did each plague begin and end?

Ibn-al-Mundhir cited Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that each punishment lasted seven days, beginning on a Saturday, followed by three weeks of relief. Imam al-Baghawī cited Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that when they were first relieved of the famine through Mūsā's prayer, they did not keep their promise to believe. So Mūsā asked Allah to send a painful punishment that would be a lesson to his people and their descendants.

Allah first sent the flood. Water filled and surrounded all the lands and houses of Pharaoh's people, leaving them nowhere to farm or live. Remarkably, the lands and houses of the Israelites were untouched. In great distress they begged Mūsā to pray for relief, promising faith and freedom for the Israelites. His prayer was answered and the flood subsided. Their fields are said to have become more fertile than before. Again they broke their promise. The flood was no punishment from Allah, they said. It had done them good, the bigger harvest came from it, and Mūsā had nothing to do with it.

They were given time to reflect. After a month the locusts came and ate all their crops and fruit, and some reports say even the wooden doors and roofs of their houses. Again they saw that the Israelites' houses and fields close by were unharmed. Once more they begged for help with firm promises, and Mūsā's prayer brought relief. Then, seeing they had enough grain for a year, they went back on their word as arrogantly as before.

After another spell of peace came the qummal, then the frogs, which filled their houses up to their necks, their beds, pans and pots. Again they came with all their old promises and were relieved. Yet those who earn Allah's anger lose the power to think straight. Now at peace, they said they were sure Mūsā was a sorcerer, not Allah's messenger, and their troubles were the work of his sorcery.

After a month's relief came the blood. Everything they used turned to blood, their drink, their food and their water, before they could use it. Water drawn from wells or tanks turned to blood. Reports say that when Egyptians and Israelites sat down to eat together, the Egyptian's mouthful turned to blood while the Israelite's did not. This punishment too lasted seven days, and was lifted by Mūsā's prayer after their usual false promises.

### In short

- With every plague, Pharaoh's people begged Mūsā to pray, swearing to believe and free the Israelites.
- Each plague is said to have lasted seven days, with weeks of relief between, while the Israelites nearby were spared.
- After each relief they explained the punishment away, as luck, as a benefit, or as sorcery.

135.text:
Their promises never lasted: "But as soon as We removed the torment from them—until they met their inevitable fate—they broke their promise". Pharaoh's people were struck by these punishments one after another, yet they persisted in their arrogance and showed no sign of learning from the warnings.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But as soon as We removed the torment from them"**: when Allah lifted the punishment from them, through Mūsā's (Moses') supplication.

**"—until they met their inevitable fate—"**: literally "for a term they were to reach". The term was their drowning. The relief was only for a set time, before they were destroyed by drowning.

**"they broke their promise"**: at once they went back on their word and broke their pledge to Mūsā. They did not believe him or send the Israelites with him, but held firm to their disbelief.

### Did they keep any of their promises?

Muhammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Yasār gave this account. After the sorcerers believed, the enemy of Allah, Pharaoh, went back defeated and humiliated, but insisted on his disbelief and kept on in his wickedness. Allah sent the signs on him one after another. First came famine, then the flood, the locusts, the qummal, the frogs and the blood.

The flood covered the face of the earth with water. When it went down, they could not use the land to farm or for anything else, and they went hungry. Then they pleaded with Mūsā and he prayed for them, yet their word was broken again. Next came locusts, which devoured the trees and even the nails in their doors, until the doors fell off their houses. Again they pleaded, he prayed and the affliction was lifted.

Still they broke their promise, and Allah sent the qummal. Mūsā was told to strike a mound with his staff. He struck a great mound, and the qummal poured out of it in vast numbers. They overran houses and food stores until no one could sleep or rest. Again they pleaded, he prayed and it was lifted.

They broke their promise, and Allah sent the frogs. These filled their houses, food and pots, so that no one could lift a garment or uncover food without finding frogs in it. When it became unbearable, they made the same promises, Mūsā prayed, and Allah removed it. They kept none of their promises, and Allah sent the blood. The water of Pharaoh's people turned to blood. Any water they drew from a well, a river or a jar turned to blood.

### How did their view of Mūsā's demand change?

Mūsā carried out his prophetic mission in Egypt for about forty years, though one report says he stayed 20 years. His mission had two parts. The first was to bring Pharaoh the message of Allah's oneness. The second was to lead the children of Israel, the descendants of Yūsuf (Joseph), out of Egypt, settle them in the Sinai desert and train them in their religion there, away from corruption. At that time the children of Israel were in the grip of the Coptic ruler, Pharaoh. The Copts used them as labourers in their farming and building, so the Coptic rulers did not want the Israelites to leave.

When Mūsā first asked Pharaoh to let the children of Israel leave with him, Pharaoh and his courtiers gave the request a political colour. They accused Mūsā of wanting to drive the Copts out of Egypt (7:110). That was absurd, since Mūsā's plan was to take himself out of Egypt. Pharaoh and his companions then had an inflated view of their power, so they saw even a straightforward request as crooked.

Later Allah struck Pharaoh and his people with every kind of calamity. For years they faced famine, along with violent storms of hail, lightning and thunder. Swarms of locusts ate their crops and gardens and destroyed all greenery. Lice multiplied until clothes and beds were full of them. Frogs hopped everywhere, in houses and along the paths, and the water of the rivers and lakes turned to blood. When Pharaoh and his people began to suffer these afflictions, they asked Mūsā to pray to his Lord to end them, promising to let the children of Israel leave with him. The demand that had once looked to the Copts like a political plot to evict them now looked like what it was, a migration of the children of Israel themselves.

### In short

- Each time the punishment was lifted, Pharaoh's people broke their word, until their appointed end by drowning.
- Ibn Isḥāq tells how the plagues came one after another and how every promise was broken.
- Mūsā's aim was to lead the Israelites out to worship Allah freely, not to overthrow the Copts.
- Under the plagues, the "political plot" they had imagined turned out to be a simple migration.

136.text:
After sign upon sign, Pharaoh's people still rebelled and overstepped every limit, so the final punishment came: "So We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them". The sixth punishment is called rijz in the Qur'an, meaning a plague or pestilence. More than seventy thousand Egyptians are reported to have died in it. They were relieved of it through Mūsā's (Moses') prayer, and again broke their promise as before. When they showed no sign of understanding, the last punishment, death, finally seized them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We inflicted punishment upon them"**: Allah took retribution from them once and for all, when the time appointed for their destruction came.

**"drowning them in the sea"**: the word al-yamm means salt water, the sea. Allah drowned them in the sea that Mūsā had parted by Allah's power, through which he and the children of Israel had passed. Leaving behind their lands, houses and possessions, Pharaoh and his soldiers went into the sea in pursuit of Mūsā and his people. When all of them were inside, the sea closed over them and every one of them drowned.

**"for denying Our signs"**: because they rejected Allah's nine signs and disbelieved in them, turning away from a truth beyond any doubt.

**"and being heedless of them"**: they paid no attention to them and did not reflect on them.

### Why do people reject plain signs?

Punishment fell on the peoples to whom prophets were sent because they denied Allah's signs (āyāt). Those who believed in the prophets, on the other hand, earned special help from Allah. They stayed patient under every kind of provocation from those around them, and remained steadfast on the path of Allah.

The "signs" are the arguments that establish the truth as true. But a person's ego and pride can keep him from accepting them. Instead of attending fully to the arguments, he turns his attention to the preacher who presents them. He cannot answer the arguments. But the one presenting them is not a figure established by history, nor is he wrapped in worldly glory, so it is easier to mock the presenter than his arguments. He feels that to listen to the arguments would be to place himself beneath the preacher. So, to keep his pride and his sense of superiority over the caller (dāʿī), he will not concede that the truth stands above him.

Here lies the real test for every human being. In this world Allah shows Himself indirectly, through signs and reason. In the Hereafter He will show His Being directly, and then no one will dare to deny Him. But only faith that comes from a person discovering the truth while Allah is still unseen has any value.

### In short

- After the plague and their broken promises, Pharaoh and his army chased Mūsā into the parted sea and were drowned.
- They perished because they denied Allah's signs and gave them no thought.
- Pride makes people mock the messenger rather than answer his arguments, and faith counts only while Allah is unseen.

137.text:
The previous verses told of Allah's warnings to Pharaoh's people. This verse tells of their shameful end and of the success of the Israelites: "And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings. ˹In this way˺ the noble Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel for what they had endured. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people constructed and what they established". Allah gave the people who were thought weak, the children of Israel, the eastern and western parts of the land as an inheritance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people"**: literally "the people who were considered weak", those humiliated by Pharaoh and his people and oppressed through bondage. The verse does not say "the people who were weak", but "those who were taken to be weak". This implies that those who have Allah's support can never be truly weak, however they may look. In the end people come to see that they are not weak, because all honour and dignity belong to Allah.

**"successors of the eastern and western lands"**: literally "We made them inherit". The word "inheritance" shows that, as a son is the rightful heir to his father's land and wealth, the Israelites became the rightful heirs to the land and wealth of Pharaoh's people. "East" and "west" are plural in the Arabic, perhaps for the different points of sunrise and sunset in winter and summer. All the experts in tafsīr say "the land" means the land of Egypt and Syria, which came under Israelite rule after Pharaoh's people and the Amalekites were destroyed. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah said it refers to ash-Shām, Greater Syria. One explanation lists the land of Jerusalem, Palestine, Jordan and Egypt, and another the lands of the Levant.

**"which We had showered with blessings."** This describes the land, which Allah blessed with water and trees, and with the best crops and fruits. The Qur'an calls Syria the land of barakah, blessing, and several traditions call Egypt a land of blessing too. The caliph ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb called the Nile the prince of rivers. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said that Egypt holds nine of the ten parts of blessing, and the tenth is spread over the rest of the earth. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ records this.

**"˹In this way˺ the noble Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel"**: the fair word of your Lord came true, O Messenger. One explanation says it was His promise to reward them with Paradise or with victory. Mujāhid and Ibn Jarīr said it refers to this promise:

> "But it was Our Will to favour those who were oppressed in the land, making them models ˹of faith˺ as well as successors and to establish them in the land; and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared" (28:5-6).

**"for what they had endured."** Because they bore patiently the persecution of their enemy, or, as some say, because they held firmly to their religion.

**"And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people constructed"**: Allah destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had produced, their farms, buildings, castles and towns. "What they constructed" may also mean their evil schemes against Mūsā (Moses).

**"and what they established"**: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said it means what they built. The verb can be read yaʿrishūn or yaʿrushūn, what they raised up. It covers the tall buildings and palaces they put up, and the trees and vines they planted.

### Which promise was fulfilled?

The verse shows how the promise of Allah and His Messenger came true, as it always does. The promise may be the one Mūsā made to his people earlier in this surah: "Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land" (7:129). Or it may be Allah's promise to the Israelites in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, quoted above. In fact the two are one, since Mūsā's promise came from Allah's.

### Why was patience rewarded?

This favour to the people of Israel was the reward for their patience, as the verse says, "for what they had endured". It quietly suggests that any people or person who follows the same example, at any time and in any place, will receive the same reward. When Mūsā promised them rule over the land, he had insisted that steadfastness, patience and seeking Allah's help were the only key to success.

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said the verse teaches that when someone is not strong enough to defend himself against an enemy, the best road to success is patience. When a wronged person tries to take revenge himself by wronging his opponent, Allah leaves him to manage his own affairs, and he may succeed or fail. But when a person asks Allah for help against what others inflict on him and stays patient, Allah opens the door of success for him.

It is not right to claim that the Israelites showed no patience because, when Mūsā urged them to be patient, they complained that they had been persecuted before and after he came. First, their patience under constant persecution by Pharaoh and his people is a proven fact. Second, their words may not have been a complaint at all, but simply an expression of grief.

### Does the promise extend to this Ummah?

As Allah fulfilled His promise of rule over the land to the Israelites, He made a similar promise to the community of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in Sūrat an-Nūr: "Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them" (24:55). As the Israelites saw Allah's promise fulfilled in their rule over the land, the Muslim Ummah saw it fulfilled in its rule over most of the earth, as Rūḥ al-Bayān notes.

### What comes next?

With Pharaoh and his people gone, the story now turns to the Israelites. The coming verses tell of their triumph and good fortune, and then of the insolence they showed in spite of Allah's many blessings. These verses also console the Prophet ﷺ in his grief at the stubbornness of the disbelievers, by showing how the earlier prophets were troubled by their own peoples.

### In short

- Allah made the Israelites, once thought weak, heirs to the blessed lands of Egypt and Syria. Those with Allah's support are never truly weak.
- This fulfilled the promise made through Mūsā and in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, as a reward for their patience.
- Patience and seeking Allah's help bring success, while taking revenge on one's own leaves a person to himself.
- Allah destroyed Pharaoh's buildings and gardens, and made a similar promise of succession to this Ummah.

138.text:
After their miraculous victory over Pharaoh and his people, and the ease that followed, the Israelites began to show the ignorance that wealthy people show when given a life of luxury. Allah records what the ignorant among them said to Mūsā (Moses) once they had crossed the sea and seen His signs and His great power: "We brought the Children of Israel across the sea and they came upon a people devoted to idols." At once they asked, "O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods." His answer was blunt: "He replied, “Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly". It was their first impertinent request.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We brought the Children of Israel across the sea"**: Allah brought them safely across when Mūsā struck the sea with his staff and it parted.

**"and they came upon a people devoted to idols."** They passed by a people who clung to their idols, worshipping them constantly instead of Allah. In the Arabic, "devoted" is read yaʿkufūn or yaʿkifūn. Some scholars of tafsīr said these people were from Canaan, or from the tribe of Lakhm. One explanation calls them al-Raqīm, remnants of the people of Ibrāhīm (Abraham). Ibn Jarīr said they worshipped idols made in the shape of cows. This later influenced the children of Israel when they worshipped the calf.

**"They demanded, “O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods.”"** Show us a god, an idol to worship, just as these people have idols to worship.

**"He replied, “Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly"**: you do not know Allah's greatness and majesty, or that He is free of any partner or anything like Him. You are ignorant of the rights due to Allah alone: belief in His oneness and the reverence owed to Him, and of how unfitting it is to ascribe partners to Him. You repay Allah's grace to you with words like these. One explanation says: you do not know Allah's command.

### Why do people long for a visible god?

Having crossed at the Red Sea's northern tip into the Sinai Peninsula, the Israelites then made their way southward along the coast. On the way they saw a people engaged in idol worship, and some of the Israelites asked Mūsā to make them an idol.

The greatest human weakness is attaching importance to what can be seen, and so failing to give one's attention to the unseen God. That is why people cannot detach themselves from things visible to the naked eye. The unenlightened bow down before gods of stone and metal. The civilised give the same devotion to a particular personality, a community, a cultural structure, or something similar.

### In short

- Soon after crossing the sea, some Israelites asked Mūsā for an idol like those of a people they passed.
- Those people worshipped cow-shaped idols, which later shaped the Israelites' worship of the calf.
- Mūsā called them ignorant of Allah's greatness and of His sole right to worship.
- People's weakness for the visible draws them to idols of stone, or to revered personalities and structures.

139.text:
Mūsā (Moses), deeply troubled by their ignorance, went on: "What they follow is certainly doomed to destruction and their deeds are in vain.”" All the effort these people put into their worship was going to waste.

### Phrase by phrase

**"What they follow is certainly doomed to destruction"**: these idol-worshippers are ruined, and their way, their idolatry, will be destroyed.

**"and their deeds are in vain.”"** All their works and devotion are false, worthless and in error, because they worship other than Allah.

### Did anything similar happen in the Prophet's ﷺ time?

Imam Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr reported from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī that the Companions set out from Makkah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for Ḥunayn. Some disbelievers had a lote tree near which they used to stay, and on which they hung their weapons. It was called Dhāt Anwāṭ. When the Companions passed a huge green lote tree, they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to appoint a Dhāt Anwāṭ for them, like the one the disbelievers had. He swore by the One in whose hand was his soul that they had said just what Mūsā's people said to him. Then he recited this verse and the one before it.

### Why could Mūsā never grant their request?

When Mūsā said that all the idol-worshippers' devotion would be wasted, he meant this. He had been sent to turn people to the worship of Allah alone. Carving idols for his own followers was unthinkable.

### In short

- Mūsā declared that the idol-worshippers' way was doomed and all their devotion worthless.
- The Prophet ﷺ likened some Companions' request for a sacred tree at Ḥunayn to the Israelites' request for an idol.
- A prophet sent to call people to the one God could never make idols for them.

140.text:
Mūsā (Moses) pressed home his reproach: "He added, “Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has honoured you above the others?”" How could he seek for them any god but Allah, when Allah had given them excellence over all the peoples of their time?

### Phrase by phrase

**"He added, “Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah"**: shall I command you to worship another lord, besides the one true God? In the Arabic, abghīkum, "shall I seek for you", stands for abghī lakum.

**"while He has honoured you above the others?”"** He has preferred you above all the peoples of your time, above all creatures then, because you surrendered to Him. You have already seen His great signs. He destroyed your enemy for you, made you leaders in the land and established you there. Those who believed in Mūsā were superior to all the people of that age.

### What did their "superiority" mean?

The superiority of the Israelites over the rest of humanity is not meant here in a racial sense. It refers to their mission. It carries the same meaning as the Qur'an's description of the community of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as "the best community". Allah's practice is to entrust His Book to one community, which then carries His message to the rest. Long ago that duty belonged to the Israelites. After the coming of the Final Prophet ﷺ, it passed to the Muslim ummah.

### In short

- Mūsā asked how he could seek another god for them when Allah had raised them above the peoples of their time.
- Their superiority was one of mission, as carriers of Allah's Book, not of race.
- That role later passed to the community of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, called "the best community".

141.text:
Mūsā (Moses) reminded the children of Israel of Allah's blessings, above all their rescue from Pharaoh's tyranny and the humiliation they had suffered: "And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment—killing your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord". He reminded them too of the honour and the justice they had seen against their enemy, when they watched him disgraced, drowned and utterly destroyed. The same subject is told in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh"**: remember, O children of Israel, when Allah saved you from Pharaoh and his people. One reading has anjaynākum, "We rescued you", and another anjākum, "He rescued you".

**"who afflicted you with dreadful torment"**: who burdened you with the worst kind of suffering and humiliation.

**"killing your sons"**: slaughtering your little sons.

**"and keeping your women."** Letting your grown women live, to use them as servants.

**"That was a severe test from your Lord"**: literally "a tremendous trial". The deliverance was a tremendous blessing from your Lord, a test to see whether you would be thankful. Or the suffering itself was a tremendous trial. Either way it was a grace or a hardship from your Lord. So will you not take the warning and stop saying what you are saying?

### Why remind them of their suffering now?

The verse reminds them of their pitiful state and their persecution by Pharaoh, when their sons were killed and their daughters kept alive as maidservants. Allah freed them from that disgraceful punishment through His prophet. Could they now show their Lord such ingratitude, setting up lifeless stones beside Him as gods? They must repent to Allah for their transgression.

### Was Pharaoh's oppression a punishment?

The power Pharaoh had to oppress the Israelites was a test for them, not a punishment. Believers are put through such trials to shake them and wake them up, as if by a shock. It then becomes clear who turns away from Allah's true religion when faced with hard times, and who holds firmly to it through patience in adversity.

### In short

- Mūsā reminded the Israelites how Allah saved them from Pharaoh, who killed their sons and enslaved their women.
- Both the suffering and the rescue were a great test from their Lord, a test of patience and of gratitude.
- Having been freed by Allah, asking for idols was gross ingratitude that called for repentance.
- Oppression of believers is a trial that shows who stays steadfast and who falls away.

142.text:
With Pharaoh and his people destroyed, the Israelites enjoyed a time of peace. They asked Mūsā (Moses) for a religious code of law that they could live by, and Mūsā prayed to Allah for a code of guidance for them. Allah now reminds the children of Israel of the guidance He sent them by speaking directly to Mūsā and revealing to him the Torah (Tawrāh), which held their law and the details of its rulings: "We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten—completing his Lord’s term of forty nights." Before leaving, Mūsā gave his brother charge of the people: "Moses commanded his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people, do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We appointed for Moses thirty nights"**: the verb can be read wa-wāʿadnā or wa-waʿadnā. It comes from waʿdah, a spoken promise of something good. Allah promised to send His word to Mūsā. The condition was that Mūsā should go to Mount Sinai and spend thirty nights there in devotion to Allah, after which Allah would speak to him, once he had fasted through that period. Those thirty nights were the month of Dhū’l-Qaʿda.

**"then added another ten"**: ten more nights, from the month of Dhū’l-Ḥijja. The scholars of tafsīr said that Mūsā fasted through the thirty, and when they ended he cleaned his teeth with a twig. Then Allah told him to complete the term by adding ten more, making forty in all. One explanation says he disliked the stale odour of his mouth at the end of the fast and so cleaned his teeth. Allah then told him to fast ten more nights, so that He would speak to him with that odour on his breath.

**"completing his Lord’s term of forty nights."** The time appointed by his Lord, the time Allah had promised to speak to him, was completed as forty nights. In the Arabic, "forty" describes a state and "nights" makes the count specific. When the term was over, Mūsā was about to go to the Mount, as Allah says: "O Children of Israel! We saved you from your enemy, and made an appointment with you on the right side of Mount Ṭûr" (20:80).

**"Moses commanded his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people"**: when he was setting out for the Mount, to be alone with his Lord, Mūsā told his brother Hārūn (Aaron) to be his deputy and lead his people in his place.

**"do what is right"**: enjoin them to do right, act rightly among them in their affairs, govern them wisely and treat them kindly. The word aṣliḥ, "set right", is given here without an object. Perhaps it was a general command meant for the Israelites and for Hārūn alike.

**"and do not follow the way of the corruptors.”"** Do not follow the path of those who spread corruption, whether by committing transgressions yourself, by going along with them in disobedience, or by helping the wrongdoers. This was only a reminder, for Hārūn was an honourable and noble prophet with a high standing before Allah.

### Why thirty nights, and then ten more?

In Allah's will the number of nights Mūsā was to spend was forty from the start. Why then was he first told thirty, and then given ten more? No one can reach all the wisdom in Allah's acts, but scholars have offered some explanations. The well-known commentary Rūḥ al-Bayān says one wisdom was to lay down commands gradually, so that people find them easier to carry out. Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī says it was to teach those in authority to grant their subordinates extra time when they fail to finish a task in the set period. On this view, the spiritual perfection required of Mūsā was not reached in thirty nights, so ten more were added to give him time to attain it.

It is reported that Mūsā kept his fast unbroken through all thirty days and nights. After completing the thirty days he ate, and then presented himself at the appointed place on Mount Sinai. Allah told him that He loves the particular odour that fasting leaves in the mouth. Mūsā had lost it by cleaning his teeth, so he was told to fast ten more days to bring it back.

### Does this mean cleaning the teeth while fasting is disliked?

The report about the lost odour cannot be taken to mean that cleaning the teeth after fasting is forbidden or disliked. First, it is cited without any chain of narrators. Second, it may have been a command meant only for Mūsā, or only for the followers of the Torah, and not for others. The permissibility of using the tooth-stick while fasting is established by the Prophet's ﷺ practice. Al-Baihaqī reported, on the authority of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said the best act of a fasting person is cleaning the teeth with the miswāk. Al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr grades this hadith ḥasan.

### How could Mūsā go thirty days without food?

One may wonder how Mūsā could fast for thirty days without even eating at night. On his journey to meet Khiẓr, he could not wait even half a day, and said: "Bring us our meal! We have certainly been exhausted by today’s journey" (18:62).

Rūḥ al-Bayān explains that the difference lay in the nature of the two journeys. The journey to Khiẓr was one created being travelling to another created being. The journey on Mount Sinai was a devoted servant travelling to his Creator, having cut himself off from creation in search of his Lord. That spiritual journey weakened the pull of hunger and thirst, and made him able to fast for thirty days and nights on end.

The inner reading says the same. On this journey Mūsā waited thirty days without a thought of food or drink, unaware of hunger, because the Real was carrying him on a journey of generosity, waiting to speak with Him in intimate prayer. The other time, when he was sent to Khiẓr on his first journey in search of knowledge, he could not bear half a day of hunger. That was a journey of learning courtesy and of hardship. At the start of that journey he was the one carrying, not the one being carried. Being with himself, he felt his own pain, and walking the road of creatures, he noticed the signs of hunger.

### Why "nights" and not "days"?

The verse also shows that in the laws of the prophets the date changed at night. That is why it speaks of thirty nights rather than thirty days. The prophets' laws reckoned time by the moon. A lunar month begins with the sighting of the new moon, which can only happen at night, so in the lunar calendar the date changes at sunset. Al-Qurṭubī reports Ibn al-ʿArabī as saying that the solar calendar serves worldly interests, while the lunar calendar serves religious observance.

According to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, the thirty nights were the nights of Dhū’l-Qaʿda, the eleventh lunar month, and the ten added nights were the first ten of Dhū’l-Ḥijja. This suggests that the Torah was given to Mūsā on the day of ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā.

### Why forty?

The verse also suggests that the number forty has a special effect in setting the heart right. A hadith says that whoever worships Allah sincerely for forty days will have his heart made a spring of wisdom, as Rūḥ al-Bayān reports.

### Why move toward a goal by stages?

The verse also teaches people to set a period for reaching their goal and to approach it step by step, for it is Allah's way to do things gradually. Allah does not approve of haste. He created the universe in six days, though He could have created it in an instant without needing a single moment. In this He gave people a wise principle: approach your goals in stages, over time, so that you can give them proper attention. In the same way, the Torah was not given to Mūsā in a moment. A period was fixed for it to stress the same principle.

By ignoring this principle the Israelites lost their faith. Mūsā had told them, as he left for Mount Sinai, to expect him back after thirty days. He was kept ten days longer, and the impatient Israelites said Mūsā was lost somewhere and they should choose another leader. So they fell prey to the sorcerer Sāmirī and began worshipping the golden calf. Had they been patient and willing to go step by step, they would not have committed that fatal act of disbelief.

### Should a leader appoint a deputy?

Mūsā made a point of appointing Hārūn as his deputy when he set out for Mount Sinai, telling him to take responsibility for his people in his absence. This makes it necessary for anyone holding a position of responsibility to appoint someone to look after the work while he is away. The Prophet ﷺ always appointed a deputy whenever he left Madinah. On different occasions ʿAlī and ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm were appointed to this role.

Mūsā also gave Hārūn instructions before leaving, which shows that giving guidelines to one's deputy is also a religious requirement. Hārūn, being a prophet of Allah, could never be imagined to take part in corruption. So the instruction not to follow the corrupters meant that he should do nothing that could help or encourage them. That is exactly what Hārūn did when he saw his people following the magician Sāmirī, until they began worshipping the golden calf. He tried to stop them and warned Sāmirī against his mischief. Later Mūsā called him to account for what had happened, thinking it was the result of some weakness on Hārūn's part. This is also a lesson for those who neglect sound management of affairs and take that neglect as a sign of piety.

### What order did Allah's commands follow?

Mūsā was given the commands of calling people to Allah (daʿwah) in Egypt, while the laws came only once he was in the Sinai desert. This shows the order of Allah's commands. In ordinary circumstances, believers are required to set their personal lives right and live as true servants of Allah. Alongside this, they must invite others to believe in Allah's oneness and to live for the Hereafter. But when believers become an independent community, free to organise themselves as the Israelites were in the Sinai desert, it becomes their duty to build their social life on Islamic law. Mūsā's charge to Hārūn, to take his place, act rightly and not follow the way of the corrupters, sets out the basic principle for anyone who bears responsibility as the head of a community.

### The inner reading: promises in friendship

How exalted it is to make promises in friendship! How great to sit at the meeting place friendship has promised! How sweet it is when a promise is put off within the religion of friendship! Of the hints in this verse, the master of the spiritual path (ṭarīqah) said, "The promises of lovers, even when put off, are a sign of intimacy." And he said, "You put me off, You delay, You promise, and You do not come."

Pushing back a promised time and adding days before the promised moment is not approved, except in the religion of friendship. There even disloyalty counts as loyalty. See what the Lord of the worlds did with Mūsā in this exchange. He promised him thirty days, and when they had passed, He added ten more. He added them because Mūsā was glad of it. Mūsā counted the thirty days as his capital and the ten days as profit. It was as if he said, "When He added those days, I heard the ready coin of the Real's speech a second time."

As the poet says: "Come, by your life! Do not stay away! Give us hope of meeting you, then put us off. Promise and delay as you please, for we love you even when you keep the longing waiting. If you keep your promise we will rejoice, but we will live on your promise, content for a while."

### In short

- Allah appointed thirty nights for Mūsā on Mount Sinai and added ten, making forty, before speaking to him and giving him the Torah.
- The report that the ten days restored the fasting odour does not make using the miswāk while fasting disliked, as a hadith praises it.
- Counting by nights reflects the lunar calendar of the prophets' laws, and the forty may have ended on the day of ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā.
- The verse teaches gradual progress, appointing and instructing a deputy, and building community life on Allah's law once believers are free to do so.
- Mūsā could fast thirty days because he was being carried toward his Lord, unlike his tiring journey to Khiẓr.

143.text:
At the appointed time Mūsā (Moses) came for his meeting, and Allah spoke to him directly: "When Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he asked, “My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You.”" The answer came with a demonstration: "Allah answered, “You cannot see Me! But look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me.”" Then: "When his Lord appeared to the mountain, He levelled it to dust and Moses collapsed unconscious." And when he came to, "he cried, “Glory be to You! I turn to You in repentance and I am the first of the believers.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When Moses came at the appointed time"**: at the time Allah had promised to speak to him, after the full forty nights. One explanation places the meeting in Midian.

**"and his Lord spoke to him"**: without any intermediary, in speech that Mūsā heard from every direction, giving him commands, prohibitions and other instructions.

**"he asked, “My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You.”"** Mūsā longed to see his Lord, and asked for it.

**"Allah answered, “You cannot see Me!"** The Arabic is lan tarānī, "you will not see Me". In this worldly life, Mūsā, seeing Allah is beyond your strength. The word lan, "never", by no means shows that seeing Allah will never happen, as the misguided sect of the Muʿtazilah claimed. The believers' vision of Allah in the Hereafter is established by hadiths of the Messenger ﷺ that come through so many chains that they are mutawātir: "On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be bright looking at their Lord" (75:22-23).

The wording also points to this. Allah did not say lan urā, "I cannot be seen", but lan tarānī, "you cannot see Me". That implies that seeing Allah is not impossible, only that Mūsā could not bear it in his present physical state. Had it been impossible, the verse would have said "I cannot be seen". So seeing Allah is logically possible even in this world, but this verse rules out its happening in this world. That is also the unanimous view of most scholars. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim contains a hadith that none of you will see his Lord until he dies. Earlier scriptures also report that Allah said to Mūsā, "O Mūsā, no living soul sees Me without perishing, and no solid thing without crumbling."

**"But look at the mountain."** Look at the mountain, which is stronger than you. One explanation says it was the highest mountain in Midian. This was a physical demonstration that, in his present state, Mūsā could not endure such an experience.

**"If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me.”"** If the mountain stays standing and is unaffected when I reveal Myself to it, then you will be able to see Me, that is, you will be able to stand firm and see Me. If it is flattened, the sight of Allah in this world is beyond you.

**"When his Lord appeared to the mountain"**: the word is tajallī, disclosure or manifestation. According to the spiritual masters (Sufis), it means seeing something indirectly, through some other means, as one sees a thing reflected in a mirror. So tajallī cannot mean "seeing". The verse itself shows this, since it denies seeing yet speaks of Allah's disclosure to the mountain.

Imam Aḥmad recorded in his Musnad from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ, explaining these words, held out the tip of his little finger and said, "Like this." At-Tirmidhī recorded it in his chapter of tafsīr on this verse and called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb. Al-Ḥākim recorded it too in his Mustadrak, through Ḥammād ibn Salamah. He said it is ṣaḥīḥ by the criteria of Muslim, though they did not record it. Another report from Anas says the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse, put his thumb on the tip of his little finger, and said that only this much of Allah's light was disclosed to the mountain, and it burst apart. One explanation speaks of the equivalent of half the nail of a little finger, in a hadith al-Ḥākim verified. As-Suddī reported, through ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said only the measure of the little finger appeared. This does not have to mean that the whole mountain was shattered. Perhaps only the part directly exposed to the light was affected.

**"He levelled it to dust"**: He made it collapse into dust. The word can be read dakkan or dakkāʾa, meaning flattened.

**"and Moses collapsed unconscious."** He fainted, losing consciousness at the awe of what he had seen. Ibn Jarīr recorded these reports because of their bearing on the word al-ghashī, fainting.

**"When he recovered, he cried, “Glory be to You!"** Once he came round, he praised, glorified and honoured Allah, declaring Him far above any flaw, for no living soul could see Him in this life and live.

**"I turn to You in repentance"**: Mujāhid said this means from having asked to see You. Others explain it as: I repent for asking what I was not commanded to ask, and I ask Your forgiveness for asking to see You in this world.

**"and I am the first of the believers.”"** Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said it means the first of the children of Israel to believe, and Ibn Jarīr preferred this view. Others say the first believer of his time, or the first of his people. Another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās says it means: the first to believe that no one will see You in this life.

### Did the Prophet ﷺ place himself above Mūsā?

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayrah each narrated a fitting hadith here. Al-Bukhārī recorded Abū Saʿīd's version in his Ṣaḥīḥ. A Jewish man came to the Prophet ﷺ, having been slapped on the face, and complained that one of his Companions from the Anṣār had struck him. The Prophet ﷺ had the man summoned and asked why he had done it. He explained that he had heard the Jew swear by the One who chose Mūsā over all humanity. When he asked, "Over Muhammad too?", he grew angry and slapped him.

The Prophet ﷺ told them not to prefer him over the prophets. On the Day of Resurrection, he said, people will fall unconscious, and he will be the first to come round. Then he will find Mūsā holding one of the pillars of the Throne (ʿArsh). He will not know whether Mūsā came round before him, or whether he was spared because of his fainting at aṭ-Ṭūr. Al-Bukhārī recorded this hadith in many places in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and so did Muslim and Abū Dāwūd. Abū Hurayrah's version was collected by Imam Aḥmad and by the two shaykhs, al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

### Why can Allah not be seen in this world?

Mūsā wanted to see Allah. When he learnt that it was not possible, he turned to Allah in repentance and placed his faith in the unseen Allah. So human beings are tested by believing in Allah without seeing Him. Seeing Allah is a reward kept for the Hereafter, so how could it happen in this world?

Mūsā received his first call to prophethood on a mountainside, and he was called to the mountain again to receive the commands of the Torah. This hints that the best place to receive inspiration from Allah is the setting of nature rather than human society. When a person leaves the din of the crowded human world for the quiet world of trees, mountains and rivers, he begins to feel closer to Allah. His mind is free of worldly problems and not taken up with worldly thoughts. This is the best moment to think without bias or complexes clouding his thinking, and then he can truly commune with Allah.

### The inner reading: the journey of longing

Mūsā made two journeys: a journey of seeking and a journey of rapture. The journey of seeking was the night of the fire, of which Allah says, "he spotted a fire on the side of Mount Ṭûr" (28:29). The journey of rapture was this one.

Mūsā came lost to himself, absorbed in his inmost secret. Love's wine, poured from the cup of holiness, had gone to his head. The pain of longing pressed on him, and the wave of "Show me" rose from the ocean of his passion. He had gone round the neighbourhoods of the children of Israel, gathering their messages and requests, so that he could lengthen his words when he reached the Presence. As the verse says, "I count it forbidden to talk with others, and whenever I talk with You, I draw out my words." When he reached the place of intimate prayer, he was drunk with the wine of longing and burnt by hearing the Real's speech. He forgot everything, and the plain truth of his state came out: "Show me, that I may gaze upon You!"

The angels cast stones of blame at his wish. Did he hope to see the Exalted Lord? What has dust to do with the Lord of lords? How can a being of dust and water speak to the Eternal? How can someone who once was not, and then came to be, seek union with the One who always was and always will be? In his rapture and selflessness, Mūsā answered in the language of solitude: "Accept my excuse, for I did not fall here of my own accord. He wanted me first, before I wanted Him. When I woke from sleep, I found the Friend at my pillow."

### In short

- Mūsā asked to see Allah, and Allah told him he could not see Him in this life, then showed him by disclosing Himself to the mountain, which crumbled to dust.
- "You will not see Me" does not deny that believers will see Allah in the Hereafter, as many hadiths affirm. It denies only that a person can bear it in this world.
- Only a fingertip's measure of Allah's light was disclosed, and Mūsā fainted, then glorified Allah and repented of his request.
- The Prophet ﷺ forbade preferring him over the prophets in a way that belittles them, and told of finding Mūsā at the Throne on the Day of Resurrection.

144.text:
After the vision was refused, Allah reminded Mūsā (Moses) of the honours he had been given: "Allah said, “O Moses! I have ˹already˺ elevated you above all others by My messages and speech. So hold firmly to what I have given you and be grateful.”" Allah was telling Mūsā that, through His message and His speaking to him, He had raised him above everyone else of his era.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah said, “O Moses! I have ˹already˺ elevated you above all others"**: I have chosen you and preferred you above other people, the people of your time, above the children of Israel.

**"by My messages and speech."** By the message I sent you with, and by My speaking to you directly. The word can be read in the plural, bi-risālātī, "by My messages", or the singular, bi-risālatī, "by My message".

**"So hold firmly to what I have given you"**: take what I have given you of My speech and My conversation with you, the great honour and bounty I have granted, and act on it.

**"and be grateful.”"** Be among those who thank Allah for My favours, and that I chose to speak to you out of all people. Thank Him for it, and stop asking for what you cannot bear.

### Where does Mūsā stand among the prophets?

Without doubt, the master of all Ādam's (Adam's) descendants, from the first to the last, is Muhammad ﷺ. That is why Allah chose him to be the Final Prophet and Messenger, whose law will remain dominant and in force until the Last Hour. His followers outnumber the followers of all the other prophets and messengers. After Muhammad ﷺ, the next in honour and virtue is Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and then Mūsā son of ʿImrān, who was spoken to directly by the Most Merciful.

A prophet is a human being like any other, not a supernatural creature. His one special quality is that he keeps his inborn abilities intact. So Allah chooses him to carry His message, and he can be trusted to represent Allah among the people. In that sense Mūsā was the best person of his community, so Allah chose him as His prophet and revealed His message to him.

### How did Allah speak to Mūsā?

The Qur'an confirms in clear terms that Allah spoke directly to Mūsā. The first time was when he was given prophethood. This was the second time, when he was given the Torah. The wording of this verse suggests that this later speech had features the first did not.

What the speech was like, and how it took place, no one can know but Allah. Reasoned suppositions about it may be allowed, so long as they go against no rule of the Sharīʿah. But none of them can be held as certain without sound proof. The best course is the one the Companions, their students and the elders after them followed. They left such matters to Allah and never tried to settle them by groundless guesswork.

### The inner reading: one thing withheld, much given

It is as if Allah said: "O Mūsā, I have held back one thing from you, the vision, but I have singled you out for many virtues. I have chosen you for messengership and honoured you with an exalted rank. Give thanks for all this and recognise these blessings. Be among the thankful, and do not put yourself in the place of complaint." A poet sang in this sense: "If they turn away, it was they who first came with tenderness. How faithful they have been, so bear with them when they keep their distance."

### In short

- Allah reminded Mūsā that His message and His direct speech had set him above everyone of his era.
- He told him to hold firmly to what he had been given, be grateful, and not ask for what he could not bear.
- After Muhammad ﷺ and Ibrāhīm, Mūsā is the next in honour, the prophet to whom the Most Merciful spoke.
- How Allah's speech took place is beyond human knowledge, and the early Muslims left it to Allah.

145.text:
Allah then gave Mūsā (Moses) the Tablets: "We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things." With them came a command and a promise: "˹We commanded,˺ “Hold to this firmly and ask your people to take the best of it. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious". The Torah was given to Mūsā inscribed on Tablets.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything"**: Allah wrote on the Tablets lessons and admonition about everything people need in their religion and their worldly affairs. According to one explanation, the Tablets were cut from the lote tree of Paradise, or else from chrysolite or emerald, and numbered either seven or ten. It is said the Tablets held advice and the detailed rules of what is lawful and forbidden. They contained the Torah, of which Allah says:

> "Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture—after destroying earlier nations—as an insight for the people, a guide, and mercy so perhaps they would be mindful" (28:43).

It is also said that Allah gave Mūsā the Tablets before the Torah, and that they were not part of it. Allah knows best.

**"commandments and explanations of all things."** Admonition for those who will take it, and a detailed explanation of the laws that needed explaining: the lawful and the unlawful, commands and prohibitions. One explanation reads "the lesson" as the prohibitions. In the Arabic, "of all things" (li-kulli shayʾin) restates the earlier "about all things".

**"˹We commanded,˺ “Hold to this firmly"**: before "hold to this" the words "We said" are understood. Take it with strength, seriously and diligently, and stand firm in obedience.

**"and ask your people to take the best of it."** Command your people to hold to its finest precepts. Act on what is clear in it, and believe in what is ambiguous. Hold to its most excellent instructions in the most complete way, with patience and forgiveness, for the greatest reward. Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah reported, through ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said Mūsā was commanded to hold himself to the hardest of what was laid on his people.

**"I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious"**: you will see the reward of those who defy My command and turn from obeying Me, and the destruction, ruin and utter loss they suffer. One explanation says it is the home of the transgressors, Hell. Others say it is Iraq, or Egypt, the home of Pharaoh and his followers, shown to them so that they might learn from it.

### Was "the home of the rebellious" Egypt or Syria?

This is a kind of promise from Allah that the Israelites would soon take over Egypt, or perhaps Syria. There are two views about which land is meant. The difference rests on whether the Israelites went back to Egypt after Pharaoh and his people were destroyed. If they did return and rule there, as the earlier verse about their inheriting the land suggests (7:137), then this verse must mean Syria. In that case they had taken Egypt before Allah's light was disclosed to the mountain. If they did not go back to Egypt after Pharaoh's destruction, the verse may mean both Egypt and Syria.

### How should Allah's words be read?

Allah's revelation gives the guidance a person needs for life. But divine messages come in the form of words, and in this world of testing it is always possible to twist those words to suit one's own desires. Someone who is serious and sincere about guidance, and fears Allah's punishment and displeasure, will draw from the words the meaning Allah intended. Only those who long for the true path receive inspiration from Allah's words.

"I will soon show you the home of the rebellious" means: on your journey you will pass the ruins of peoples who were destroyed. They had been given Allah's guidance but went astray. They could not stand firm in their faith, because they gave in to the pressure of circumstances and to their own desires and ambitions. So they earned Allah's displeasure and were destroyed. The children of Israel would meet the same fate if they disobeyed Allah. In the scales of divine justice Allah favours no community over another. In this world a person can interpret Allah's words by his own whims and even distort them. But that kind of insolence puts even those who claim to obey on Allah's list of the disobedient.

### The inner reading: the admonitions of the Tablets

The traditions say that among the admonitions Allah wrote on the Tablets for Mūsā was this: "O Mūsā, if you want to be honoured at the threshold of My majesty and singled out for My nearness, be good to orphans and do not humiliate the poor. O Mūsā, I am the One who is tender to orphans and wishes them well, the Loving One who is generous to the poor. Be tender to those I am tender to, and do not drive away those I call."

Al-Muṣṭafā said of the poor that those who stay patient will sit in Allah's company on the Day of Resurrection. Of orphans he said that the weeping of an orphan makes the All-Merciful's Throne shake, and Allah says that whoever makes him content, He will make content.

"O Mūsā, if you want Me to speak proudly of you among the angels, harm no one, and keep stones and thorns off the path of those who have submitted." Al-Muṣṭafā said that faith has seventy-odd branches, the highest being "There is no god but Allah" and the lowest the removal of harm from the road.

"O Mūsā, if you want Me to answer your supplications, deal well with people, learn knowledge and teach it to others, for I have honoured those who know by giving them knowledge. For them I make the dust sweet and light and widen their graves, and tomorrow I will gather them among the ranks of the prophets." Al-Muṣṭafā told of what Jibrīl (Gabriel) said to him: "O Muḥammad, do not look down on a servant to whom Allah has given knowledge, for Allah did not look down on him when He gave it to him." He added that Allah will gather the people of knowledge in one place and tell them that He placed His knowledge in them only because He wished them good, and that He forgives them what came from them.

### In short

- Allah gave Mūsā the Torah written on Tablets, holding admonition and detailed rulings for every need of faith and life.
- Mūsā was to hold it firmly and command his people to keep its finest teachings, holding himself to its hardest demands.
- "The home of the rebellious" promised them the lands of the destroyed, Egypt or Syria, as a lesson about the fate of the disobedient.
- Allah's words guide only those who read them sincerely. Twisting them to suit one's desires counts as disobedience.

146.text:
Allah describes what arrogance does to a person's understanding: "I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land. And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them." It also bends their choices: "If they see the Right Path, they will not take it. But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it. This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them". Those too proud to obey Allah, and arrogant toward people without any right, are kept from understanding the signs and proofs of His might, His law and His commands. Just as they were proud without cause, Allah has disgraced them with ignorance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will turn away from My signs"**: I will turn them from believing in My revelations and from reflecting on My signs, the proofs of My power in creation, on the horizons and within themselves. Other verses say the same: Allah turns hearts and eyes away from the truth because people refused it the first time (6:110). And: "So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5).

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah explained it as: I will take away from them the understanding of the Qur'an and turn them away from My signs. Ibn Jarīr took Sufyān's words to mean that this part of the verse is addressed to this Ummah. That is not necessarily so. Ibn ʿUyaynah meant that this happens in every Ummah, with no difference between one Ummah and another. Allah knows best.

**"those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land."** Those who are proud on earth without any right, proud toward Allah's servants and toward the truth. Allah humbles them, so that they cannot magnify themselves. One explanation says the arrogant meant here are Pharaoh and his people. Another says Abū Jahl and his people. The same explanation links the "home of the rebellious" promised just before to the site of Badr, or to Makkah.

**"And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them."** A similar verse says, "Indeed, those against whom Allah’s decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe— even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment" (10:96-97).

**"If they see the Right Path, they will not take it."** Even if the way of guidance and safety appears before them, the way of Islam and goodness that leads to Allah's pleasure, they will not take it or like it.

**"But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it."** If the road of error, disbelief and idolatry that leads to ruin and Allah's displeasure appears, they take it.

**"This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them"**: they rejected Allah's scripture and messengers in their hearts, opposed Allah and His Messenger, and paid the signs no attention, learning nothing from them. A similar statement came earlier in the surah.

### Is all pride condemned?

The words "unjustly", literally "without right", show that answering the arrogant with a show of pride is justified. It is pride in appearance only, not in reality. As a saying recorded in Masāʾil as-Sulūk puts it: showing pride to the proud is an act of humility.

### What does arrogance do to a person?

"I will turn away from My signs those who act with arrogance" means that people with an offensive sense of superiority are deprived of knowledge and understanding. They cannot benefit from Allah's signs. These signs may be the revealed verses of the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, and also the signs placed in everything in the heavens and the earth. A false sense of superiority is the worst of habits, because it keeps a person from reflecting on Allah's signs and coming to know the truth.

Rūḥ al-Bayān says that arrogance is so wicked a trait that it raises a wall between a person and knowledge from Allah. Divine knowledge comes only through Allah's mercy, and His mercy visits the humble. The spiritual guide Rūmī said: "Water flows down toward the slope, and the remedy goes where the hardship is."

There are two ways to live in this world. One is to keep one's eyes and ears open. Then a person sees things as they are, and when the truth appears he recognises it, for Allah's signs are everywhere in the universe and lessons are sure to be found in them. The other way is to live with a superiority complex. Such a person lives as if he owned the world. He cares for nothing but his own interests. He thinks every good thing he receives comes from his own ability and effort, so he gives no thought to others' needs. This attitude blocks him from recognising and accepting the truth.

The first kind of person is open to the world around him. With an open mind he grasps the meaning of Allah's signs and quickly shapes himself by them. The second, because of pride and self-righteousness, is closed. He meets the truth, thinks it unimportant and ignores it. Nature sings its melodies in a silent language, but he does not listen. Any truth that lies beyond his own beliefs holds no appeal for him. People of his kind have no place in the world to come. As he ignored Allah's message in this world of testing, so Allah will ignore him in the eternal world, while the first kind will be richly rewarded.

The path of error comes from following the desires of one's self. The path of guidance is reached by rising above the pull of the self and one's surroundings, and choosing it purely for Allah's sake. The self-centred person, who values nothing but his own desires, rushes headlong down the path of transgression. The right path seems odd and foreign to his temperament, so he does not follow it. Someone who feels superior readily accepts any idea that does not lessen his sense of superiority. Where he senses he will not be given due importance, he loses interest.

### The inner reading: two kinds of pride

Pride is of two kinds, one with the Real and one without the Real. The first kind, pride with the Real, is what the poor feel toward the rich. Their aims are lofty, and their hearts are made rich by the Real. Their aspiration has turned away from the Throne and all beneath it. They have cut their hearts off from creatures and occupied themselves with loving the Real. What they aspire to is greater than this world and better than the next, and they long for the vision of their Master. Wāsiṭī said that the pride which is with the Real is directed at the rich and the sinful, toward disbelievers and the people of innovation. The traditions say, "Meet the wicked with stern faces." Pride without the Real is the pride of the rich and the rulers of the world toward the poor, and that is what this verse means.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said of this verse: "I will hold back their hearts, their inmost selves and their spirits from roaming the realm of holiness." In other words: I will tie their hearts and inmost selves so they cannot travel. I will make their own being their veil and turn them from My road, so that their inmost selves cannot roam the world of holiness and the unseen kingdom. They will be kept from seeing its wonders and will grow familiar only with their own selves and with this world's creatures. They will never taste the joy of finding, and will know nothing of the gifts given to the chosen. They will never see a day of good fortune, and the rose of union will never bloom for them. Poor is the wretch who has never caught the scent of these words! How can he have any share of the ocean, when he has not even a stream?

### In short

- Allah turns the arrogant away from understanding His signs, so that they disbelieve whatever they see.
- They reject the path of guidance and choose the path of error, because they denied the signs and ignored them.
- Answering the proud with pride is humility in disguise, but unjust pride raises a wall between a person and knowledge from Allah.
- A closed, superior mind meets the truth and ignores it, and so is shut out of the Hereafter's reward.

147.text:
The verse states the end of those who deny: "The deeds of those who deny Our signs and the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter will be in vain. Will they be rewarded except for what they have done?”" Whoever lives this way and stays on that path until death will find all his deeds wasted.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The deeds of those who deny Our signs"**: those who reject Allah's scripture and His messengers, and the signs that prove the messengers true.

**"and the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter"**: who deny the resurrection after death and their meeting with Allah on the Day of Judgement.

**"will be in vain."** Their good deeds will fail and earn no reward.

**"Will they be rewarded except for what they have done?”"** The question means they will not. They are repaid only for what they did and said of evil in this world, their denial and their disobedience. Allah repays people according to their deeds, good for good and evil for evil. As you sow, so you reap.

### Why are their good deeds lost?

Even the good they did in this world, such as keeping family ties or giving voluntary charity, is void and will not be rewarded. Those deeds were not built on faith, and their idolatry cancelled them. The loss is complete for whoever keeps to this denial until death. What remains is the repayment for their disbelief and for joining partners with Allah, which is to live forever in the Fire.

### In short

- Those who deny Allah's signs and the meeting with Him will find even their good deeds void, since these were not built on faith.
- Allah repays each according to his deeds, and their denial earns them the Fire.

148.text:
While Mūsā (Moses) was away on the Mount, his people fell into the worship of a calf: "In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound." The verse rebukes their folly: "Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path? Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers". The calf was the work of as-Sāmirī, who shaped it from ornaments the people had borrowed from the Copts, and the verse describes how far astray its worshippers went.

### Phrase by phrase

**"In the absence of Moses"**: after Mūsā had left them for his retreat on the mountain, to speak with Allah. Allah told him what had happened while he was on Mount Ṭūr: "We have indeed tested your people in your absence, and the Sâmiri has led them astray" (20:85).

**"his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery"**: from their ornaments of gold, of a saffron colour, which they had borrowed from Pharaoh's people on the pretext of a wedding and still had with them.

**"an idol of a calf"**: literally "a calf, a body". The word "body" (jasadan) stands in for "calf" (ʿijlan), meaning a body of flesh and blood, or, by another view, a statue with no soul. In the Arabic, the second object of "they made", "as a god", is left unsaid.

**"that made a lowing sound."** It made audible sounds like a cow, a sound the Sāmirī produced for them.

**"Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path?"** Did Mūsā's people not know that the calf had no speech for them, and no guidance toward any good, worldly or spiritual, and could bring them no benefit or remove any harm? Another verse says, "Did they not see that it did not respond to them, nor could it protect or benefit them" (20:89). So how could it be taken as a god?

**"Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers"**: they worshipped the calf out of ignorance, and wronged and harmed themselves by doing so.

### How was the calf made?

When Mūsā did not come back from Mount Sinai after thirty days, because he was to spend ten more nights there, the hasty and impatient Israelites began to make a fuss. Among them was a man named Sāmirī, a prominent figure who also held superstitious beliefs. He told the people that the Egyptians' jewels and ornaments in their possession were unlawful for them. Spoils taken from a defeated enemy were also unlawful for the Israelites. They gathered all their jewels and handed them to him. He melted them down and cast a golden calf from them.

It is reported that he had once collected some dust from where the hooves of the horse of Jibrīl (Gabriel) had trodden. Allah had given this dust a kind of life-giving effect. As-Sāmirī mixed it into the molten metal, or threw a handful of it into the calf's mouth, and the calf began to low like a cow. The scholars of tafsīr hold two views here. One is that the calf actually came alive and lowed. The other is that it remained gold, and air passing through it made it seem to low. Allah knows best. Another account says the sculpting art of the ancient Egyptians was such that air passing through such a figure made a bellowing sound come from its mouth.

Having made this satanic invention, Sāmirī called the people to worship the calf, declaring it a god. Mūsā, he said, had gone off to the mountain to speak with his Lord, but their god had come to them here, in the shape of this calf. It is reported that when the statue lowed, they began dancing around it and fell into error through their love of it. "This is your god and the god of Mūsā," they said, "but Mūsā has forgotten it." Sāmirī already enjoyed respect among them, and this unusual display increased their trust in him, so they began to worship the calf and took it as their god.

Allah condemned them for this error, for worshipping a calf and ignoring the One who created the heavens and the earth, Lord and Sovereign over everything. They worshipped besides Him a statue shaped like a calf that seemed to low, yet it neither spoke to them nor did them any good. Their very reason was blinded by ignorance and error.

### Why did the people follow Sāmirī?

Sāmirī was a clever man. When Mūsā left for the mountain, leaving his people in Hārūn's (Aaron's) care, Sāmirī set about misleading them. People are generally awed by unusual things, so this "miracle" of the calf made them think there was something sacred about it, and they began to worship it. Sāmirī's persuasive speech drew people to him. His influence grew until he had a large following, with only Hārūn and a few companions holding out. No one dared protest openly. Against this mass following, even Hārūn's protests were not strong enough to sway the people, and no one else had the courage to speak.

This has always been the public's way, from ancient times to the present. A clever person can draw a huge crowd by sheer eloquence, even over a non-issue. People drawn to trivialities, unconnected to the facts, cannot think deeply enough to sort truth from falsehood. So they rally to such a person and add to his popularity and importance. Anyone who tries to reveal the truth is simply ignored, as Hārūn was.

### The inner reading: every person's calf

Sahl ibn ʿAbdallāh said, "Whatever in this world turns a servant away from the Real and keeps him from obeying Him is his calf, and he is its worshipper." The calf-worshippers among the children of Israel were saved when, by Allah's command, they put themselves to death: "turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves" (2:54).
