In the same way, a servant is saved on the road of the Ḥaqīqah when he is cleansed of his own shares and of secondary causes. Better still, when he renounces all that is not the Real. As someone said: "Disown everything in the realm of being, and be that Heart-taker's companion of the cave."

"Did they not see that it could neither speak to them" points to what is rightly due to the Real. He is a speaker who addresses His creatures and speaks to His servant. The kings of the earth, in their grandeur, disdain to speak to their servants with their own tongues. But the Real has His own custom with His faithful servants. To His enemies He says, "Be despised in there! Do not ˹ever˺ plead with Me ˹again˺" (23:108). Of the faithful the Prophet ﷺ said that every one of them will be spoken to by his Lord, with no interpreter between them. On this theme it has been sung: "His majesty does not keep them from ease when they speak to Us and We speak a little to them."

### In short

- In Mūsā's absence, as-Sāmirī cast a calf from the borrowed gold jewellery, and it gave out a lowing sound.
- Whether it truly came alive through Jibrīl's dust or merely made noise as air passed through it, it could neither speak nor guide nor help.
- The people, awed by a novelty and swayed by Sāmirī's eloquence, worshipped it, while Hārūn's warnings went unheeded.
- Whatever turns a servant from Allah is his calf, and a god who cannot speak to his worshippers is no god at all.

149.text:
When Mūsā (Moses) returned from the Mount, the calf-worshippers came to their senses: "Later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried, “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.”" They regretted what they had done, and did not know how to make up for their wrong.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Later, when they were filled with remorse"**: when they were at a loss, regretting that they had worshipped the calf and fearing its consequences. They felt sorrow for what they had done.

**"and realized they had gone astray"**: they saw, knew for certain, that they had strayed from the truth, from guidance and the straight path, by worshipping the calf besides Allah. This came after Mūsā's return from his meeting with his Lord.

**"they cried, “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us"**: the mercy they hoped for was help to carry out His commands, and the forgiveness was pardon for worshipping the calf instead of punishment. The two verbs can be read in the third person, "if our Lord does not have mercy", or in the second, "if You, our Lord, do not have mercy".

**"we will certainly be losers.”"** We will be among the lost and the destroyed, losers in this world and in the Hereafter, overtaken by the punishment.

### What made their words a turning point?

This verse records their remorse over that guilt, and their repentance. Their words admitted the sin and sought salvation from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Not knowing how to undo what they had done, they placed themselves at the mercy of their Lord, and saw that without His forgiveness they had lost everything.

### In short

- Once Mūsā returned, the calf-worshippers realised their error and were filled with remorse.
- They admitted that without Allah's mercy and forgiveness they would be lost in this world and the next.
- Their plea admitted the sin and asked Allah for salvation, the start of their repentance.

150.text:
Mūsā (Moses) came down from his meeting with Allah to find his people worshipping the calf: "Upon Moses’ return to his people, ˹totally˺ furious and sorrowful, he said, “What an evil thing you committed in my absence! Did you want to hasten your Lord’s torment?”" In his anger he set down the Tablets and seized his brother: "Then he threw down the Tablets and grabbed his brother by the hair, dragging him closer." Hārūn (Aaron) answered him, "O son of my mother! The people overpowered me and were about to kill me." He went on, "So do not ˹humiliate me and˺ make my enemies rejoice, nor count me among the wrongdoing people.”" Allah had already told Mūsā on Mount Sinai what his people had done. Seeing it with his own eyes filled him with indignation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Upon Moses’ return to his people, ˹totally˺ furious and sorrowful"**: when he came back after speaking with his Lord and heard the noise of their revolt. He was angry with them and bitterly grieved. Abū ad-Dardāʾ said that the word used here for sorrow, asif, means the most intense kind of anger.

**"he said, “What an evil thing you committed in my absence!"** Evil is what you did after I left you for the mountain, worshipping the calf. Literally: evil is the way you have taken my place after me. It is an evil state that leads only to ruin and misery.

**"Did you want to hasten your Lord’s torment?”"** Literally, "Did you hasten your Lord's matter?" Several meanings are given. Mūsā was saying: you wanted me to rush back to you, though my staying there was Allah's decision. Or: were you so tired of waiting out the forty nights your Lord had appointed for me that you turned to the calf? Or: did you act in haste against your Lord's command, when you should have waited for Allah's Book to reach you? Or: did you rush to bring on your Lord's promised judgement by worshipping the calf? Some say it means they hastily decided that Mūsā had died.

**"Then he threw down the Tablets"**: the Tablets of the Torah. He did this out of anger at his people, anger for the sake of his Lord, according to most scholars of earlier and later times. Some reports say the Tablets broke, two of them, or into pieces.

**"and grabbed his brother by the hair, dragging him closer."** He seized Hārūn by the hair of his head with his right hand and by the beard with his left, and pulled him close in anger. Hārūn had been with them and had not managed to stop them, and Mūsā feared he had not tried hard enough to forbid them. Another passage records the exchange: "O Aaron! What prevented you, when you saw them going astray from following after me? How could you disobey my orders?”" (20:92-93). Hārūn replied, "O son of my mother! Do not seize me by my beard or ˹the hair of˺ my head. I really feared that you would say, ‘You have caused division among the Children of Israel, and did not observe my word.’" (20:94).

**"Aaron pleaded, “O son of my mother!"** The two were full brothers, sons of the same father too. Hārūn spoke of their mother so that Mūsā would feel more tender and gentle toward him. Naming the mother is the more affectionate appeal to the heart. The words can be read ibna ummi or ibna umma, both meaning "son of my mother".

**"The people overpowered me and were about to kill me."** They judged me weak, humiliated me and showed me no respect. They nearly killed me because I opposed them.

**"So do not ˹humiliate me and˺ make my enemies rejoice"**: do not punish or humiliate me in a way that lets my enemies, the calf-worshippers, gloat over me and spite me.

**"nor count me among the wrongdoing people.”"** In your anger and your reproach of them, do not treat me as one of those who did wrong by worshipping something other than Allah. Do not put me on their level, as if I were one of them.

### Why did Mūsā react only on seeing it?

This verse shows the meaning of the hadith, "Hearing about something is not the same as seeing it." Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: may Allah have mercy on Mūsā. One who sees a thing is not like one who is only told of it. His Lord told him that his people had been tested after he left, and he did not throw down the Tablets. When he saw them with his own eyes, then he threw them down.

### Did Mūsā show disrespect to the Torah?

The Arabic word used here, ilqāʾ, means dropping or throwing. That raises a doubt: did Mūsā show disrespect to the Tablets of the Torah by throwing them down? Throwing down the Tablets would plainly be a grave sin. It is equally plain that all the prophets are innocent and free of sin. The meaning, therefore, is that Mūsā put the Tablets aside very quickly to free his hands so he could take hold of his brother, so quickly that it looked as if he had dropped them. The Qur'an uses this word as a sign of warning.

### Why did he blame Hārūn?

Mūsā had left Hārūn among the people as his deputy. When he saw the Israelites worshipping the golden calf, he held Hārūn responsible, thinking he had neglected his duty as a reformer. He turned to his people first, then to his brother, and took hold of him in anger. Hārūn then explained his position. He had tried everything he could to set them on the right path, but they would not listen.

### In short

- Mūsā returned furious and grieved, and rebuked his people for the evil they had done in his absence.
- Being told of the calf did not move him to throw the Tablets, but seeing it did, for hearing is not like seeing.
- He set the Tablets down so fast that it seemed he had thrown them, and seized Hārūn, fearing he had not done enough.
- Hārūn appealed to him as "son of my mother", explaining that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him.

151.text:
Once Mūsā (Moses) was satisfied that his brother was innocent, he turned to Allah in prayer: "Moses prayed, “My Lord! Forgive me and my brother! And admit us into Your mercy. You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”" Hārūn (Aaron) had given him the true account. It was not his fault. He had tried to stop the people from this wicked act, but they would not listen, and they were so stubborn they almost killed him. Hārūn asked Mūsā not to count him among the ignorant or let his enemies laugh at him, and Mūsā's anger cooled.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses prayed, “My Lord! Forgive me"**: forgive me for what I did to my brother.

**"and my brother!"** Forgive Hārūn any shortcoming in his duties, including that he did not fight them. Mūsā included him in the supplication to make peace with him and to deny the enemies any chance to gloat over his misfortune.

**"And admit us into Your mercy."** Enclose us in Your mercy and bring us into Your Garden.

**"You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”"** You show us more mercy than anyone who shows mercy.

### What showed Hārūn was innocent?

Hārūn had warned the people before Mūsā returned: "O my people! You are only being tested by this, for indeed your ˹one true˺ Lord is the Most Compassionate. So follow me and obey my orders." (20:90). When Mūsā saw that his brother had not failed in his duty, he checked himself and began praying for him.

Misunderstandings often arise between believers. Once things are made clear, they return to normal, as if no misunderstanding had ever happened.

### Why did Mūsā ask forgiveness for himself?

He had done nothing like what the people did, yet he named himself first. One reason may be the haste with which he set down the Tablets of the Torah, which the Qur'an called "throwing" as a sign of warning. Another may be to teach people that when they seek forgiveness for others, they should include themselves, so that they do not grow complacent.

### The inner reading: asking forgiveness for sins not committed

In this prayer lies the lesson that the servant must ask forgiveness in every state. It is Allah's right to punish even the innocent, since all creation belongs to Him and the Owner's decree runs through all He owns. The children of Israel sinned, yet Mūsā and his brother were the ones who apologised and asked forgiveness. This is the path of the chivalrous and the road of the Sufis. They take the sin upon themselves and apologise for sins they did not commit. As the verse goes: "When we are ill, we come to You and visit You. They sin, and we come to You and apologise."

### In short

- After Hārūn showed he had warned the people, Mūsā's anger cooled and he prayed for them both.
- He sought forgiveness for his own haste and for any shortcoming of his brother, and asked to be enclosed in Allah's mercy.
- Including oneself when asking forgiveness for others guards against complacency.
- The servant asks forgiveness in every state, even for sins committed by others.

152.text:
Allah warns the calf-worshippers who persisted in their worship of a grim end in the Hereafter and a disgraced life in this world: "Those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath as well as disgrace in the life of this world. This is how We reward those who invent falsehood". The verse covers them and whoever follows their example. They displeased their Lord and did not act on His command.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who worshipped the calf"**: those who took the calf as a god.

**"will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath"**: the wrath that struck the children of Israel for worshipping the calf. Allah did not accept their repentance until some of them, those who had not worshipped the calf, killed others who had. Sūrat al-Baqarah tells this story (2:54). Their punishment was the command to slay themselves.

**"as well as disgrace in the life of this world."** This is the disgrace and humiliation the Jews suffered in this world. One explanation names the poll tax imposed on them. Another says abasement was stamped on them until the Day of Resurrection.

**"This is how We reward those who invent falsehood"**: those who invent lies against Allah, through idolatry and in other ways. As Allah repaid them, so He repays every such inventor.

### Who are "those who invent falsehood"?

The phrase covers everyone who invents an innovation in religion. The disgrace of inventing an innovation and defying Allah's message settles in the heart and from there spreads to the shoulders. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that the disgrace of innovation weighs on their shoulders even as they gallop on their mules or trot on their workhorses.

Ayyūb as-Sakhtiyānī narrated that Abū Qilābah al-Jarmī said of this verse: "By Allah! It applies to everyone who invents a lie, until the Day of Resurrection." Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said that every inventor of an innovation in religion will taste disgrace. Those who bring new things into the Sharīʿah commit the sin of fabrication and deserve this punishment. Imām Mālik also concluded from this verse that such people deserve Allah's wrath in the Hereafter and disgrace in this life.

### Why is the calf called a falsehood?

The Israelites' deed is called iftirāʾ, a false attribution. They did this wrong in the name of the truth. Theirs was not a rejection of the truth but an exploitation of it for worldly gain, justified in religious terms. Like the idolaters, they claimed that Allah had taken bodily form in the idol they had made with their own hands, so worshipping it was as good as worshipping Him. Sāmirī also invented a dream. In it, he claimed, he had seen Gabriel and taken a handful of earth from his horse's footprint, which he put into the calf, making it give out a sound. Sāmirī and his companions made up falsehoods and attributed them to Allah. When the People of the Book commit such irreligious acts in the name of religion, they bring Allah's wrath upon themselves, and they are punished in this life as well as the Hereafter.

### Are sins punished in this world?

Part of the punishment for some sins comes in this life. That is what happened to Sāmirī. Mūsā (Moses) ordered him to live apart from the people, touching no one and touched by no one. For the rest of his life he lived in desolate seclusion, wandering among animals, and no human came near him. Al-Qurṭubī reports from Qatādah that his punishment from Allah was a fever that struck both him and anyone he touched or who touched him. The author of Rūḥ al-Bayān observed that his descendants still inherit signs of this illness.

### In short

- The calf-worshippers met Allah's wrath, the command to slay themselves, and lasting disgrace in this world.
- Inventing falsehood includes every innovation in religion, and its disgrace weighs on the innovator wherever he goes.
- The calf was a false attribution to Allah, a wrong done in the name of truth.
- Sāmirī's lonely life, untouched by anyone, shows that some sins are punished in this world.

153.text:
Allah opens the door of repentance even after the worst of sins: "But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers, your Lord will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful". Allah tells His servants that He accepts repentance for any sin, even shirk, kufr, hypocrisy and disobedience.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who commit evil"**: those who do wrong by joining partners with Allah and committing sins.

**"then repent"**: then turn back after their idolatry, or after their transgressions, and give them up.

**"and become ˹true˺ believers"**: and believe in Allah, affirming His Oneness. They repent from shirk to faith in Him alone and from disobedience to good deeds, leaving every kind of sin while seeking His forgiveness.

**"your Lord"**: addressed to Mūsā (Moses), or, by another view, to Muhammad ﷺ, the Messenger of Repentance and the Prophet of Mercy.

**"will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful"**: after they have repented and believed, after that evil deed, He overlooks and erases what they have done and shows them mercy. Sūrat al-Baqarah ends the story the same way: "That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" (2:54).

### How were the Israelites forgiven?

The verse speaks of those who repented after their prophet's warnings and met the hard condition set for their forgiveness, that they kill one another. They did so as Allah had commanded. Mūsā then called them and told them that Allah had accepted their repentance. Those killed were granted martyrdom, and those who survived were forgiven.

Another account says Mūsā told the leaders of each tribe to find those who had first started the wrongdoing. Once found, the guilty were executed by men of their own tribe. Only those who were deeply ashamed, admitted their guilt and sincerely repented were spared. The Israelites were punished by their own people. Such punishment is sometimes carried out by other peoples, especially when they can also inflict humiliation and disgrace.

### What is true repentance?

Whoever falls into sin and then repents and sets his belief right, Allah forgives in His mercy, however grave the deed. So it is wise to turn to Allah at once after every sin.

Real shame for a sin is the essence of tawbah, repentance. That deep shame guarantees that, in the depths of his heart, a person resolves never to do the deed again. When a sinner shows this shame and proves his resolve, it is as if he had embraced faith anew. After a time of backsliding, he comes back into the fold of Allah's religion.

### Ibn Masʿūd and the verse

Someone once asked ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd about a man who had committed fornication with a woman and afterwards married her, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported. Ibn Masʿūd recited this verse ten times, neither permitting nor forbidding it.

### In short

- Allah accepts repentance for any sin, even shirk and kufr, from those who turn back and truly believe.
- The Israelites' repentance was accepted after the hard command was carried out, and the slain were counted as martyrs.
- Sincere shame and a firm resolve never to return are the heart of repentance, and they restore a person to faith.

154.text:
Once Hārūn's (Aaron's) explanation had calmed him, Mūsā (Moses) returned to the Tablets: "When Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the Tablets whose text contained guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord". He had cast them down out of jealousy for Allah and anger for His sake, because his people had worshipped the calf. Now that his anger at his people had died down, he picked them up again.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When Moses’ anger subsided"**: when his anger with his people abated and he grew calm.

**"he took up the Tablets"**: the Tablets of the Torah that he had thrown down in anger.

**"whose text"**: literally "in their copy", meaning what was inscribed on them. The Arabic word nuskhah means a piece of writing copied from a book or from other writings. One explanation takes it as what remained on the Tablets. Another takes it as what was given back to him of the two Tablets.

**"contained guidance and mercy"**: guidance away from error and a clear explanation of the truth, and mercy that shields from punishment.

**"for those who stand in awe of their Lord"**: those who fear Him and keep in mind the outcome He will bring. In the Arabic, a small particle, lām, is placed before "their Lord", the object of awe, because that object comes ahead of its verb.

### What happened to the broken Tablets?

Several scholars of tafsīr said that when Mūsā threw the Tablets to the ground, they shattered, and he gathered up the pieces afterwards. He found guidance and mercy in what was inscribed on them, but the detailed rulings of the Law were lost, or so they said. They also claimed that the broken pieces were kept in the treasuries of certain Israelite kings until the rise of the Islamic state. Only Allah knows whether these reports are true.

Other reports say that the Tablets broke when Mūsā set them aside in haste, and that Allah then gave him the Torah written on some other material.

### Who benefits from Allah's Book?

Allah's Book is a book of guidance and grace. It is the best guide for a person in this world and a sure source of Allah's grace in the Hereafter. Yet it benefits only those who fear Allah and keep thinking about how He will decide their fate. These are the real seekers of truth. When the truth comes before them, they accept it, with no inner complexes holding them back.

For such people Allah becomes the centre of their hopes and fears, and their lives and wealth are devoted to Him. Their fear of Allah awakens their awareness and lifts every barrier from their eyes, so they do not miss His signs when these appear. In short, they live in fear of their Lord, not in contentment and complacency.

### In short

- When his anger calmed, Mūsā took up the Tablets he had cast down for Allah's sake.
- What was written on them held guidance from error and mercy from punishment.
- Some reports say the Tablets shattered and part of the Law was lost, but only Allah knows if this is true.
- Allah's Book benefits those who stand in awe of their Lord, for that fear opens their eyes to the truth.

155.text:
After the calf, Mūsā (Moses) took the best of his people to meet their Lord: "Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment" and, at the meeting, disaster struck: "and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried, “My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well." He went on pleading, "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? This is only a test from You—by which You allow whoever you will to stray and guide whoever You will." And he ended, "You are our Guardian. So forgive us and have mercy on us. You are the best forgiver".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses chose seventy men from among his people"**: seventy of the best men, chosen by Allah's command from those who had not worshipped the calf.

**"for Our appointment"**: for the time and place Allah had set, when they were to come and apologise for the calf-worship of the foolish among them.

**"and, when they were seized by an earthquake,"** A violent tremor seized them, struck them down and killed them.

**"he cried, “My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well."** Had You wished, You could have destroyed them before this day, before I set out with them, so that the children of Israel would have seen it and not accused me falsely. You could have destroyed me with them back when I killed the Copt. One reading of his words is: they were foolish, so will You now destroy every one of the children of Israel who comes after me?

**"Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?"** The question is a plea for compassion: do not punish us for the sins of others. Mūsā thought they had been destroyed because of the calf-worship.

**"This is only a test from You"**: the trial that the ignorant fell into, the worship of the calf, was only Your test and Your affliction upon us.

**"by which You allow whoever you will to stray and guide whoever You will."** You send astray whom You will, and You guide whom You will away from the turmoil.

**"You are our Guardian."** You are our Protector who looks after our affairs, and You have more right than anyone to show us mercy.

**"So forgive us and have mercy on us."** Forgiveness here means covering the mistake and not punishing the sin. Whenever mercy is asked alongside forgiveness, it includes the hope that Allah will keep one from falling into the same act again.

**"You are the best forgiver"**: the best of those who forgive and overlook, for no one but You can forgive sins.

### What brought the seventy to the mountain?

One account says that when Mūsā brought the Torah and told his people to follow it, they, being crooked and contrary, said they were not sure it was Allah's word. Mūsā might have written it himself. Mūsā prayed for them to be made certain. Allah told him to choose seventy men and bring them to Mount Sinai, where He would let them hear His speech. As-Suddī said that Allah told Mūsā to bring thirty men of the children of Israel to apologise for the calf-worship, and set them a time and place. Mūsā then chose seventy and went with them so they could apologise.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related that Mūsā told the seventy to go to the meeting with Allah and repent of what they had done, and to ask forgiveness for those they had left behind. They were to fast, purify themselves and wash their clothes. He took them to Mount Ṭūr in Sinai, at the time and place his Lord had set, and only with Allah's leave and knowledge. On the way they asked to hear their Lord's words too, and he agreed.

As Mūsā drew near, the mountain was wrapped in columns of cloud, and he went into it, telling the people to come close. When Allah spoke to Mūsā, a dazzling light surrounded his cloak that no human could bear to look at, so a screen was placed below him. The people came near, entered the cloud and fell down in prostration. They heard Allah speaking to Mūsā, giving him commands and prohibitions. When the cloud lifted, they faced Mūsā and said they would not believe him until they saw Allah directly. The thunder shook them, their souls were taken, and every one of them died.

### Why were they seized?

There are several accounts. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the seventy went with Mūsā to pray to their Lord. In their supplication they asked Allah to give them what He had never given anyone before them and would never give anyone after them. Allah disliked this request, and the earthquake seized them.

In as-Suddī's account they demanded to see Allah. They told Mūsā they would never believe him until they saw Allah plainly, since he had spoken to Him, so he should show Him to them. As two other verses put it: "We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes" (2:55), and "Make Allah visible to us!” So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing" (4:153). They died, and Mūsā stood weeping and calling on Allah. What would he tell the children of Israel when he returned to them, now that Allah had destroyed their best men?

Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Mujāhid and Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī said that the tremor or the lightning seized them because they neither kept away from the calf-worshippers among their people nor forbade them. Mūsā's words, "for what the foolish among us have done", support this. Ibn ʿAbbās added that these were not the same people who asked to see Allah and were struck by the thunderbolt (2:55).

### Earthquake or thunderbolt?

In Sūrat al-Baqarah the punishment is called a thunderbolt, while here it is an earthquake. The two can be reconciled: they were struck by an earthquake from beneath and a thunderclap from above. Their demand came from ignorance and stubbornness, so it drew Allah's wrath. They fell to the ground lifeless. They either looked dead or were truly dead.

Mūsā was deeply grieved. They were the leading men of the Israelites, and he did not know how he would face his people. They would accuse him of killing these men, and might even kill him. So he pleaded: My Lord, I know it is not Your will to kill them. There were earlier occasions better suited to it. They could have drowned with Pharaoh, or died when they worshipped the calf, yet You spared them. You mean only to warn them. Nor would You destroy all of us for what a few fools did. I know this is only a trial from You. Through it some go astray, while those who see the wisdom and lesson in it are guided. You are the Wise, the All-Knowing, the Most Merciful and Most Forgiving, so forgive the insolence of these people. Through his prayer, all seventy were brought back to life.

### What does "test" mean here?

The word is fitnah. Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and many of the Salaf and later scholars said it means affliction, test and trial. This is the only plausible meaning. Mūsā was saying: the decision and the judgement are Yours, and whatever You will comes to pass. No one can guide those You leave astray, or lead astray those You guide. No one can give what You withhold or hold back what You give. Sovereignty, judgement, creation and command all belong to You.

### The inner reading: chosen by Mūsā, chosen by Allah

The community of Mūsā differs from the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Mūsā's community was chosen by Mūsā, as the verse says, "Moses chose seventy men". Muhammad's community was chosen by Allah. Those Mūsā chose demanded to see Allah openly, and here the earthquake took them. Of those Allah Himself chose, He said that their faces will be bright on that Day, looking at their Lord (75:22-23). The wanting is the Real's wanting and the choosing is His choosing: "Your Lord creates and chooses whatever He wills—the choice is not theirs" (28:68).

Mūsā was bold on the carpet of nearness, in the station of intimate prayer. Anguish and bewilderment had left him broken and poor, and from that state of realisation he voiced his remorse: "This is only a test from You." Then he became aware of himself and returned to helplessness, entering by the door of awe and reverence. He handed the decree back to the Real entirely: You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. Not content with that, he let loose his tongue in praise joined to pleading and weeping: "You are our Guardian. So forgive us and have mercy on us." He laid his need and lowliness before Allah and begged for mercy and forgiveness.

The traditions say that on the day of the intimate prayer, Mūsā reached the edge of Mount Sinai praising Allah, calling on Him and showing his need with every step. The Pir of the Ṭarīqah said, "The needy are never turned away. There is no deceit behind the door of need. And there is no way of approach to the Friend like need."

### In short

- Mūsā took seventy of the best men to seek forgiveness for the calf, and an earthquake seized them at the meeting.
- They were seized for asking to see Allah, for asking an unprecedented gift, or for not shunning the calf-worshippers, depending on the account.
- Mūsā pleaded that Allah would not destroy them for the deeds of fools, and through his prayer they were brought back to life.
- The calf-worship was a test by which Allah guides and leaves astray whom He wills, and Mūsā submitted the decree wholly to Him.

156.text:
Mūsā (Moses) ended his prayer with a request for good in both worlds: "Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next. Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺.”" Allah answered with a statement about His punishment and His mercy: "Allah replied, “I will inflict My torment on whoever I will. But My mercy encompasses everything." He then said for whom that mercy would be written: "I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations". The first part of Mūsā's prayer asked Allah to ward off what should be avoided. This part asks for what is sought.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next."** Write down every good thing for us, in both lives, and give it to us. Good in this world means knowledge, worship and protection from sin. It also means being among those blessed with favour and well-being, and enabled to do good works. Good in the next world is Paradise and its bliss, among the righteous servants for whom it has been prepared. The meaning of "good" was explained earlier, in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

**"Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺.”"** The word is hudnā. Qatādah, as-Suddī, Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Ibrāhīm at-Taymī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others said it means: we repent and come back to You. It can also mean: we are betaking ourselves to You, admitting our faults.

**"Allah replied, “I will inflict My torment on whoever I will."** This answers Mūsā's words, "This is only a test from You." I single out for My punishment whom I will, those who do the deeds that lead to misery. I do what I will and decide as I will, and there is wisdom and justice in all I do. All the disobedient deserve punishment. Yet out of His mercy, which reaches everything, even His wrath, He strikes only a few whom He wills.

**"But My mercy encompasses everything."** His mercy covers every created thing, righteous or sinful. Nothing has been left out of it, and all is immersed in His grace and kindness in this world. Even those who rebel against Allah and deny Him are shown some of His mercy, though only in this world. The angels who carry the Throne and those around it pray, "Our Lord! You encompass everything in ˹Your˺ mercy and knowledge." (40:7).

**"I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil"**: I will write My mercy for them as a favour and a kindness from Me. Another verse says, "Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful." (6:54). Those who shun evil are those who keep away from shirk, disbelief, indecency and the major sins, doing what Allah commands and avoiding what He forbids. They are the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ.

**"pay alms-tax,"** The zakah here may mean purifying oneself, or the zakah paid on wealth, giving the poor their due. Both meanings may be meant, since this verse was revealed in Makkah, before zakah was fixed in set shares.

**"and believe in Our revelations"**: who believe in Allah's scripture and His Messenger, and hold firmly to His verses without excuses or false interpretations.

### The hundred mercies

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Jundub ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī that a bedouin came, made his camel kneel and tied it, then prayed behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the prayer ended, the man untied his camel, mounted it and called out, "O Allah, have mercy on me and on Muhammad, and give no one else a share in it." The Messenger ﷺ asked his Companions whether this man was more misguided or his camel, and whether they had heard what he said. They said they had. He told the man that he had narrowed a vast mercy. Allah created a hundred mercies and sent down one of them, through which all creation, people, jinn and animals, show mercy to one another. The other ninety-nine He kept with Himself. Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd collected this hadith.

Imām Aḥmad also recorded from Salmān that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has a hundred mercies. Through one of them His creatures show mercy to each other, and even wild animals are gentle with their young. Ninety-nine He has kept for the Day of Resurrection. Muslim recorded it.

### Was Mūsā's prayer answered?

Opinions differ on how to read this exchange. Here, unlike elsewhere, the verse gives no plain words of acceptance. On another occasion Allah said, "All that you requested has been granted, O Moses" (20:36). Of the prayer of Mūsā and Hārūn (Aaron) He said, "Your prayer is answered!" (10:89). No such words appear here. So some suggested that this prayer was answered not for the Israelites but for the Muslim Ummah. The author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī called that a remote possibility.

The correct reading is that the prayer held two requests. The first was mercy and forgiveness for those who had been punished. The second was that good be written for Mūsā and his people in this world and the next. The first is granted in this verse, and the next verse answers the second. To the first request Allah replied that He does not punish everyone who sins, only a few whom He wills for their transgression, so these people would not be punished either. His mercy is so great that it covers all He has created. Even those who are punished are not wholly cut off from it, since they could have received something harsher.

The second request was made conditional. In this world Allah may extend His mercy to all, believers and disbelievers alike. The Hereafter is a separate world, where His mercy is kept for those who meet certain conditions. They fear Allah and live piously, carrying out every religious duty and avoiding what He forbids. They pay zakah regularly from their earnings. And they believe firmly in His verses without pretexts or false interpretations. If Mūsā's people met these conditions, the full favour would be written for them in both worlds. The next verse shows that those who would fit this description perfectly are people to come in the last age, following the last Prophet ﷺ.

Mūsā prayed for his whole community, but Allah's reply made clear that salvation and success do not depend on belonging to a particular community. They are decided for each individual according to his deeds. Allah is the Most Merciful, yet someone who does not do righteous deeds cannot escape His punishment, whatever group he belongs to.

### Does a mercy that encompasses everything include Iblīs?

Hearing this, Iblīs seized his chance and said, "I am one of the things." In Qatādah's report too, Satan claimed a share in the mercy, since it reaches everything and he is one of those things. But the conditions that follow, beginning with those who shun evil, and above all the condition of īmān (faith), excluded him. Then the People of the Book seized their chance. They said they were the people of fear of Allah and of scripture, who believed in Allah and paid zakah, and so the full mercy would be theirs in both worlds. The next verse excluded them by making faith in the final Prophet ﷺ and in the Qur'an's verses a condition, which the Jews and Christians who rejected him did not have.

Shaykh Anwar Kashmīrī said that the verse shows that Allah's mercy can embrace everything. It does not say that it will embrace everything. Another verse says it more plainly: "Your Lord is infinite in mercy, yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people." (6:147). The vastness of His mercy does not stop sinners from being punished.

### The inner reading: coming back to Allah entirely

"We have turned to You" means: we have turned toward Your religion and come home to You entirely, keeping nothing back for ourselves. O Lord, we have come back to You wholly. We have given up our own power and strength and are content with whatever You decree. Do not leave us to ourselves, and lift our self-regard out of our way. This is what al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ asked: "Do not leave me to myself for the blink of an eye, or less." He also asked to be shielded as a son is shielded.

Revelation came to Dāwūd (David): O Dāwūd, what have My friends to do with the sorrows of this world? Worldly sorrow takes the sweetness of intimate prayer from their hearts. I love My friends to be spiritual, to grieve over nothing, to cut their hearts off from this world, to leave all their affairs to Me and to be pleased with My decree. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that being pleased with the decree is Allah's greatest gate.

Among the children of Israel was a worshipper who had spent long days in devotion. In a dream he was shown that his close companion in Paradise would be a certain man. He went looking for him to see what his worship was. He found that the man neither prayed at night nor fasted by day, doing only what was obligatory. He asked what he did. The man said he did little worship beyond what had been seen. But he had one trait. In trial or illness he did not wish to be well, and in the sun he did not wish for shade. He was pleased with whatever Allah decreed and did not add his own wish to Allah's will. The worshipper said, "That is what brought you to this station."

### In short

- Mūsā asked for good in this world and the next, and declared that his people had turned back to Allah in repentance.
- Allah punishes whom He wills, but His mercy reaches everything, one part of it shared among all creatures and ninety-nine kept for the Day of Resurrection.
- Mercy in the Hereafter is written only for those who shun evil, pay zakah and believe in Allah's revelations, which shuts out Iblīs and those who reject the last Prophet ﷺ.
- Salvation depends on each person's faith and deeds, not on belonging to a favoured group.

157.text:
Allah now names the people who will receive the mercy promised in the previous verse: "“˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel." The verse then lists what this Messenger does: "He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil, permits for them what is lawful and forbids to them what is impure," and he "relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them." It ends with the condition for success: "˹Only˺ those who believe in him, honour and support him, and follow the light sent down to him will be successful.”"

The people who truly deserve the full mercy and favour that Mūsā (Moses) asked for his people, and who truly meet the conditions of the previous verse, are those who follow the unlettered Messenger of Allah ﷺ. While describing them, the verse names some distinctive qualities of the Prophet ﷺ. It then requires not only belief in him but also following his commands and his practice. So, together with belief in Allah, following the Sunnah and the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ is necessary for lasting success in the Hereafter. This is how Muhammad ﷺ was described in the books of the earlier prophets. They gave their nations the good news of his coming and commanded them to follow him. His description was still plain in their books, as their rabbis and priests well knew.

### Phrase by phrase

**"“˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger,"** They are the ones just described, who follow the religion of the Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ.

**"the unlettered Prophet,"** The Prophet who could neither read nor write, and who was taught only by revelation from his Lord.

**"whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel."** They find him there by name and by description, with his traits, in the Torah revealed to Mūsā and the Gospel revealed to ʿĪsā (Jesus).

**"He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil,"** He commands decency, belief in Allah's Oneness and fine character. He forbids disbelief, harming others, and whatever sound minds and sound natures know to be bad.

**"permits for them what is lawful"**: literally "the good things". He makes clear to them that things in their scripture are lawful, such as the meat and milk of camels, sheep and other animals. He permits good things that had been forbidden to them under their law. He also makes lawful the baḥīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah and ḥām, animals the idolaters had banned by their own invention, prohibitions that only made life hard for themselves. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported this from Ibn ʿAbbās. In all, he allows good food, drink and relationships that do no harm.

**"and forbids to them what is impure,"** He forbids foul things such as carrion, the flesh of the pig, blood, liquor and all the prohibited animals. He forbids riba, and foods they treated as lawful though Allah had forbidden them. Impure earnings are included too, such as gambling, interest and bribes. Some scholars count immorality and bad manners among impure things as well.

**"and relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them."** He came with gentleness and an easy religion, lifting the hard rules laid on earlier peoples. The details follow below.

**"˹Only˺ those who believe in him,"** Those who believe in Muhammad ﷺ, from among the Israelites and others, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his followers.

**"honour and support him,"** They respect and revere him, and help him against the disbelievers who were his enemies, even with the sword.

**"and follow the light sent down to him"**: the Qur'an, sent down with Jibrīl (Gabriel), along with the revelation the Prophet ﷺ delivered to people, his Sunnah. They hold lawful what it makes lawful and unlawful what it forbids.

**"will be successful.”"** They will succeed in this life and the Hereafter. They will be saved from Allah's wrath and punishment, gain what they hope for and be safe from what they fear.

### Why is the Prophet ﷺ called "unlettered"?

The phrase "the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet" names three qualities of the Prophet ﷺ. The Arabic word ummī means someone who has not learned to read and write. The Qur'an calls the Arabs ummiyyīn because, in general, they had little to do with reading and writing. Not being able to read and write is plainly not a merit in itself. It is a sign of a lack. Yet, unusual as it may seem, this very lack became a sign of the Prophet's perfection of the highest degree, given the matchless knowledge, wisdom and learning he taught and showed.

When an educated person shows perfect wisdom and wise conduct, it is seen as the fruit of his education. When such perfections, of the highest degree a human can imagine, come from someone who could not even read and write, it is a miracle as clear as daylight. It is all the more remarkable that he lived forty years in Makkah al-Mukarramah with no chance to learn. Then, at exactly forty, he suddenly began to speak words of such wisdom, in such language and style, that no one in the world could match even the smallest part of them. That speech is the Qur'an. Its challenge stands: "And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true" (2:23).

The Arabs were so proud of their eloquence that they called all other peoples ʿajam, "the mute", yet they could not meet this challenge. That is clear proof of the Qur'an's miraculous nature. It plainly testifies that the Prophet ﷺ was Allah's true Messenger and the Qur'an is Allah's true word. Being unlettered may be a defect in others, but in him it is praiseworthy. The verse lists it alongside his being Messenger and Prophet, which shows it too was a great quality of his.

He was unlettered so that no one could doubt his honesty. Had he been educated, people would have suspected that he composed everything himself and attributed it to Allah. According to Jewish tradition, the scriptures had also predicted an unlettered Final Prophet, which would make it easy for people to recognise him as sent by Allah.

### What does it mean to "find him" in the Torah and the Gospel?

This is the fourth quality the verse mentions. The verse does not say they will find his qualities or signs written in their books. It says, literally, that they will find him written there. This hints that his qualities would be described in the Torah and the Gospel so vividly and in such detail that reading them would be like seeing the Prophet ﷺ himself. The Torah and the Gospel are named, and not the Zabūr, the book revealed to Dāwūd (David), because these were the books the Jews and the Christians believed in. The Zabūr also contained his description.

As far as the Israelites knew, every prophet who had come had been from their own people, without exception. But according to Allah's plan, the last prophet was to come from the children of Ismāʿīl, and Allah had already told the Israelites so through their prophets. They were given this news so that when the last prophet appeared, they would not face a great trial. They could recognise him at once and rally to his cause. Many such prophecies still survive in their books.

The present versions of the Torah and the Gospel have been greatly changed and distorted, and have lost their originality and reliability. Even so, they still contain passages that point to the Prophet ﷺ. Moreover, the Qur'an declared in clear terms that the Torah and the Gospel described him. Had this claim been false, the Jews and Christians of his time would have used it against the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. Yet neither group ever tried to refute it. That itself shows that the Torah and the Gospel of that time contained clear references to him.

Some of the qualities described in those books are reported in the Qur'an itself, with reference to the Torah and the Gospel. Others are reported in the hadith, by people who read them in those books and later accepted Islam because of those descriptions.

### The dying boy who recognised him

Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Ṣakhr al-ʿUqaylī heard from a bedouin who had brought a milk camel to sell in Madinah in the Prophet's lifetime. Having sold it, the bedouin decided to go and meet this man and hear from him. He found the Prophet ﷺ walking between Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and followed them. They came to a Jewish man reading from an open Torah. He was grieving over his son, a very handsome boy, who lay dying.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked the father, by the One who sent down the Torah, whether he did not find his description and his coming in his book. The father shook his head. His son said, "Yes indeed, by the One who sent down the Torah! We find your description and your coming in our book." The boy then bore witness that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that he was Allah's Messenger. The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to take charge of their brother and keep the Jew away from him. He himself saw to the boy's funeral and led the funeral prayer. This hadith is sound, and a similar hadith from Anas in the Ṣaḥīḥ supports it.

Al-Baihaqī gives a version from Anas in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah. In it, the Jewish boy used to serve the Prophet ﷺ. When the boy fell ill, the Prophet ﷺ visited him and found his father reciting the Torah beside his bed. The father denied the description, the boy affirmed it and declared his faith, and the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to give him an Islamic funeral, since he had died a Muslim.

### The creditor who tested him

ʿAlī reported that the Prophet ﷺ owed some money to a Jewish man. The man came demanding it back, speaking harshly, and said he would not let the Prophet go until he was paid. The Prophet ﷺ said the man had a right over him, and sat down beside him, saying he would not leave until the man willingly let him go. He stayed there a whole day and night, praying Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ and the next morning's Fajr in that place. The Companions were deeply upset and quietly rebuked the Jew to make him release the Prophet ﷺ. Sensing this, the Prophet ﷺ asked what they were doing. They said they could not bear to see him held by a Jew. He replied that his Lord had forbidden him to wrong anyone under a covenant.

The next morning the Jew, deeply moved, came and declared his faith in Allah and His Messenger. He explained that he had held the Prophet ﷺ only to test the qualities the Torah gave him, and he pledged half his wealth in Allah's cause. He was a wealthy man, so this was a large sum for the Muslims. The description he had read was this. Muhammad, son of ʿAbdullāh, would be born in Makkah, his place of migration would be Madinah and his realm Syria. He would not be harsh by temper or rough in speech. He would not raise his voice in the markets, and he would keep far from indecency. The man said he had found all of this true of him. Al-Baihaqī reported the incident in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah.

### How did the earlier books describe him?

Ibn Jarīr recorded that ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār met ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr and asked him about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Torah. He said, "Yes, by Allah! He is described in the Torah just as he is described in the Qur'an." The Torah, he said, contains the words "O Prophet! We have sent you as a witness, and a deliverer of good news, and a warner" (33:45), and calls him a refuge for the unlettered. It says: You are My servant and Messenger. I have named you al-Mutawakkil, the one who trusts in Allah. He is not harsh or coarse. He does not use foul language in the markets, and does not repay evil with evil, but forgives and pardons. Allah will not take his soul until He has straightened the crooked religion through him, so that people declare that none is worthy of worship but Allah. Through him He will open sealed hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes.

When ʿAṭāʾ later put the same question to Kaʿb, the reply matched ʿAbdullāh's to the letter. Al-Bukhārī recorded this from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, in one version as far as "forgives and pardons". It was common in the speech of the Salaf to call the books of the People of the two Scriptures "the Torah", as some hadiths also show. Allah knows best.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, a great scholar of the Jews, reported almost the same words from the Torah, as Ibn Saʿd recorded in his Ṭabaqāt, ad-Dārimī in his Musnad and al-Baihaqī in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah. In his version the Prophet ﷺ is sent as a witness over all the nations, a bearer of good news to the righteous, a warner to wrongdoers and a protector of the unlettered Arabs. He neither quarrels nor shouts in the markets, and Allah will not let him die until he has set the crooked straight and brought people to believe in Allah alone.

Imām al-Baghawī reported from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār that the Torah described the Prophet ﷺ as Allah's Messenger and chosen servant. He is neither harsh in temper nor unpleasant in speech. He does not shout in the markets, and he does not repay a wrong with a wrong, but forgives or overlooks. He is born in Makkah and migrates to Ṭaybah, which is Madinah, and his realm is Syria. His people are ḥammādūn, "constant praisers", who praise Allah in ease and in hardship. They say the takbīr as they climb on their journeys, and watch the shadows to know the times of prayer. He wears a cloth around his waist and keeps his hands and feet clean with wuḍūʾ. His caller to prayer raises his voice high in the air. In battle his people stand in rows as close as their rows in prayer. At night their recitation is heard like the humming of bees.

Ibn ʿAsākir and Ibn Saʿd recorded, with a full chain of narrators, that Sahl, the freed slave of Khuthaimah, said he had read this description in the Gospel (Injīl). He would be neither short nor tall, fair in colour, with his hair in two locks. Between his shoulders would be the seal of prophethood. He would not accept charity, would ride a camel, milk his own goat and wear patched clothes. He would be of the line of Ismāʿīl, and his name would be Aḥmad.

Al-Baihaqī reported in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah from Wahb ibn Munabbih, a great expert in the earlier scriptures, that Allah revealed to Dāwūd in the Zabūr: A prophet named Aḥmad will come after you. I will never be displeased with him, and he will never disobey Me. I have forgiven him all his slips and omissions. I have enjoined on his people the voluntary and obligatory prayers I enjoined on the earlier prophets. On the Day of Judgement they will come before Me with a light like the light of the prophets.

The revelation went on: O Dāwūd, I have favoured Muhammad and his people above the followers of other prophets, with six concessions I gave to no one before. They will not be punished for slips made in error. I will forgive their unintended sins when they ask My forgiveness. What they spend willingly in My way, I will repay many times over, even in this world. Whoever says "We belong to Allah and to Him we return" when distress strikes, I will turn that distress into blessing and mercy and a guide to Paradise. And I will answer their prayers, sometimes by giving what they ask, and sometimes by storing it up for them for the Day of Judgement.

These are only a few of hundreds of such reports, which scholars have gathered in separate volumes. Among them is Shaykh Raḥmatullāh Kairānwī of India, who treated the subject thoroughly in his book Iẓhār al-Ḥaqq. He gave specific examples of such descriptions in the current versions of the Bible, even though these have lost their originality through countless changes and distortions.

### What do "good" and "evil" mean here?

The Arabic word for good, maʿrūf, literally means something recognised, acknowledged or known. The word for evil, munkar, means unfamiliar or unrecognised. So maʿrūf refers to acts known and recognised in Islam, and munkar to acts not recognised in it. This shows that only what the people of the first century of Islam recognised counts as a good deed. Anything else is munkar, rejected. Any act not approved by the Companions and their followers cannot be considered a good deed, however positive or appealing it looks. That is why the authentic traditions call such acts bidʿah, innovation.

Commanding good and forbidding evil was a quality of all the prophets, as it had to be, since that is the very purpose of their being sent. So there must be a reason it is named here as a special mark of the Prophet ﷺ. A little reflection on his way of preaching, speaking to each person according to his state of mind, shows the difference. Bedouins who knew nothing but herding camels and goats were addressed so simply and plainly that they grasped even complex and abstract ideas without effort. He received delegations from the great powers of the day, Rome and Persia, and from other tribes, and they were struck by how easily he made his point clear. The gift Allah gave him of moving people by his words was miraculous, and even his enemies admitted it. The Torah's words about opening blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts through him may also refer to this effective way of teaching.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said that whenever you hear Allah say "O you who believe!", give it your full attention, for it is either a good you are being commanded or an evil you are being forbidden. The greatest of these commands and prohibitions is that Allah sent the Messenger ﷺ to call people to worship Him alone, without partners, and to forbid the worship of anything besides Him. This is the message Allah sent with every messenger before Muhammad ﷺ, calling every community to worship Allah and shun false gods (16:36).

### What are the burdens and shackles?

The Arabic word iṣr means a burden so heavy that it stops a person from moving. Aghlāl is the plural of ghull, a shackle that binds a criminal's hands to his neck. Both refer to punishments. They were not religious requirements in themselves. These hard rules included the following:

- Cloth stained with impurity had to be cut away, not simply washed.
- Spoils taken in jihad against disbelievers were not lawful for them. It is reported that fire came down from heaven and burned them up.
- Hunting on the Sabbath, Saturday, was forbidden.
- The limbs used in committing a sin had to be cut off.
- A killer had to be put to death in return, whether the killing was deliberate or accidental, with no option of paying compensation.
- Repentance required killing oneself.
- Breaking their pledges made good things unlawful for them, and other hardships included tearing their clothes.

These heavy commands are what the verse calls burdens and shackles. The Prophet ﷺ would cancel them and replace them with commands that are easy to carry out. He described this side of the Sharīʿah when he said that he was leaving them an easy, practical law, neither burdensome nor open to going astray. In another tradition he said that Islam is easy. A hadith reported through many routes has him say that he was sent with the easy way of pure monotheism, the ḥanīfiyyah.

When he sent Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī as governors to Yemen, he told them to bring good news and not drive people away, to make things easy and not hard, and to cooperate and not quarrel. Abū Barzah al-Aslamī, his Companion, said that he had accompanied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and seen how easygoing he was. The nations before had been given hard laws, while Allah made the law broad and easy for this Ummah. So the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has forgiven his Ummah the thoughts that pass through their minds, as long as they do not speak of them or act on them. He also said that his Ummah has been forgiven unintentional mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are forced to do.

That is why Allah guided this Ummah to pray: "“Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us." (2:286). Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records that after each supplication in this prayer, Allah the Exalted answered that He would accept it.

### Why does the verse require honour along with obedience?

The verse ties success to four conditions: believing in the Prophet ﷺ, revering him, readily helping him, and following the commands of the Qur'an.

The word for honour here, ʿazzarūhu, comes from taʿzīr. Lexically it means to hold someone back from something out of love and affection, and to protect him. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās explained it as reverence. Al-Mubarrad said it means the highest degree of reverence. So lasting success belongs to those who not only love and respect him but are always ready to help him against his enemies. In his lifetime, helping him meant helping him in person. After his passing, helping his message and supporting the Sharīʿah takes the place of helping him.

The words "honour and support him" come between "those who believe in him" and "follow the light". This placement shows that the obedience owed to the Prophet ﷺ is not like obedience to a high official, given out of necessity. It is obedience in the true sense, born of love and respect, so that a person loves and reveres him enough to make obeying him the dearest thing to him. The Prophet ﷺ stands in many relations to his people. He is their prophet, their master, their commander and the object of their deep love, all at once. Being above all of them in knowledge, wisdom and social and moral conduct, he also calls for deep respect.

The Prophet ﷺ is perfect in every one of these respects, so Muslims must honour all of them. He is to be believed as a prophet, obeyed as a commander, revered as a man of great knowledge and wisdom, and loved and cherished for his great kindness to them. Obeying him is a religious duty for Muslims, because the purpose of his being sent is left unfulfilled without it.

In his case Allah added further duties. Believers are to "support and honour him" (48:9). They are told: "O believers! Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you do to one another, or your deeds will become void while you are unaware" (49:2). And: "O believers! Do not proceed ˹in any matter˺ before ˹a decree from˺ Allah and His Messenger." (49:1). This warns Muslims not to speak ahead of the Prophet ﷺ in his presence. Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh took it to mean that people should not start talking before he speaks, and should stay silent while he talks. Another verse is understood to forbid calling the Messenger as people call one another: "Do not treat the Messenger’s summons to you ˹as lightly˺ as your summons to one another." (24:63). The Qur'an warned the Muslims that all their good deeds would be wasted if they showed him disrespect.

### How did the Companions honour him?

The Companions, who spent most of their time with the Prophet ﷺ, kept to the respect the Qur'an taught. It is reported that after this verse came down, Abū Bakr spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as quietly as if telling him a secret. ʿUmar al-Fārūq did the same.

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said that no one on earth was dearer to him than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, yet he could never bring himself to look at him fully. If asked to describe him, he could not, because he had never looked at him enough.

At-Tirmidhī reported from Anas that whenever the Prophet ﷺ came into a gathering of his Companions, they lowered their eyes out of respect. Only Abū Bakr and ʿUmar would raise their eyes to him and smile at him.

ʿUrwah ibn Masʿūd was once sent to Madinah to spy on the Muslims. Back in Makkah he reported that he had seen the courts of great kings, of Rome and Persia, and had met the Negus. Yet nowhere in the world had he seen anything like the respect and veneration the Muslims had for their prophet. He told them he did not think they would ever defeat such people.

Al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah reported that the Companions thought it disrespectful to call the Prophet ﷺ from outside his house. They knocked on his door with their fingernails so as not to make a loud noise. Even after his passing, they avoided loud talk in his mosque and did not raise their voices even when preaching there. Many could not hold back their tears when he was mentioned. This remarkable love and respect let them share a large part of prophetic perfection and reach the highest religious rank after the prophets.

### What is the light, and why follow both?

The Qur'an is called a light. Light needs no outside proof of its existence. In the same way the Qur'an is its own proof that it is divine, Allah's word. Its supreme wisdom and eloquence are as plain as sunlight, all the more because it came from an unlettered man. Light is not only bright in itself but brightens the dark, and the Qur'an lit up a humanity lost in darkness.

The verse begins with "the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet" and ends with "follow the light sent down to him". The first phrase calls for obeying the Prophet ﷺ, the second for obeying the Qur'an's commands. So lasting salvation depends on obeying both the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and obeying the Prophet ﷺ is achieved only by following his way of life, the Sunnah.

### Why is believing in a new prophet so hard?

The real spirit of religion is fear of Allah and concern for the Hereafter. In the later generations of a prophet or reformer, that inner spirit cools and form becomes all-important. At such a time Muhammad ﷺ came with religion in its pure form, cleared of every human addition and alteration. When a prophet appears, the greatest virtue is to believe in him. This faith is not the ritual recital of a few words. It means leaving a lifeless structure of rituals for a living religion that speaks directly to human nature.

A person's ties to the old religious structure rest only on historical tradition and ancestral custom. Accepting the religion of a new prophet takes a conscious decision. He leaves lifeless rituals behind and chooses reality. This looks simple, but in every age it has proved the hardest step to take, because people find it so hard to see beyond appearances.

### In short

- The full mercy asked for by Mūsā belongs to those who follow the unlettered Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, whose description the Torah and the Gospel contained.
- His being unlettered made the Qur'an's wisdom and eloquence an undeniable sign of his truth.
- He commands what Islam recognises as good, permits the pure, forbids the impure, and lifts the heavy burdens of earlier laws.
- Success requires believing in him, honouring and supporting him out of love, and following the Qur'an and his Sunnah.
- The Companions' deep reverence for him raised them to the highest rank after the prophets.

158.text:
Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to make a declaration to the whole of humanity: "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! I am Allah’s Messenger to you all." The One who sent him is the Lord of everything: "To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He gives life and causes death.”" The call that follows is addressed to everyone: "So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His revelations." And then: "And follow him, so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided". This verse sets out one of the fundamental beliefs of Islam about prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ was sent as Allah's Messenger to all mankind and to the jinn, to everyone who will exist until the Day of Judgement.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity!"** Say, O Muhammad, to all people, red and black, Arabs and non-Arabs alike.

**"I am Allah’s Messenger to you all."** This shows the Prophet's honour and greatness, for he is the Final Prophet, sent to all mankind and to the jinn. He was told to declare openly that his prophethood was not limited to one people or place.

**"To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth."** The One who sent him is the Creator, Lord and King of all things. All the treasures of the heavens and the earth are His, and Allah alone controls them.

**"There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him."** Nothing besides Him deserves worship, glory be to Him. One explanation renders it: there is no provider except Him.

**"He gives life and causes death.”"** He brings the dead to life at the resurrection and causes the living to die in this world. Control, life, death and judgement are all in His hand, so He alone is Lord of the universe.

**"So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet,"** Allah proclaims that Muhammad ﷺ is His Messenger and confirms it by commanding people to believe in him and follow him. He is the unlettered Prophet whom they were promised, and whose coming was announced, in the earlier scriptures. Those books described him fully, including as the unlettered Prophet. He cannot read or write, and he brought only what his Lord revealed to him, to guide people to what is good for them in this world and the next.

**"who believes in Allah and His revelations."** His deeds match his words, and he believes in what his Lord gave him. His Lord's words here are the Qur'an. Another reading, in the singular, takes "His word" as ʿĪsā (Jesus), who came into being through a word, "Be", and he was.

**"And follow him, so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided"**: take up his path and guidance and his religion, so that you may be led out of error into faith and onto the Straight Path.

### Was the Prophet ﷺ sent to everyone?

Allah says elsewhere: "And this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches." (6:19). And: "But whoever from the ˹disbelieving˺ groups rejects it, the Fire will be their destiny." (11:17). And: "And ask those who were given the Scripture and the illiterate ˹people˺, “Have you submitted yourselves ˹to Allah˺?” If they submit, they will be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, then your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺." (3:20). There are many other verses on this subject, and more hadiths than can be counted. Every Muslim knows that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came for all mankind and for the jinn too.

The earlier prophets came to a particular people in a particular place, for a limited time. Another tradition, which Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, has the Prophet ﷺ say that anyone who hears of his coming, Jew or Christian or otherwise, must believe in him, or he will be put in Hell. So this verse is clear proof that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all of humanity. His message is for every generation, every age to come and every place. No one can reach salvation without believing in him, even if he devotedly practises some other faith or follows some other book.

### "Abū Bakr said: You speak the truth"

Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū al-Dardāʾ that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar once had a sharp argument in which Abū Bakr angered ʿUmar. ʿUmar walked off in anger. Abū Bakr followed him, asking his forgiveness, but ʿUmar refused and shut his door in Abū Bakr's face. Abū Bakr went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, where Abū al-Dardāʾ and others were sitting. The Prophet ﷺ remarked that their companion had been in a quarrel. Later ʿUmar regretted what he had done. He came to the Prophet ﷺ, greeted him with salām, sat beside him and told him what had happened.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ grew angry with ʿUmar. Seeing this, Abū Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah, I was the one in the wrong," and that his own fault was greater. The Prophet ﷺ said: will you not leave my Companion alone for my sake? When I said, "O people, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all," you all said, "You lie." Abū Bakr alone said, "You speak the truth."

### Five things given to no prophet before

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said he had been given five things that no prophet before him was given, and that he did not say this out of pride. The chain of this hadith is acceptable, though the two Ṣaḥīḥs did not record it. Imām Aḥmad's Musnad also reports, through reliable narrators, that this was said during the campaign of Tabūk. The Prophet ﷺ was praying Tahajjud late at night, and his Companions formed a circle around him to guard him from any attack. When he finished, he told them that five distinctions had been given to him that night:

1. He was sent to all mankind, black and white alike, while each earlier prophet's message was limited to his own people.
2. Allah gave him victory through fear, which seized his enemies from as far as a month's journey away.
3. The spoils of war were made lawful for him and his people, though they had been unlawful for everyone before.
4. The whole earth was made a place of prayer for him and his followers, and its soil a means of purification. The earlier peoples could pray only in their churches and synagogues, not at home or out in the open. When water is lacking, his people may use clean earth instead, in tayammum, a concession no one before was given.
5. The fifth, he stressed, was the greatest and most helpful. Every prophet was given one supplication that was certain to be answered, and each used it for his own purpose. He kept his supplication back as intercession for his Ummah on the Day of Resurrection. It will reach everyone who bears witness that there is no god but Allah and associates no partner with Him.

### Why does this verse show the finality of prophethood?

Because the Prophet ﷺ came at the end of all the prophets, the belief in the finality of prophethood follows naturally. Since he is the last of them and came to guide all people of all times to come, there is no room for any other prophet. The verse is thus taken as proof that he is the seal of the prophets, since his message is for all the world and all the ages to come. Some authentic traditions say that ʿĪsā (Jesus), when he descends from heaven in the last age, will also follow the law of the Prophet ﷺ. Many other verses state the finality of prophethood just as plainly. The verse of the Holy Qur'an quoted above (6:19) makes following the Qur'an binding on all who come after the Prophet ﷺ, and with it the duty of learning it.

The same fact explains a special quality of the Muslim Ummah. According to a tradition of the Prophet ﷺ, there will always be a group among the Muslims who stand up to the forces against Islam and resist irreligious ideas and practices. They will also correct false interpretations of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Allah will favour this group with His special help, and in the end it will prevail over its opponents. These people are the true heirs of the prophetic mission, faithfully carrying out its duty after the Prophet ﷺ.

Imām al-Rāzī, explaining the Qur'anic command "Be with the truthful", remarked that it guarantees there will always be a group of truthful people available. Otherwise the command to keep their company would make no sense. Al-Rāzī drew the principle of consensus from this phrase. The presence of the truthful is enough to prevent the whole Ummah from agreeing on an error.

### Another view: directly and through his Ummah

Another view holds that "I am Allah’s Messenger to you all" is no claim that every other prophet went only to his own people while Muhammad ﷺ went to all nations. The statement does not compare one prophet with another. It is simply a statement of fact. His prophethood works in two ways, directly, and by way of his community, the Ummah. His direct task was to bring the divine message to the people of Arabia: "so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it" (6:92). And he was to convey it to the whole world indirectly: "so that the Messenger may be a witness over you, and that you may be witnesses over humanity" (22:78).

In principle, this was the task given to every prophet of Allah. But the religion the other prophets brought did not stay in its original, pure condition. So it could no longer give good news, or warn people of the results of their deeds in the life to come, which is a prophet's main duty. The Bible foretells that through the Arab Prophet every tribe on earth will receive blessing. His blessings have been able to reach all nations because the religion he brought has been preserved in its original state. The religion brought by Mūsā (Moses) and ʿĪsā has been distorted. Its voice may reach everyone, but its blessings will not.

### Why "believe" and then "follow"?

Having established that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all the people of the world and all times to come, and that no one has any choice but to follow his law, Islam, the verse calls for belief in Allah and His unlettered Messenger. He himself believes in Allah and His words, so people should follow him to stay on the right path. Allah's words here are the scriptures revealed to His prophets, such as the Torah, the Gospel revealed to ʿĪsā, and the Qur'an.

The command to believe in him is followed by a command to follow him. This shows that belief alone, or saying the words of faith, is not enough for guidance or salvation. Living by the Sharīʿah of Islam is necessary for salvation in the Hereafter. The great saint and spiritual guide Shaykh Junayd of Baghdad said that every road to Allah is closed except the path the Prophet ﷺ marked out.

"The unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His revelations" also shows the difference between the philosopher's idea of the Divine and the prophet's. The philosopher's deity is an abstract spirit. Accepting it is like accepting the force of gravity in the universe. But gravity neither speaks nor gives commands. The Lord of the prophets is living and conscious. He speaks to human beings, commands His servants and decides reward and punishment by their obedience or disobedience to His commands.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ was told to declare that he is Allah's Messenger to all mankind, unlike earlier prophets sent to one people.
- No one can reach salvation without believing in him, and Abū Bakr was the first to say, "You speak the truth."
- He was given five unique gifts, among them the whole earth as a place of prayer and his intercession kept for his Ummah.
- As the last Prophet sent to all ages, he seals prophethood, and a truthful group of his Ummah will always uphold his message.
- Belief must be joined with following him, for every road to Allah is closed except his.

159.text:
