After so much about the failings of the Israelites, Allah does justice to the righteous among them: "There are some among the people of Moses who guide with the truth and establish justice accordingly". Among the children of Israel there is a group who stand for the truth, guide people to it and judge fairly between people by it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There are some among the people of Moses"**: a group, a community, from among the Israelites, the people of Mūsā (Moses). One explanation says they are the people who live beyond the river al-Raml, the river of sand.

**"who guide with the truth"**: who call others to the truth, follow it and act on it themselves.

**"and establish justice accordingly"**: who act justly by that truth when they pass judgement, settling their disputes by what the truth demands, which is Islam.

### Who are these people?

Allah says the same of some of the People of the Book in other verses: "there are some among the People of the Book who are upright, who recite Allah’s revelations throughout the night, prostrating ˹in prayer˺" (3:113). And: "Indeed, there are some among the People of the Book who truly believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you ˹believers˺ and what was revealed to them. They humble themselves before Allah—never trading Allah’s revelations for a fleeting gain. Their reward is with their Lord." (3:199).

Allah also says: "˹As for˺ those ˹faithful˺ to whom We had given the Scripture before this ˹Quran˺, they do believe in it. When it is recited to them, they declare, “We believe in it. This is definitely the truth from our Lord. We had already submitted ˹even˺ before this.” These ˹believers˺ will be given a double reward for their perseverance" (28:52-54). And: "when it is recited to those who were gifted with knowledge before it ˹was revealed˺, they fall upon their faces in prostration and say, ‘Glory be to our Lord! Surely the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.’ And they fall down upon their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.”" (17:107-109).

These are the people who faithfully followed the commands of the Torah and the Injīl in the times when those books were revealed. They also include those who readily accepted Islam once the Prophet ﷺ appeared, as the Torah and the Injīl had foretold. The Qur'an praises this group in a number of verses.

A number of Jewish tribes were settled in Arabia, proud of possessing Allah's holy Book. Such people resist accepting any truth from outside. The feeling that they already hold the greatest truth keeps them from accepting a truth brought by anyone else. Most of the Jews were blinded by stubbornness and prejudice. Only a few, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, could look at Islam with an open mind. They affirmed that it was true, without caring for their worldly standing, and gave themselves to it wholeheartedly.

### The people beyond the river of sand

Ibn Jarīr records a narrative under this verse. A group of Israelites, disgusted by the corrupt practices of the rest, prayed to Allah for a land of their own, apart from the other tribes, where they could practise the original faith that Mūsā had taught. Allah took them away to a distant land in the far east, and there they lived by their faith without fail.

Allah favoured them further by letting them accept Islam directly at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ. On the night of the Ascension, Jibrīl (Gabriel) took the Prophet ﷺ to them on the way to the heavens. They accepted the faith, and he taught them some surahs of the Qur'an.

The Prophet ﷺ asked whether they had weights and measures, and how they made their living. They said they farmed the land and gathered the whole harvest into one heap, and people came and took from it what they needed. So they had no need of weights and measures. He asked whether any of them ever lied. They said no one did, because anyone who told a lie was burned up by fire from heaven. He asked why all their houses were alike. They said it was so that no one could show off his wealth over others. He asked why they had built their graves in front of their houses. They said it kept them mindful of death at all times. When the Prophet ﷺ returned from the heavens to Makkah, this verse was revealed to him.

Al-Qurṭubī related this story under the verse along with other suggestions, and remarked that the narrative is not authentic. Others called it an unusual report but did not reject it. Either way, the verse teaches that the Israelites have never been without some who followed the truth. They may be the people described in this story, or those who embraced Islam after the Prophet ﷺ appeared.

### The inner reading: the hidden friends of Allah

This is the story of Allah's friends, a description of the chivalrous and of how the travellers on the path conduct themselves. The Lord of the worlds has shown them the road of happiness, singled them out for the special favours of nearness, and honoured them with the pull of His generosity. Awareness of Allah lives on through them. The well-trodden path of truthfulness rests on their firmly planted feet, and the good fortune of the religion is joined to the blessing of their breaths. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that if the light of one of them were divided among the people of the earth, it would be enough for them all.

If the light of their hearts were given free rein, and its radiance fell on the world and its people, every stubborn soul would become a voice of tawḥīd. They would trade the sashes of unbelief for belts of passion for the religion. Yet such people are rare and precious. Allah shows them to no one, and gives them over neither to this world nor to the next. He keeps them like refugees under His own protection and nurtures them with love beneath the domes of His jealousy.

Revelation came to Mūsā: O companion in conversation, do not open the shell that holds the pearl of your pain before those who have no eyes. Do not recite the verses of passion for My majesty to those not admitted to the secret, or to those shut out from true hearing. If you wish to reveal My mystery to anyone, reveal it to those in whom the covenant of My secrets is kept. They serve at My threshold night and day, the tent of their passion pitched in contemplation of My majesty. The threshold of Lordship has branded them with the mark of worthiness: "a community that guides by the truth and does justice thereby".

This brand of worthiness is one of the divine secrets, a subtle gift of the Lord that came down from the world of the unseen and settled only behind the veils of the clay of the poor. To catch its scent, go behind the veils of the soul until you reach the heart. Then go behind the veils of the heart until you reach the spirit, and behind the veils of the spirit until you reach union with the Beloved. You will find it nowhere but in the spirits of His friends.

### In short

- Among the people of Mūsā has always been a group that guides by the truth and judges justly by it.
- They include those who kept faithfully to the Torah and the Injīl in their time, and those, like ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, who accepted Islam.
- A report about a hidden people beyond a river of sand who met the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the Ascension is judged not authentic by al-Qurṭubī.
- Allah keeps His true friends hidden and protected, and the light of their hearts could guide the whole world.

160.text:
Allah lists the favours He showed the Israelites in the wilderness: "We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community. And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, “Strike the rock with your staff.”" The rock answered at once: "Then twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place." He protected and fed them: "We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves". This verse and the two after it recount Allah's favours to the Israelites, then their turning from His commands, which brought punishment from heaven.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We divided them into twelve tribes"**: Allah separated the children of Israel into twelve tribes, tribe by tribe. In the Arabic, "twelve" describes their state, asbāṭan, "tribes", stands in for it, and umaman, "communities", stands in for "tribes".

**"each as a community."** Each tribe formed its own distinct nation. One explanation says nine and a half of the tribes live toward the east, beyond China, on the river al-Raml, while two and a half are spread across the world.

**"And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water,"** Allah commanded Mūsā (Moses), when his people in the wilderness asked him to pray to Allah for water.

**"“Strike the rock with your staff.”"** Strike it with the staff you carry.

**"Then twelve springs gushed out."** He struck it, and twelve springs, or streams, burst out of the rock, one for each tribe.

**"Each tribe knew its drinking place."** Every tribe knew its own spring, which no other tribe shared.

**"We shaded them with clouds"**: a white cloud that went with them wherever they moved and stopped when they stopped. By day it shielded them from the heat of the sun, and by night it gave them light like a lamp.

**"and sent down to them manna and quails,"** The manna was something like gum with a sweet taste, said to be a kind of turunjabīn. The quails were quails, or a bird like them.

**"˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.”"** Eat the manna and quails We have given you.

**"They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves"**: their disobedience and their ingratitude for these blessings did Allah no harm. They harmed only themselves, bringing ruin on themselves by going against Allah's commands and failing to value His gifts as they should have.

### How were the Israelites provided for?

Allah took the Israelites out of the idol-worshipping atmosphere of Egypt and settled them in the desert of Sinai. There they were organised into twelve groups, each with its own leader, all under the charge of Mūsā. The children of Israel were given everything they needed to live. Water came from mountain springs. For food, manna and quails were sent down and lay ready for them right in front of their tents.

Allah then reminded them that He had arranged for all their needs. So they should stop being greedy for worldly and bodily pleasures and not rush toward unholy things. Instead they should take the way of contentment and gratitude to Allah.

### Where else is this story told?

These verses were discussed in Sūrat al-Baqarah, which was revealed in Madinah, while these verses were revealed in Makkah. The details, and the differences between the two tellings, were set out there and need not be repeated here.

### The inner reading: twelve rivers from the wellspring of recognition

On the realities behind this verse, Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad said that Allah made twelve streams flow from the wellspring of recognition and made each the drink of one group. At that watering place He let each group draw the water of the religion's good fortune. Allah said the same briefly elsewhere, by way of allusion: "Had the deniers followed the Right Way, We would have certainly granted them abundant rain to drink—" (72:16). The Right Way there is the Ṭarīqah, and the meaning is: We would grant them an unfailing watering place.

There are twelve rivers. The first is familiarity and the last is friendship. The ten between them are:

1. sincere belief
2. purity in deeds
3. contentment with the decree
4. the eye of certainty
5. the joy of ecstasy
6. the lightning of unveiling
7. bewilderment in witnessing
8. the dissolving of the signs that bear witness
9. the vision of togetherness
10. the reality of being alone with Him

Once the servant's spirit has drunk from these rivers and known their sweetness, and the divine pull is joined to that, he himself becomes the Wellspring of Life. Whoever sips from his hand will prosper forever.

The Pir of the Ṭarīqah said: "O Allah, I know the drinking place, but I cannot drink. Thirsty at heart, I weep in hope of a drop." No fountain could quench him, he said, for he sought the ocean, and he had passed a thousand springs and streams in search of it. He likened himself to one drowning in the fire of passion, to one dying of thirst in the middle of a lake, and to one lost in the desert. "Help me! I am at my wits' end. I have lost my heart."

### In short

- Allah organised the Israelites into twelve tribes and, when they asked for water, made twelve springs gush from a rock, one for each tribe.
- He shaded them with a cloud, fed them with manna and quails, and told them to eat of His good provision.
- Their ingratitude and disobedience harmed only themselves, never Allah.
- In the inner reading, Allah lets each group drink from its own river of recognition, from familiarity to friendship.

161.text:
Allah reminds the Israelites of the city He opened to them and the simple conditions He set: "And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them, “Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please." They were to enter humbly, asking forgiveness: "Say, ‘Absolve us,’ and enter the gate with humility. We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them,"** Remember, O Messenger, when Allah told the Israelites.

**"“Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺"**: dwell in the Holy House of Jerusalem. Another explanation names the town of Jericho. For their settlement, a whole city, Jericho in the Jordan valley, was given to them.

**"and eat from wherever you please."** Eat of the town's fruits wherever and whenever you wish.

**"Say, ‘Absolve us,’"** The word is ḥiṭṭah. It means: our plea is for release from our sins. In other words, ask Allah to lift your disobedience from you, saying, "Forgive our sins." One explanation takes it as the declaration that there is no deity except Allah.

**"and enter the gate with humility."** Literally, "enter the gate prostrating", meaning bowing or kneeling. This was the gate of the city. The prostration here is really a bow. They were to enter their place of worship with humility and modesty and worship their Lord. They were to remember Allah's majesty and supremacy, and confess their shortcomings before Him.

**"We will forgive your sins,"** We will forgive you your transgressions. The verb can be read "We will forgive" or "your sins will be forgiven".

**"˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers.”"** Those who do good through obedience will be given more reward for their good works, in the good things of this world and of the Hereafter.

### What was asked of them?

Very little was asked of them in return for a city and its produce. They were to walk in humbly, with their heads bowed, and ask forgiveness. Entering the gate this way was meant to show their humility before Allah, and the plea "Absolve us" to admit their sins. In return Allah promised to forgive them and to add to the reward of those who did good. Their test lay in whether they would keep to this path of humility.

### In short

- The Israelites were told to enter the city, Jerusalem or by another view Jericho, and eat freely of it.
- They were to enter its gate bowing in humility and say, "Absolve us", asking Allah to forgive their sins.
- Allah promised forgiveness, and more reward in this world and the next for those who did good.

162.text:
The Israelites answered even this easy command with insolence: "But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their wrongdoing". They changed both the word and the deed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But the wrongdoers among them"**: those among them who sinned.

**"changed the words they were commanded to say."** They were told to say ḥiṭṭah, "Absolve us", or as another explanation has it, that there is no deity except Allah. Instead they said ḥinṭah, "wheat". Other explanations report their words as "a grain inside a hair". They also changed what they were told to do. Instead of entering humbly with lowered heads, they came in dragging themselves on their backsides.

**"So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them"**: a chastisement and terror from the sky, which one explanation identifies as a plague.

**"for their wrongdoing"**: for their disobedience, and for changing what they had been commanded to say.

### Why did they change the words?

The Jews forgot Allah's admonition. Instead of taking the way Allah had shown them, they followed a path they invented themselves in Allah's name. They chose arrogance over the path of humility. Their words were not words of gratitude but of insolence. When the Jews went this far in their wrongdoing, Allah withdrew His grace from them. Instead of His blessings, all kinds of punishment closed in on them.

### In short

- The wrongdoers among the Israelites changed "Absolve us" into an insolent word, and entered the gate dragging themselves instead of bowing.
- They replaced the way Allah showed them with arrogance and insolence.
- So Allah withdrew His grace and sent a punishment from the sky for their wrongdoing.

163.text:
Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ to remind the Jews of his time of a story from their own past: "Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath." The fish behaved in a way that tested them: "During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen. In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness". This verse explains another passage: "You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath." (2:65). The events are discussed in detail in Sūrat al-Baqarah, and they are clear enough to need little explanation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask them ˹O Prophet˺"**: ask the Jews who are with you, O Muhammad, by way of rebuke. Ask them about their fellow Jews who defied Allah's command, so that His punishment struck them suddenly for their evil deeds, their transgression and their defiance through deceit. Remind them how Allah punished some of the Israelites. Warn them, too, not to conceal how their books describe you, or they may meet the fate of their forefathers.

**"about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea,"** The town was Aylah, or Eilat, on the shore of the Qulzum, the Red Sea. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq recorded, through Dāwūd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn and ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās placed this village, Aylah, between aṭ-Ṭūr in Sinai and Madyan. ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Qatādah and as-Suddī said the same.

**"who broke the Sabbath."** They overstepped Allah's limits on the Sabbath by fishing, which they had been forbidden to do that day, defying His command to keep the day sacred.

**"During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible,"** On their Sabbath day great fish came in scores, rising from the depths up to the shore and floating openly on top of the water. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbās.

**"but on other days the fish were never seen."** On the days when they did not keep the Sabbath, the fish did not come to them.

**"In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness"**: Ibn Jarīr explained that Allah tested them by making the fish swim near the surface on the day they were forbidden to fish, and hiding them on the days fishing was allowed. This trial came because of their disobedience and their rebellion against His command.

### How did they break the Sabbath?

Eventually they decided to fish by a trick. They set up their nets so that the fish would fall into them on Saturday, and then took them out and ate them on Sunday. So these were people who used a ruse to break Allah's prohibitions. On the surface their action looked lawful, but in reality it was meant to violate the prohibition.

The imam and scholar Abū ʿAbdullāh Ibn Baṭṭah reported from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: do not commit what the Jews committed, making lawful what Allah has forbidden by cunning tricks. This hadith has a reasonable chain.

### Why is a trick worse than a plain sin?

It is a sin to do anything Allah has forbidden. But to do a forbidden act while trying to make it lawful through some trick adds insult to injury. By breaking the rule of the Sabbath in this way, the Jews committed a double sin. Such people must suffer divine retribution. They lose the blessings Allah has reserved for human beings alone, and in this world they fall from the level of humanity to the level of animals.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ was told to remind the Jews of the Sabbath-breakers of Aylah, and to warn them against hiding his description.
- Allah tested that town by sending fish openly on the Sabbath and withholding them on other days.
- They used nets as a trick to catch the fish on the Sabbath, a sin made worse by pretending it was lawful.

164.text:
When some of the townspeople broke the Sabbath, the rest divided over how to respond: "When some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺, “Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?”" The warners had their answer: "They replied, “Just to be free from your Lord’s blame, and so perhaps they may abstain.”" When the fishing began, the town split into three groups.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺,"** A group among them who neither fished nor forbade it spoke to those who were forbidding it.

**"“Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺"**: why do you keep admonishing and cautioning these people?

**"who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?”"** Allah is going to destroy them in this world for their disobedience, by turning them into animals, or punish them severely on the Day of Judgement with the Fire. Since they had already earned Allah's punishment, these people said, there was no point in forbidding them.

**"They replied, “Just to be free from your Lord’s blame,"** We admonish them to clear ourselves before your Lord and have a plea before Him. We were commanded to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. By doing so we keep Him from holding us to account, and from blaming us for failing to forbid them in any way.

**"and so perhaps they may abstain.”"** Perhaps they will take our advice, fear Allah, stop fishing on the Sabbath and give up their disobedience. If they repent to Allah, He will accept their repentance and grant them His mercy.

### Who were the three groups?

The people of the town were divided into three groups:

1. Those who broke the prohibition and caught fish on the Sabbath, and encouraged others to do the same.
2. Those who did not fish, but forbade the others and kept away from them.
3. Those who did not fish but did not warn others against it either.

The first group's fishing is described in Sūrat al-Baqarah. It was the third, silent group who asked the warners why they bothered.

### In short

- When the Sabbath-breaking began, the townspeople split into those who fished, those who warned against it, and those who stayed silent.
- The silent group asked why anyone should warn people already doomed to Allah's punishment.
- The warners spoke out to clear themselves before Allah, as He had commanded, and in the hope that the sinners might yet stop.

165.text:
The warning went unheeded, and the outcome separated the groups: "When they ignored the warning they were given, We rescued those who used to warn against evil and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment for their rebelliousness". Allah saved those who had forbidden the sin and seized those who had committed it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they ignored the warning they were given,"** Literally, "when they forgot what they had been reminded of". The wrongdoers overlooked the admonition, turned away from it and refused the advice. They abandoned what they had been commanded and did not desist.

**"We rescued those who used to warn against evil"**: Allah saved from the punishment the group that had forbidden the sin, catching fish on the Sabbath.

**"and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment"**: Allah struck those who transgressed by fishing on the Sabbath with a grievous punishment. The word used is baʾīs. Mujāhid said it means "severe", and Qatādah said "painful". The two meanings come to the same thing, and Allah knows best. Naming only the wrongdoers as seized suggests that the others were spared.

**"for their rebelliousness"**: because they disobeyed Allah and persisted in rebelling against His command.

### What became of the silent group?

Allah stated that those who forbade evil were saved and those who committed the transgression were destroyed. He did not mention the end of the third group, who stood by. The reward matches the deed. They did nothing that deserved praise, nor any wrong that called for blame.

Forbidding evil is, in effect, a declaration that one has done one's duty. So when Allah's scourge falls on a people, those so disgusted by evil that they actively try to stop it are spared the punishment.

### In short

- When the Sabbath-breakers ignored the warning, Allah saved those who had forbidden the sin.
- He seized the wrongdoers with a severe, painful punishment for their persistent rebellion.
- Those who actively forbid evil discharge their duty, and so are spared when punishment falls.

166.text:
The final stage of their punishment came when they kept on sinning: "But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”" This is the detail of the "dreadful punishment" mentioned in the previous verse, and the same words are recorded of them in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But when they stubbornly persisted in violation,"** When they overstepped the limits and arrogantly refused to give up what had been forbidden to them, rebelling against Allah out of pride and stubbornness, and would not accept advice.

**"We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”"** Allah said to them, "O you disobedient ones! Be apes, despised!", humiliated, disgraced, rejected and loathed. And so they became, for when Allah wills something, He only says to it "Be!" and it is.

### Were the silent ones saved?

Ibn ʿAbbās said he did not know what happened to the group that stood aside, those who had asked, "Why do you warn them?" ʿIkrimah said that group was not destroyed, because they had disliked what the others were doing, and had asked that question. ʿIkrimah recalled that he kept discussing it with Ibn ʿAbbās until he convinced him that they had been saved, and Ibn ʿAbbās then gave him a garment as a gift. Al-Ḥākim reported in a hadith that ʿIkrimah put this opinion to Ibn ʿAbbās, who was delighted with it.

### What does it mean to become an ape?

One view, recorded by al-Qurṭubī, holds that "Be apes" does not mean their faces became the faces of apes. It means their character became ape-like, so that their hearts and minds were those of apes instead of human beings.

A person becomes an ape when, after acting again and again against the dictates of his wisdom and conscience, he grows so callous that every fine feeling is driven out of him. Whatever desire forms in his heart, he acts on it. Whoever comes within his reach, he attacks that person's honour and property. If he has a grievance against someone, he sets about degrading him at once. If he disagrees with someone, he starts to belittle him. If he finds someone in his way, he immediately fights him. A true human being is one who puts the bridle of Allah on himself. An ape is one who does whatever his lower self demands, without restraint.

The Creator has placed intelligence and conscience within every human being. When a desire forms in a person, his wisdom and conscience come alive at once and ask whether fulfilling it is right or not. In an ape, nothing stands between the wish and its fulfilment. Whatever comes to its mind, it does at once. It need not think about its wish, nor feel any shame after following it.

### In short

- When the Sabbath-breakers persisted in arrogance, Allah commanded them to be despised apes, and they became so.
- The fate of the silent group is debated, but ʿIkrimah persuaded Ibn ʿAbbās that they were saved because they disliked the sin.
- One view sees the change as one of character, the state of a person who follows every desire without the bridle of conscience.

167.text:
Allah reminds His Prophet ﷺ of a declaration He made about the Jews: "And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment." The verse then balances its warning with hope: "Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". This verse and the next describe two punishments given to the Israelites. The first is that Allah will keep sending, until the Day of Judgement, people who punish and disgrace them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺"** Mention, O Messenger.

**"when your Lord declared"** The word is taʾadhdhana. Mujāhid said it means "declared", while others said "ordained". Allah made it known in clear terms, in words that carry the force of an oath.

**"that He would send against them others"**: against the Jews.

**"who would make them suffer terribly"**: who would humiliate and humble them in this life and afflict them with a degrading torment. This was for their disobedience, their defiance of Allah's commands and Law, and their tricks for getting round His prohibitions. Al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that this torment includes disgrace and the payment of the jizyah, the tribute tax. One explanation says the reference is to Muhammad ﷺ and his Ummah, who imposed the capitation tax and other measures on them.

**"until the Day of Judgment."** For as long as the world lasts.

**"Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment,"** He is swift to requite those who disobey Him, defy His Law and refuse to believe in Him, and sometimes punishes them in this worldly life.

**"but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**: forgiving to every servant who repents and turns back to Him, and merciful to those who believe and obey.

### How has this declaration been fulfilled?

It is reported that Mūsā (Moses) made the Jews pay a land tax for seven or thirteen years, and that he was the first to do so. Allah later sent Sulaymān (Solomon) against them. After him came Nebuchadnezzar, who killed some of them, took others captive and imposed the jizyah on them. They fell under the humiliating rule of the Greeks, then the Chaldeans, and later the Christians, who subdued and disgraced them and made them pay tribute. They went on paying this tax to the Magians until the Prophet ﷺ was sent. When Islam came, they came under his authority and paid the jizyah to him as well. History records that they have been dominated and treated with contempt by one people after another, down to this day.

It is also said that in the last age the Jews will side with the Dajjāl, the False Messiah. The Muslims, together with ʿĪsā (Jesus) son of Maryam, will kill them. This will happen shortly before the end of this world.

### Why are warning and mercy joined?

This verse mentions both punishment and mercy, so that no one falls into despair. Allah often places encouragement and warning side by side, so that hearts always hold both hope and fear.

### Why was their punishment so severe?

When a great reward is promised for a task, the punishment for failing in it is equally great. This is true of a community made the bearer of a holy Book. Allah raised the Jews to this rank. Besides promises of blessings in the Hereafter, they were given extraordinary benefits in this world. But they kept on disobeying, committing irreligious acts in the name of religion. So Allah removed them from their high position. It was decreed that as long as the world lasts they would taste Allah's punishment, with whatever awaits them in the Hereafter still to come.

This does not mean they would never see good fortune until the Last Day. As these verses themselves make clear, they would have spells of good times. But even these would be a kind of curse, since they would give them the chance for more insolence and so make them liable to more punishment.

### In short

- Allah declared that He would keep sending, until the Day of Judgement, people who would humble the Jews for their disobedience and tricks.
- History bears this out, from the tax under Mūsā through Nebuchadnezzar to the jizyah paid in the Prophet's time.
- A people raised to bear a holy Book is punished all the more severely for betraying it.
- The verse joins swift punishment with forgiveness and mercy, so that hearts hold both fear and hope.

168.text:
The second punishment follows: "We dispersed them through the land in groups—some were righteous, others were less so." Then come their trials: "We tested them with prosperity and adversity, so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺". Allah broke the Jewish people into fragments scattered across the world, so that they could not hold together as one solid nation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We dispersed them through the land in groups"** The verb means to cut into pieces. "Groups" renders umam, the plural of ummah, a community or party. Allah split them into separate nations, sects and factions across the earth, after they had been united. He also said: "And We said to the Children of Israel after Pharaoh, “Reside in the land, but when the promise of the Hereafter comes to pass, We will bring you all together.”" (17:104).

**"some were righteous,"** Some were rightly guided and upheld the rights of Allah and of His creatures. They followed the commandments of the Torah faithfully and did not distort them as others did. One explanation identifies them as the tribes beyond the river al-Raml. On another view, the righteous are those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ and followed the guidance of the Qur'an once it was revealed.

**"others were less so."** Some were moderate, and some went to excess in disobedience. Those "less so" include disbelievers and wicked people, and those who stubbornly disobeyed their prophets and even killed them. On the second view, they are those who believed the Torah to be Allah's word, yet disobeyed it or distorted its commands, selling their eternal salvation for petty worldly gains. One explanation takes them as the remaining believers among the children of Israel, and another as their disbelievers. The jinn described themselves in the same terms: "Among us are those who are righteous and those who are less so. We have been of different factions" (72:11).

**"We tested them with prosperity and adversity,"** With good things and bad: times of ease and difficulty, eagerness and fear, health and affliction. The good things were fertile land, abundance and comfort. The bad things were drought, failed harvests and hardship, or the persecutions and disasters that run through their history, or a famine sent as punishment.

**"so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺"**: so that they might turn back from their wickedness and repent of their transgression and disbelief.

### Why is scattering a punishment?

This verse shows that being united as a nation is a blessing from Allah, while being broken into scattered pieces is a punishment He sends. Muslims, for their part, have always had the blessing of a collective identity, recognised in the world as an organised people. From Madinah in the time of the Prophet ﷺ to this day, they have held independent rule in various parts of the earth. Muslim lands stretching from the Far East to the West are clear proof of this.

The Jews, by contrast, have been persecuted by one people after another from the time of Sulaymān (Solomon) onward. Their captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, their persecution by later kings, and their defeat at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ and his Caliph ʿUmar al-Fārūq are clear examples.

Their gathering in Palestine in the last age does not contradict this. The Prophet ﷺ foretold in authentic traditions that ʿĪsā (Jesus) will come down from heaven before the end of the world, in the land of Syria, and that the Christians will then accept Islam. He will fight the Jews, as mentioned under the previous verse. Allah does not summon those who have earned His punishment through police or other agents. The causes He creates drive them to the place of their end. Their gathering in one land spares ʿĪsā the trouble of seeking them across the world.

### A law for every community

This law of Allah was not for the Jews alone. It applies equally to the later community raised, after the Jews were removed, to the high rank of Allah's witnesses. If Muslims find themselves dominated by those who deny the truth and by polytheists, and their groups scattered, they must turn back to Allah. That state is a sign that they have earned His displeasure.

### What are prosperity and hardship for?

Both kinds of test were used on them. They were given prosperity and wealth to see whether they would thank their Lord. When they failed that test, they were made to suffer the many punishments described in the preceding verses. Their thinking and conduct became so twisted that in prosperity they said what Allah records: "Indeed, Allah has heard those ˹among the Jews˺ who said, “Allah is poor; we are rich!”" (3:181). And in hardship: "˹Some among˺ the Jews said, “Allah is tight-fisted.”" (5:64).

The verse also implies that prosperity and poverty, joy and suffering, are sent to people as tests of the faith and love of the created for the Creator. People of understanding should not set real store by either, since both are temporary and must end. So it is unwise to grow arrogant in prosperity or despondent in poverty. A Persian poet said that happiness brought him no real gain and sorrow did not make him weep, for both came only as guests to his steadfast spirit.

### The inner reading: the exiles of the path

For those who taste these realities, the verse alludes to the travellers among the community, the exiles of the Ṭarīqah. They wander the world from one region to another and from one cave to another. They hide their spiritual state from people and struggle for their religion against the harm others would do it. Al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ pointed to this when he said that a time will come when the religious will not stay safe unless they keep away from people. You will see them like travellers fleeing from people, now in the mountains, now in the desert.

They rush and wail across the world, in mountain monasteries and desert caves, lost in the ocean of thought, and they say of themselves to all: "No home, no possessions." The story of the Companions of the Cave bears witness to this. So does the story of the Prophet ﷺ and Abū Bakr in the cave: "he was only one of two. While they both were in the cave, he reassured his companion, “Do not worry; Allah is certainly with us.”" (9:40).

Their travel and exile is also explained as yearning. Through most of their days and states, those who yearn have no settled place or rest. Perhaps they will reach somewhere they can see a trace of the Friend, or ask someone about Him. In this sense they have sung: our traces will point to us after we are gone, so look at our traces.

The Pir of the Ṭarīqah said: "O Allah, the homeland of Your exiles is exile, so when will this end?" How, he asked, can one You are testing deserve relief, and how can one whose homeland is exile ever reach home? "The yearner is slain by friendship, and the shroud of those slain by friendship is the vision of You."

"We tested them with prosperity and adversity" means: We tested them with pleasure and disappointment. Pleasure does not deceive them, and disappointment does not turn them away from Allah. They have before them a concern more important than their own pleasure or disappointment. Among people they are only on loan, and to themselves they are strangers. They are free of attachment, their hearts joined to their Protector and their innermost selves aware of Him. With the tongue of poverty and in a state of brokenness, they keep saying: "O Lord, we have come to Your threshold as servants. Raise us up if You wish, and if You wish, bring us low."

### In short

- Allah's second punishment of the Israelites was to scatter them across the earth, for unity is a blessing and scattering a punishment.
- Among them were the righteous, the moderate and the wicked.
- Allah tested them with prosperity and hardship so they might return, but many answered with insolence in both states.
- The same law applies to the Muslims, who must turn back to Allah if they find themselves scattered and dominated.
- In the inner reading, the exiles of the path wander in yearning, unmoved by pleasure or disappointment.

169.text:
Verse 169 turns to the generation that came after the mixed one, and it was worse still: "Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture." Their attitude to the Book is laid bare: "They indulged in unlawful gains, claiming, “We will be forgiven ˹after all˺.” And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it." Allah confronts them with their own pledge: "Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth?" They knew better: "And they were already well-versed in its teachings." The verse ends by setting the next life against this one: "But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then they were succeeded by other generations"** In the time of Mūsā (Moses), many of the Jews feared Allah and did righteous deeds. After that generation of righteous and unrighteous people came another in which there was no goodness. The verb khalafa means to succeed someone, acting as his deputy in his absence. The noun khalf, with a still lām, usually means a successor marked by wickedness, unlike the good ways of his elders. Qatādah said: by Allah, this is an evil generation. Allah says the same in another verse: "But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their lusts and so will soon face the evil consequences" (19:59).

**"who inherited the Scripture."** The word comes from inheritance. They received the Torah from their forefathers, after their prophets and messengers, and studied it. This was the job Allah had entrusted to them by His command. One explanation adds that they took the Scripture and hid the traits and description of Muhammad ﷺ found in it.

**"They indulged in unlawful gains,"** The Arabic speaks of the ʿaraḍ of "this lower world". ʿAraḍ means something bought with money, or sometimes anything owned. Using it for wealth shows that whatever is owned in this world is temporary. As the opposite of jawhar, "substance", it means an accident, which needs something else in order to exist, as colour needs a thing to appear in. The word for "lower", adnā, comes either from a root meaning nearness or from one meaning lowliness, in which case it describes something base. Mujāhid said they would consume anything they could in this life, lawful or unlawful, and still wish for forgiveness. They took bribes and other unlawful gains to hide the description of Muhammad ﷺ, to distort Allah's Scripture and to give judgements against what was revealed.

**"claiming, “We will be forgiven ˹after all˺.”"** They convinced themselves that Allah would forgive what they had done. One explanation reports them saying that sins committed by night would be forgiven by day, and sins committed by day would be forgiven at night. They kept hoping in Allah while deceiving themselves.

**"And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it."** If the same kind of unlawful gain came to them again, they would take it every time, even declaring it lawful. They hope for forgiveness while repeating the same offence and persisting in it. Yet the Torah holds no such promise for those who persist in sin. Nothing stops them, for whenever they get the chance they consume, whether it is allowed or not.

**"Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture"** "The covenant of the Scripture" means the covenant in the Scripture. The question is really an affirmation: a covenant was certainly taken from them. Allah took a pledge from them to proclaim the truth to people and not hide it, without distorting or changing anything.

**"that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth?"** Ibn Jurayj reported that Ibn ʿAbbās identified the untruth here as their claim of forgiveness for sins they go on committing without repentance.

**"And they were already well-versed in its teachings."** They had read what was in it, so why did they ascribe lies to it, claiming it promised forgiveness for persisting in sin? Their failure to act on the Scripture came not from ignorance but from full knowledge, which made their disobedience greater. One explanation says they studied the traits and attributes of Muhammad ﷺ in it. Another says they studied its rulings on the lawful and the unlawful but did not act on them.

**"But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺."** Paradise and its eternal bliss are far better than any passing gain they were given as a bribe. They are for those who have taqwā, following what Allah commands and avoiding what He forbids. Such people guard against disbelief, idolatry, indecency, bribery and altering the Prophet's description in the Torah. Allah says, in effect: My reward, and what I have, is better for those who avoid what is forbidden, abandon their lusts and are active in obeying their Lord. This both encourages them to seek His immense reward and warns them of His severe torment.

**"Will you not then understand"** Do these people, who prefer this life to what is with Allah, have no sense to restrain them from their foolish and extravagant ways? Do they not realise that this world is vanishing and the Hereafter lasts forever, and so prefer it? The verb can be read "Do they not understand?" or "Do you not understand?"

### The judges who took bribes

As-Suddī said that every time the children of Israel appointed a judge, he would take bribes. The best of them met and made one another promise not to take bribes. Yet when one of them took a bribe for a judgement and was asked why, he replied, "I will be forgiven." His people would rebuke him for it. But when he died or was replaced, his successor took bribes as well. So Allah says that if those who rebuked him had their own chance at worldly gain, they would seize it too.

### How did they trade the Book?

Allah says elsewhere: "˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain. What a miserable profit" (3:187).

Among the early Jews there were two groups, the righteous and the wrongdoers. But the later generations who inherited the Torah did the opposite of their elders. They turned the Book into an object of trade and a means of earning a living. For money they would twist and distort the text of the Torah. Gradually they made the world the goal of their lives and piled up wealth without caring whether it was lawful. They still read the Holy Book, but through interpretations of their own making they coloured it so that Allah Himself seemed to support their rebellious way of life. Their callousness grew until they took comfort in declaring: we are a pious community and the descendants of prophets, and Allah will forgive us for the sake of His favourites.

### Can one sin and count on forgiveness?

Despite a sin as grave as distorting the Book of Allah, they claimed His forgiveness. The very next words expose this: offered money to change another passage, they would readily take it. Allah's forgiveness is always open to those who recognise their error and turn to their Lord in repentance. They show remorse for what they have done and firmly resolve not to repeat it. To persist in sin while claiming forgiveness is sheer self-deception.

Then comes the question whether they had not made a covenant with Allah to say nothing about Him but the truth. Indeed they had, and they read this pledge in their own Book. Only their impudence and obstinacy keep them from grasping the truth of the Hereafter, which belongs to those who fear Allah.

### In short

- A later generation inherited the Torah but used it for gain, taking bribes to distort it and to conceal the Prophet's description.
- They claimed forgiveness while persisting in the same sins, though the Torah promises no such thing.
- They broke a covenant to say only the truth about Allah, and did so knowingly, which made their sin greater.
- Forgiveness is for those who repent sincerely, and the Hereafter is far better for the mindful than any passing gain.

170.text:
Not all of them were like this, and Allah honours the faithful: "As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture and establish prayer—surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously". The previous verse (7:169) mentioned the covenant taken from the religious leaders of the Israelites in particular. They were to change nothing in the Torah and say nothing about Allah but the truth, yet they broke that pledge and distorted the Torah for petty sums. This verse continues the theme. Some of their religious leaders do follow the Torah truthfully and hold firmly to its guidance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture"**: those who hold fast to the Book, carry out its commands and keep away from what it forbids. They declare lawful what it makes lawful and unlawful what it forbids, and they bring into the open the traits and description of Muhammad ﷺ. Allah praises them because their Book directs them to follow His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. The verb can be read yumassikūn or yumsikūn. One explanation names ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions as examples.

**"and establish prayer"**: who perform the prayer as it should be performed, at its appointed times, the five daily prayers.

**"surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously"** Allah does not let the reward of those who do good in deed and word go to waste. Grammatically, this sentence is the predicate of alladhīna, "those who". An explicit noun, al-muṣliḥīn, "the righteous" or "reformers", stands in place of a pronoun, so the meaning is "their reward". This assures such people that they will not lose their reward. Those who have been true to their faith and met its demands are the righteous among them.

### Which Book, and why "hold fast"?

The Book most probably means the Torah. It may also mean all of Allah's revealed books, such as the Torah, the Injīl and the Qur'an. Simply keeping Allah's Book and showing it respect, without following its commands, does not fulfil the purpose for which it was revealed. That is why the verse says "hold fast", and not "take it" or "read it". Holding fast to the Book means following all of its rulings and commands.

### Why is prayer singled out?

Of all the Torah's teachings, the verse mentions only the establishment of prayer, the ṣalāh. Prayer is the most important and purposeful of the acts Allah has commanded. It is the most basic expression of faith in Allah and obedience to Him. Praying regularly makes a person able to keep up other acts of worship more willingly and easily. The Prophet ﷺ called prayer the pillar of Islam, on which the whole structure rests. Whoever sets it up properly has built the whole edifice of his faith on firm ground. Anyone who does not pray regularly is of no worth to Allah, even if he seems always to be repeating His name, sees unusual visions or performs extraordinary feats.

### What does holding fast look like?

This happens in every prophet's community. At first its members are pious and mindful of Allah, but in later generations that spirit fades and they become like other worldly people. Religion is still among them. The Holy Book is still read and taught, but as a national heritage, not as the real fulfilment of a pledge to Allah. They follow the ways of the world and, in practice, forget the Hereafter. Heedless of right and wrong, they make their desires their religion. Yet they pride themselves on being the best of communities, the followers of Allah's favourite, the heirs of the Book, sure of salvation by virtue of their belief in the oneness of Allah.

The truth is that a person must hold fast to Allah's Word and pray regularly. The sign that he holds fast to Allah's Book and prays sincerely is that he becomes a maintainer of peace and harmony, one of the muṣliḥūn. Closeness to Allah's Book and His worship are what set a person against anyone who disturbs the peace.

### In short

- Allah honours those who hold fast to their Book, act on it and establish prayer, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions.
- Holding fast means following the Book's commands, not merely keeping and revering it.
- Prayer is singled out because it is the pillar of the religion.
- The sign of true devotion is that a person becomes a maker of peace.

171.text:
Allah recalls an earlier moment when the Israelites were made to take their covenant seriously: "And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them." With it came a command: "˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”" This incident, when the Israelites were made to promise obedience to the law of the Torah, is also mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them"** Mention, O Muhammad, when Allah raised the mountain above the Israelites after they refused to accept what was in the Torah. The word here, nataqnā, means to pull or lift up. In Sūrat al-Baqarah the word is rafaʿnā, "We raised", and so Ibn ʿAbbās took it to mean lifting high. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as raising the mountain, as another verse testifies: "We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant" (4:154). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reported from him that the angels raised the Mount over their heads. One explanation says it was wrenched up from its roots and fixed above their heads.

**"as if it were a cloud"** The word is ẓullah, a sunshade or canopy. The mountain spread over them like a cloud, casting its shadow.

**"and they thought it would fall on them."** They were certain it would fall on them if they did not accept the Scripture, for Allah had threatened that it would. They had at first refused its rulings as too burdensome, but then they accepted them.

**"˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you"** Take what Allah revealed to you, the Torah, firmly, seriously and earnestly, and act on it with diligence.

**"and observe its teachings"** Remember what is in it by acting on it, and do not forget it. One explanation says: remember the reward and punishment it contains. Others say: recall its commands and prohibitions, or act on what it makes lawful and unlawful.

**"so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”"**: so that you may fear Allah and obey Him, guard yourselves against His wrath and torment, and believe in Him.

### What happened at the mountain?

Al-Qāsim ibn Abī Ayyūb narrated, through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that Ibn ʿAbbās said Mūsā (Moses) later set out with them for the Sacred Land. He took the Tablets with him once his anger had passed, and commanded them to keep the orders Allah had given him to deliver. But these orders weighed heavily on them, and they would not carry them out until Allah raised the mountain over them like a canopy. That was when the angels lifted the mountain over their heads. An-Nasāʾī collected this report.

Another account says that when Mūsā came back from Mount Sinai with the Torah, they found in it many injunctions they considered too hard, and showed they were unwilling to obey. Allah commanded the angel Jibrīl (Gabriel) to raise Mount Sinai over their town, whose area is said to have been three square miles. When the mountain hung over their heads, they fell down in prostration out of fear and promised to obey the law of Mūsā, the Torah. Yet later events saw them stray from that Law again and again.

Receiving the commandments at the foot of the mountain was meant to impress on them that a pledge to Allah is a very serious matter. If they failed to keep its conditions, they should remember who the other party was. He is the Majestic Being who could, if He willed, bring the mountain down on them.

### Was this not compulsion in religion?

The incident raises a question. Why were the Israelites forced to promise obedience, when the Holy Qur'an declares: "Let there be no compulsion in religion" (2:256)? The answer is simple. No disbeliever has ever been forced to accept the faith, and no one is permitted to use force for that purpose. But those who have entered the covenant of faith of their own free will, and later turn from Allah's commands to escape their obligations, must be made to keep the rules of the Law. If they abandon their duty, they are liable to the penalties the Law prescribes. That is exactly what happened here. They had already believed in Allah and His Prophet and entered the covenant of faith. What they refused was obedience to the law of the Torah, and they were rightly made to fulfil their commitment.

### In short

- When the Israelites refused the burdensome rulings of the Torah, Allah raised the mountain over them like a canopy.
- Certain it would fall, they fell in prostration and promised to obey, though they later strayed again.
- They were told to hold the Scripture firmly and act on it so that they might become mindful of Allah.
- This was no compulsion into faith, since they had already believed and were being held to a covenant they had made.

172.text:
Allah recalls a moment before human history began: "And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify regarding themselves." He put a question to them: "˹Allah asked,˺ “Am I not your Lord?” They replied, “Yes, You are! We testify.”" And He closed off any future excuse: "˹He cautioned,˺ “Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day, ‘We were not aware of this.’" This verse and the next describe the great covenant that the Creator made with all of His creation even before they took on their existence. It is known as the covenant of Alast.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth"** Mention, O Muhammad, when your Lord took out their seed on the Day of the Covenant.

**"from the loins of the children of Adam"** In the Arabic, "from their loins" (min ẓuhūrihim) is an inclusive substitute for "from the children of Adam" (min banī Ādama), repeating the same preposition. Allah brought them out of one another's loins, all of them ultimately from the loins of Adam, offspring after offspring, in the way they multiply.

**"their descendants"** The word is dhurriyyah. Imām Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī said it comes from a root meaning "to create", and the Qur'an uses it in that sense in a number of verses. So dhurriyyah means all who are created. The covenant therefore included every human being, since all are the progeny of Adam.

**"and had them testify regarding themselves."** They bore witness that Allah is their Lord and King and that no one but He deserves worship. Allah set up proofs of His Lordship for them and gave them the faculty of reason. He made acknowledging that He created them and is their Lord part of their innate nature. He created them on this fiṭrah. As another verse says: "Let there be no change in this creation of Allah." (30:30). The two reports quoted under 7:30 make the same point. One, in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Hurayrah, says that every child is born on the fiṭrah. In the other, which Muslim recorded from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, Allah says He created His servants pure in faith, ḥunafāʾ.

**"˹Allah asked,˺ “Am I not your Lord?”"** This was the pledge Allah took from all humankind. Its aim was to have them acknowledge that He is their Nourisher and Sustainer, the Lord of all created beings.

**"They replied, “Yes, You are! We testify.”"** We know and acknowledge that You are our Lord. Allah then told the angels to bear witness over them, and told them to bear witness over one another.

**"˹He cautioned,˺ “Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day,"** The testimony was taken so that they could not say otherwise. The verb can be read "lest they say" or "lest you say". Allah said, in effect, that He asked them this so that they would not deny His proofs on the Day of Judgement.

**"‘We were not aware of this.’"** "This" is tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah, and the covenant. They cannot claim that they knew nothing of it, or that no pledge was taken from them. The pledge Allah took lit a candle of faith in their hearts. With a little reflection they can easily recognise Him as their Lord, so the excuse of ignorance will be of no use to them on the Day of Judgement.

### Was the testimony spoken or shown?

Allah made them testify about themselves both by their condition and in words. Testimony is sometimes given in words, as in: "They will say, “We confess against ourselves!”" (6:130). At other times a person's state is itself the testimony. Allah says: "It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they openly profess disbelief." (9:17). That verse means their disbelief bears witness against them, not that they literally testify against themselves there. Another example is: "and they certainly attest to this—" (100:7), meaning by their deeds.

Asking works the same way. It is sometimes done in words and sometimes through a person's situation. Allah says: "And He has granted you all that you asked Him for." (14:34).

### What do the hadiths add?

Several hadiths tell how Allah drew Adam's offspring out of his loins and set some on the right side and some on the left. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ said a man of the Fire will be asked on the Day of Resurrection whether he would give the whole earth as ransom if he owned it. He will say yes. Allah will tell him that He asked far less of him while he was still in Adam's loins: to associate nothing with Him. But he insisted on associating others with Him. This is also recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.

Commenting on this verse, at-Tirmidhī recorded a hadith from Abū Hurayrah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that after creating Adam, Allah wiped his back, and every soul He would create from him until the Day of Resurrection fell out of it. Allah placed a gleaming light between the eyes of each, on their foreheads, and showed them to Adam. Adam asked who they were, and Allah said they were his offspring. Adam was pleased by the light of one man and asked about him. Allah said he was a man from the later generations of his offspring, named Dāwūd (David).

Adam asked how long Dāwūd would live, and was told sixty years. He said: My Lord, I give him forty years of my own life. When Adam's life came to its end and the angel of death came for his soul, Adam said: do I not still have forty years left? The angel replied: did you not give them to your son Dāwūd? Adam denied it, and so his offspring deny. Adam forgot, and his offspring forget. Adam erred, and his offspring err.

At-Tirmidhī graded this hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ and said it was reported through several chains from Abū Hurayrah. Al-Ḥākim also recorded it in his Mustadrak. He said it is ṣaḥīḥ by Muslim's criteria, though they did not record it.

Imām Mālik, Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Imām Aḥmad reported from Muslim ibn Yasār that some people asked the Caliph ʿUmar al-Fārūq about this verse. ʿUmar said the same question had been put to the Prophet ﷺ, and he heard his answer. Allah first created Adam, then passed His hand over his back and drew out all the righteous descendants who would come into being. He said: I have created these for Paradise, and they will do the deeds of its people. Then He passed His hand over Adam's back again, and all his wicked descendants appeared. He said: I have created these for the Fire, and they will do the deeds of its people.

One of the Companions asked: if Allah has already decided people's fate, what use are good deeds? The Prophet ﷺ replied that whoever is created for Paradise takes up the deeds of its people and dies doing them. Whoever is created for the Fire falls into the deeds of its people and dies doing them. Since no one knows which group he belongs to, he should put all his effort into the deeds of the people of Paradise and hope to be among them.

The Tradition reported by Imām Aḥmad from the Companion Abū al-Dardāʾ adds that those who came out the first time were shining white, and those who came out the second time were dark. These and similar hadiths show that Allah brought Adam's offspring out of his loins and separated the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire.

### From Adam's back, or from his children's?

The hadiths describe Adam's children coming out of Adam's own back. The verse describes them coming out of the backs of his children. There is no real conflict. Adam's direct offspring are described as coming from his back, and the generations after them as coming from the backs of his descendants.

### Spirits alone, or bodies too?

This suggests that the children of Adam who came out of his back were not spirits alone. They also had some kind of body made of fine elements. Nourishing, the work of a Lord, concerns the body, which is brought from one stage to the next. Spirits need no such nourishment, since they remain in one state from the moment of their creation. The hadiths support this. Their mention of colours, and of brilliance on the forehead, requires some material form, since spirits plainly have no colour.

### How could all humanity fit in one place?

One may wonder how all the human beings to be created until the Last Day could gather in one place. The tradition from Abū al-Dardāʾ answers this. They did not appear in their usual size but as tiny as small ants. In an age of scientific knowledge, it should be no surprise that a full-sized person can be reduced to the size of an ant. Science has found a system like the solar system at work around the nucleus of an atom. Books of hundreds of pages can be reduced to a small dot on microfilm. So there is nothing surprising in Allah, the All-Powerful, reducing them to the size of ants on this occasion.

### When and where was it taken?

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās answered this, as Imām Aḥmad and an-Nasāʾī reported through authentic chains. The covenant was taken when Adam was sent down from heaven to earth. The place was the valley of Naʿmān, the plain of ʿArafāt near Makkah. Another explanation places it in that valley on the Day of ʿArafah, where the multitude looked like small ants.

### How could the unborn recognise their Lord?

This pledge was taken before any human being except Adam had been created. So how could Adam's children have the knowledge and reason to acknowledge Allah as their Lord and Nourisher? Recognising that seems to need the experience of being nourished, which was impossible before coming into the world.

The answer is simple. Allah has power to do anything He wills. If He could make every human being appear in the size of an ant, He could far more easily give them enough knowledge and reason to recognise their Lord. He brought them forth in a small size, with body and soul and every function a complete human being needs. Reason and understanding, the most important of those functions, must have been included.

### What use is a covenant no one remembers?

One more question remains. What value can a covenant have when it came before people's actual creation and they do not remember it on earth? Some individuals have in fact remembered it. The great spiritual master Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said that he remembered this covenant as clearly as if he were hearing it at that very moment. Some elders are said to have remembered even the people standing near them. Such cases are rare, though, and do not answer the question.

The real answer is that many acts work by their very nature, whether or not anyone remembers or understands them. They leave their mark naturally. One clear example is the Muslim practice of saying the adhān in a newborn's right ear and the iqāmah in his left. The adhān is the call to ṣalāh, a bold declaration that Allah is One, has no partner and is the Greatest. The iqāmah repeats it and adds that the prayer is about to begin.

The baby neither understands this call nor remembers it as an adult. Its wisdom is to revive the pledge he made with Allah and to sow the seed of faith in his heart by repeating the covenant's message in his ears. Its effect can be seen in every Muslim, even one who does not practise. He is proud to call himself a Muslim and would hate to lose that identity. The command to recite the Qur'an even to those who know no Arabic may have the same reason. The impact of its words lights up their hearts and renews their faith in Allah.

The wisdom of the covenant is likewise to sow the seed of faith in every human heart. That seed draws nourishment from the soil of the heart whether people are aware of it or not. Its fruit is the love and reverence for the Creator that is part of human nature. This love may take wrong forms, such as worshipping idols or created beings. Yet all worship, true or false, is in itself an expression of love and reverence for the Creator. Billions of people hold this love for Allah and express it in worship shaped by their knowledge or their ignorance. Only a few, absorbed in worldly pursuits, have dulled their natural understanding and forgotten the pledge they made.

### Why does Allah record what He already knows?

Allah created all the worlds, the heavens and the earth and whatever lies between them. His infinite wisdom and all-embracing knowledge designed this universe so perfectly that no room remains for doubt or question. He created everything according to wise laws. Following them leads to eternal success and lasting peace, while turning from them brings the punishments Allah has set.

His knowledge and wisdom would have been enough to decide the fate of every creature. He had no need for angels to watch and record His servants' deeds, nor to weigh those deeds in the Balance on the Day of Judgement. He knows every deed, even His servants' hidden thoughts and intentions, with no possibility of a wrong judgement.

But His grace and perfect justice chose that no one should be punished without documentary proof of his sins. The evidence will be such that the sinner has no choice but to admit what he did. So He appointed angels to record every act of each person: "not a word does a person utter without having a ˹vigilant˺ observer ready ˹to write it down˺" (50:18). According to Ibn ʿAbbās, everything good or bad about a person is recorded by his guardian angels: "Every matter, small and large, is written ˹precisely˺" (54:53). Then, on the Day of Judgement, the Balance will be set up to weigh everyone's good and bad deeds. Those whose good deeds weigh heavier will be saved, and those whose bad deeds weigh heavier will be punished.

When Allah, the Best of Judges, holds His court on that Day, He will also call witnesses to each person's deeds. Some wrongdoers will try to discredit them. Then Allah will make the person's own limbs speak and testify against him. The very places where he did his deeds will bear witness too. In the end he will find no way to deny the witnesses and will confess his evil deeds: "And so they will confess their sins." (67:11).

### How has Allah helped people to obey?

Allah, the Most Kind and Loving, did not leave His servants with bare laws and regulations. Out of kindness He gave them complete guidance through His prophets and His Books, to save them from eternal punishment. Loving parents make it compulsory for their children to go to school every morning. But they also make sure everything the children need is ready in time, so that keeping the rule is as easy as possible. Allah, who is beyond all comparison, is more loving and kind to His servants than parents are to their children. He did not merely lay down laws but made them a source of real guidance. With His commands, He also taught how to carry them out with ease and readiness.

Besides sending His messengers and Books, He appointed many angels to help and guide people to the right path. He also scattered plain signs of His might and wisdom everywhere, so that people could use their own observation and understanding to tell right from wrong and to remember their Creator. He repeatedly invites them to reflect on the signs spread around them: "There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith, as there are within yourselves. Can you not see" (51:20-21).

This verse speaks of two kinds of signs, outer and inner. The outer signs are everywhere: the heavens and the earth, the oceans and mountains, plants and trees, fruits of many colours and tastes. All of them point unmistakably to the Lord. The inner signs include the way human beings are reproduced, their bodies, their thoughts and intentions, and their feelings of joy and sorrow. A little reflection on these signs leads a person to the Creator and moves him to thank Him.

### What other covenants has Allah taken?

Another way Allah moved people to act righteously was to have them enter covenants with Him through His prophets. The Holy Qur'an mentions a number of such covenants, made with different people in different circumstances. The prophets were made to promise that they would convey Allah's message to their people, whatever hardship or reproach they met. This pious group did convey His message as faithfully as possible and sacrificed all they had in doing so. The people of every prophet, in turn, were made to promise to obey him, and in some cases to spend all their energy carrying out particular commands. Some kept their promise and some did not.

The most significant of these is the covenant all the prophets made concerning the Holy Prophet ﷺ. They pledged to follow the last of the prophets and to help him whenever they had the chance: "˹Remember˺ when Allah made a covenant with the prophets, ˹saying,˺ “Now that I have given you the Book and wisdom, if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.”" (3:81). By implication, this pledge binds the followers of every prophet to believe in the Holy Prophet ﷺ, follow him and support his aims. It also binds them to follow the law given by the last of the prophets.

### What is a pledge of allegiance worth?

The traditional pledge of allegiance, the bayʿah or pledge of discipleship that a guide takes from devoted followers, is modelled on this way of Allah. Prophets, their companions and spiritual leaders have all taken such pledges from their followers. The Holy Qur'an mentions the Bayʿat al-Rizwān: "Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree." (48:18). The Holy Prophet ﷺ took such pledges from his Companions on many occasions. The Bayʿat al-ʿAqabah is a famous covenant made with the Anṣār of Madinah before the migration.

The Sufi custom of taking a pledge from followers is a covenant to practise Allah's commands regularly and to strengthen faith through frequent remembrance of their Lord. Swearing allegiance in this way has many benefits and draws barakah, blessing, from Allah. After pledging himself to a Shaykh, a spiritual master, a follower feels more willing to carry out his religious duties and more careful to seek Allah's pleasure.

This also clears up a misconception common among people of little knowledge, that placing one's hand in the hand of a Shaykh is enough for salvation in the Hereafter. That notion is entirely wrong. The pledge is a commitment to follow practical guidance as the Shaykh instructs. Merely placing one's hand in his is of no use at all. In fact, it betrays the pledge and may bring on Allah's wrath.

### The inner reading: the first day of friendship

In the tongue of the Reality, the verse holds another hint and another taste. It alludes to the beginning of the friends' states, and to the binding of the compact of friendship with them on the first day, in the beginningless past, when the Real was present and the Reality was there. A poet sang: "How blessed were Laylā and those nights when we used to meet her!" What a fine day was the day the foundation of friendship was laid, and how exalted the hour when its compact was made! Whoever desired on that first day will never lose that desire. Whoever yearned when union with the Friend came has come to know life's crown and the direction of all his days. Another line runs: "How blessed was the time of Your covenant, without which my heart would have no room for longing!"

The command came: "remind them of Allah’s days ˹of favour˺" (14:5). These servants, Allah says, have forgotten His covenant and busied themselves with others. They are to be reminded of the day their pure spirits made the covenant of friendship with Him, when He anointed their yearning eyes with the kohl of "Am I not your Lord?"

O needy one! Remember the day when the spirits of the friends drank the wine of passion for Allah from the cup of love in the assembly of intimacy. The angels drawn near, of the Higher Assembly, said that these were a people of high aspiration. The angels themselves had never tasted this wine nor caught its scent. Yet the clamour of these beggars rose as high as Capella, crying, as the verse has it, "Are there any more?" (50:30). As the poet says: "Of that wine, which my religion does not forbid, my lips will never be dry until I return to nonexistence." One day the paragon of the world and master of the children of Adam ﷺ said of a mountain: this is a mountain that loves me and that I love.

### In short

- Before their earthly life, Allah drew all of Adam's descendants from their fathers' loins and had them testify that He is their Lord.
- The hadiths describe them drawn from Adam's back as tiny beings, with body and reason, at Naʿmān near ʿArafāt, divided into the people of Paradise and of the Fire.
- Though forgotten, the covenant sowed a seed of faith in every heart, which is why the excuse of ignorance will not be accepted.
- Allah, who knows all, still records deeds and calls witnesses out of justice, and He guides through prophets, Books and signs.
- The covenant of Alast stands at the head of the covenants Allah took through the prophets, and of every true pledge of allegiance.

173.text:
The covenant also closes off a second excuse, that of blind imitation: "Nor say, ‘It was our forefathers who had associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺ and we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps."
